docs.title: negative_ml
docs.text:
Companion code for the SciPy talk Just Throw It Away? Class Imbalance Lessons from Molecules to Meatballs — a study of the role of majority-class (negative) examples in imbalanced machine learning.

Most real-world classification problems are heavily imbalanced: the majority of labeled examples are negatives, and standard practice is to downsample or discard them. This project asks whether that majority-class data is redundant, and whether it can be chosen more carefully under a fixed labeling or experimental budget. See the full research plan for the hypotheses and methodology.

docs.title: Install from source
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:jackievaleri/negative_ml
cd negative_ml
micromamba env create -f environment.yml
micromamba activate negative_ml
python -m pip install -e .

docs.title: Run an experiment
docs.text:
negative_ml prepare --all
negative_ml saturation molecules --scaffold
negative_ml selection molecules --budget 2000 --scaffold

docs.title: Reproduce the figures
docs.text:
Each domain has a reproducible script under scripts/ that generates result tables and redraws every figure from them:

python scripts/molecules_eda.py                  # generate + plot
python scripts/molecules_eda.py --plot-only       # replot saved artifacts
python scripts/molecules_eda.py --generate-only   # compute tables, no figures

The same plotting helpers back the notebooks/*.ipynb EDA notebooks, so a notebook and its matching script always draw the same figures.

docs.title: The three domains
docs.text:
Domain Question Notebook Molecules — ~40,000 antibacterial screening compounds, ~97% inactive The core case study: do we need all of the inactive majority class? 01_molecules_eda.ipynb Baseball — MLB batted-ball outcomes (home runs, triples) An intuitive, geometrically separable minority class for a general audience 02_baseball_eda.ipynb Sandwiches — Roll-for-Sandwich ingredient ratings A tiny, sparsely sampled combinatorial problem recast as good-vs-bad classification 03_sandwiches_eda.ipynb

Why these questions matter, in short:

  • How can we best leverage negative data in model training?
  • If we were to collect less negative data, what negative data should we collect?
  • Does losing negative data hurt model performance near the decision boundary?
  • What is the role of negative data in active learning loops?

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text:
• negative_ml/core/ — domain-agnostic building blocks: the Dataset abstraction, configuration, splitting, selection strategies, evaluation metrics, and experiment plumbing.
  • negative_ml/molecules/, negative_ml/baseball/, negative_ml/sandwich/ — per-domain I/O, featurization, and evaluation-split builders.
  • negative_ml/models/ — model wrappers behind a task-based factory.
  • negative_ml/viz/ — plotting helpers shared by the scripts and notebooks.
  • scripts/ — reproducible generate/plot entry points, one per domain.
  • notebooks/ — the EDA notebooks referenced above.

See the API reference for the full module-by-module documentation.

docs.title: Dataset dataclass
docs.text:
A featurized dataset plus the metadata needed to study imbalance.

Attributes: X: Feature matrix, shape (n_samples, n_features). y: Targets. Binary {0, 1} labels for classification (1 == minority / class of interest), or continuous values for regression. task: Either "classification" or "regression". feature_names: Optional column names for X. groups: Optional group id per row (e.g. molecular scaffold) used for grouped / scaffold splits. None when not applicable. meta: Optional raw rows / identifiers (SMILES, player, ingredients) kept alongside the features for inspection and matched-pair eval. label_y: Optional binary {0, 1} label array that overrides y for minority_mask / majority_mask when y holds continuous values (e.g. a regression Dataset whose model trains on continuous ratings but whose minority class is still defined by a threshold-derived binary label). When None, mask logic falls back to y and task as usual. distance_metric: Which distance the selection/mmp code should use over X, one of DISTANCE_METRICS. Defaults to "euclidean" (z-scored L2); domains built entirely from nominal/multi-hot features (currently only sandwich) set this to "hamming".

Source code in negative_ml/core/dataset.py 
@dataclass
class Dataset:
    """A featurized dataset plus the metadata needed to study imbalance.

    Attributes:
        X: Feature matrix, shape (n_samples, n_features).
        y: Targets. Binary {0, 1} labels for classification (1 == minority /
            class of interest), or continuous values for regression.
        task: Either "classification" or "regression".
        feature_names: Optional column names for X.
        groups: Optional group id per row (e.g. molecular scaffold) used for
            grouped / scaffold splits. None when not applicable.
        meta: Optional raw rows / identifiers (SMILES, player, ingredients)
            kept alongside the features for inspection and matched-pair eval.
        label_y: Optional binary {0, 1} label array that overrides y for
            minority_mask / majority_mask when y holds continuous values (e.g.
            a regression Dataset whose model trains on continuous ratings but
            whose minority class is still defined by a threshold-derived binary
            label). When None, mask logic falls back to y and task as usual.
        distance_metric: Which distance the selection/mmp code should use over
            X, one of DISTANCE_METRICS. Defaults to "euclidean" (z-scored L2);
            domains built entirely from nominal/multi-hot features (currently
            only sandwich) set this to "hamming".
    """

    X: np.ndarray
    y: np.ndarray
    task: Task
    feature_names: list[str] | None = None
    groups: np.ndarray | None = None
    meta: pd.DataFrame | None = field(default=None, repr=False)
    label_y: np.ndarray | None = field(default=None, repr=False)
    distance_metric: str = "euclidean"

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        """Validate that shapes line up."""
        self.X = np.asarray(self.X)
        self.y = np.asarray(self.y)
        if len(self.X) != len(self.y):
            raise ValueError(
                f"X has {len(self.X)} rows but y has {len(self.y)} entries."
            )
        if self.distance_metric not in DISTANCE_METRICS:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Unknown distance_metric {self.distance_metric!r}; "
                f"choose from {DISTANCE_METRICS}."
            )

    @property
    def n_samples(self) -> int:
        """Number of rows in the dataset.

        Returns:
            The number of samples (length of y).
        """
        return len(self.y)

    def minority_mask(self, threshold: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray:
        """Boolean mask selecting the minority / class-of-interest examples.

        When label_y is set it takes precedence: the mask is label_y == 1,
        which lets a regression Dataset (continuous y for model training) keep
        a correct binary minority definition without changing its y. Otherwise
        for classification this is y == 1, and for regression the minority is
        the low-value tail y <= threshold (threshold must then be supplied).

        Args:
            threshold: Cutoff for the regression minority tail. Ignored when
                label_y is set.

        Returns:
            Boolean array of length n_samples.
        """
        if self.label_y is not None:
            return self.label_y == 1
        if self.task == "classification":
            return self.y == 1
        if threshold is None:
            raise ValueError("A threshold is required for the regression minority.")
        return self.y <= threshold

    def majority_mask(self, threshold: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray:
        """Boolean mask selecting the majority examples (complement of minority).

        Args:
            threshold: Cutoff for the regression minority tail; forwarded to
                minority_mask. Ignored when label_y is set.

        Returns:
            Boolean array of length n_samples (complement of minority_mask).
        """
        return ~self.minority_mask(threshold)

    def subset(self, indices: np.ndarray) -> "Dataset":
        """Return a new Dataset containing only the given row indices.

        Args:
            indices: Integer row indices into this dataset.

        Returns:
            A new Dataset restricted to the given rows.
        """
        indices = np.asarray(indices)
        meta = (
            None
            if self.meta is None
            else self.meta.iloc[indices].reset_index(drop=True)
        )
        groups = None if self.groups is None else np.asarray(self.groups)[indices]
        label_y = None if self.label_y is None else np.asarray(self.label_y)[indices]
        return Dataset(
            X=self.X[indices],
            y=self.y[indices],
            task=self.task,
            feature_names=self.feature_names,
            groups=groups,
            meta=meta,
            label_y=label_y,
            distance_metric=self.distance_metric,
        )

docs.title: make_model(task, kind='xgboost', class_weight=None, **params)
docs.text:
Construct an estimator for the given task.

Args: task: "classification" or "regression". kind: Model family — "xgboost" (default), "ridge" (the L2-regularized linear model behind the good-vs-bad sandwich classifier; a RidgeClassifier for classification and a Ridge regressor for regression), "logistic" (an alternative linear classifier exposing probabilities), or "correlation" (the single-feature negative control, which requires a feature_index). class_weight: Optional class weighting to test the "weighting can substitute for data" hypothesis (H4) without deleting examples. Forwarded to scikit-learn directly for the logistic classifier (including the string "balanced"); a numeric value becomes XGBoost's scale_pos_weight. **params: Extra hyper-parameters forwarded to the estimator.

Returns: An unfitted sklearn-compatible estimator.

Source code in negative_ml/models/base.py 
def make_model(
    task: str,
    kind: str = "xgboost",
    class_weight: str | dict | None = None,
    **params: Any,
) -> Estimator:
    """Construct an estimator for the given task.

    Args:
        task: "classification" or "regression".
        kind: Model family — "xgboost" (default), "ridge" (the L2-regularized
            linear model behind the good-vs-bad sandwich classifier; a
            RidgeClassifier for classification and a Ridge regressor for
            regression), "logistic" (an alternative linear classifier exposing
            probabilities), or "correlation" (the single-feature negative control,
            which requires a feature_index).
        class_weight: Optional class weighting to test the "weighting can
            substitute for data" hypothesis (H4) without deleting examples.
            Forwarded to scikit-learn directly for the logistic classifier
            (including the string "balanced"); a numeric value becomes XGBoost's
            scale_pos_weight.
        **params: Extra hyper-parameters forwarded to the estimator.

    Returns:
        An unfitted sklearn-compatible estimator.
    """
    if kind == "correlation":
        return CorrelationModel(feature_index=params["feature_index"])
    if kind == "logistic":
        if task != "classification":
            raise ValueError(
                f"kind='logistic' is a classifier; task must be 'classification', "
                f"got {task!r}."
            )
        return logistic_classifier(class_weight=class_weight, **params)
    if kind == "ridge":
        if task == "classification":
            return ridge_classifier(class_weight=class_weight, **params)
        if task == "regression":
            return ridge_regressor(**params)
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unknown task {task!r}; expected 'classification' or 'regression'."
        )
    if kind != "xgboost":
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unsupported model kind {kind!r}; expected 'xgboost', 'logistic', "
            "'ridge', or 'correlation'."
        )

    if task == "classification":
        # "balanced" weighting is resolved against the data later (it needs the
        # class ratio); accept it here as an explicit scale_pos_weight instead.
        scale_pos_weight = (
            class_weight if isinstance(class_weight, (int, float)) else None
        )
        return xgb_classifier(scale_pos_weight=scale_pos_weight, **params)
    if task == "regression":
        return xgb_regressor(**params)
    raise ValueError(
        f"Unknown task {task!r}; expected 'classification' or 'regression'."
    )

docs.title: Dataset
docs.text:
The shared Dataset abstraction used across every domain.

Antibacterial molecules, baseball batted balls, and sandwich ratings look nothing alike, but the central experiment is the same in all three: hold the minority / high-value examples fixed and vary how the majority class is sub-selected. Wrapping each domain in a single Dataset lets the splitting, selection, experiment, and evaluation code be written exactly once.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Project-wide configuration: paths, seeds, and shared constants.

Domain-specific constants live in their respective domain packages: - baseball/config.py: OUTLIER_BALLPARKS - molecules/config.py: MOLECULE_, GONORRHEA_, MORGAN_, MOLECULES_EDA_ - sandwich/config.py: SANDWICH_*

Centralizing shared values here keeps the domain loaders, experiments, and scripts from each hard-coding their own paths or magic numbers.

docs.title: Splitting
docs.text:
Domain-agnostic train/test splitting strategies (plan.md 3.1, 4.x).

Two regimes matter for the study, and both apply across every domain (unlike a domain's own held-out-group splits, e.g. baseball's ballpark_split or sandwich's season_split, which live in that domain's split.py):

- Random splits: the easy, optimistic baseline.
- Scaffold / grouped splits: hold out entire structural families (via
  Dataset.groups) to measure generalization under distribution shift. This
  is where curated majority data is expected to pay off. Despite the name
  (from its original use on Bemis-Murcko molecular scaffolds), it is a
  generic grouped-random split wired through core.experiment's
  resolve_split and exposed as the CLI's cross-domain --scaffold flag, so
  any domain with dataset.groups set can use it.

Splitters return integer index arrays so they compose cleanly with the selection and experiment code.

def random_split(
    dataset: Dataset,
    test_size: float = TEST_SIZE,
    stratify: bool = True,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Random train/test split, optionally stratified by label.

    Stratification is only applied for classification (it is meaningless for the
    continuous regression target).

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset to split.
        test_size: Fraction of samples held out for the test set.
        stratify: Whether to stratify the split by label (classification only).
        seed: Random seed controlling the split.

    Returns:
        (train_idx, test_idx) integer index arrays.
    """
    indices = np.arange(dataset.n_samples)
    stratify_on = dataset.y if (stratify and dataset.task == "classification") else None
    train_idx, test_idx = train_test_split(
        indices,
        test_size=test_size,
        random_state=seed,
        stratify=stratify_on,
    )
    return train_idx, test_idx

Requires dataset.groups to be set (e.g. Bemis-Murcko scaffolds for molecules). Tests generalization under distribution shift. Not used by the baseball domain, which has no natural grouping.

def scaffold_split(
    dataset: Dataset,
    test_size: float = TEST_SIZE,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Grouped split that keeps each dataset.groups family on one side.

    Requires dataset.groups to be set (e.g. Bemis-Murcko scaffolds for
    molecules). Tests generalization under distribution shift. Not used by the
    baseball domain, which has no natural grouping.

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset to split; its groups attribute must be set.
        test_size: Fraction of groups held out for the test set.
        seed: Random seed controlling the split.

    Returns:
        (train_idx, test_idx) integer index arrays.
    """
    if dataset.groups is None:
        raise ValueError("scaffold_split requires dataset.groups to be set.")
    splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=test_size, random_state=seed)
    train_idx, test_idx = next(
        splitter.split(np.arange(dataset.n_samples), groups=dataset.groups)
    )
    return train_idx, test_idx

docs.title: Selection strategies
docs.text:
Majority-class selection strategies under a fixed budget (plan.md 4.2).

Given a training Dataset and a budget (how many majority examples we are allowed to keep), each strategy returns the row indices of the majority examples to retain. Minority examples are always kept; the experiment code combines kept_minority + selected_majority into the final training set.

This is the heart of the study: it isolates whether boundary proximity (H2), distributional coverage (H3), or simply volume is what matters.

All strategies share the signature (dataset, budget, **kwargs) -> np.ndarray so they can be looked up by name and compared uniformly. Each returns indices into the full dataset (a subset of the majority rows).

def clamp(budget: int | None, n_available: int) -> int:
    """Clamp a requested budget to [0, n_available].

    Args:
        budget: Requested number of examples; None means keep all.
        n_available: Total number of available examples.

    Returns:
        The clamped budget as an int in [0, n_available].
    """
    if budget is None:
        return n_available
    return int(min(max(budget, 0), n_available))

docs.title: density_aware_diversity(dataset, budget, seed=RANDOM_SEED, **_kwargs)
docs.text:
Diversity selection that also respects local density / structure.

Clusters the majority into budget groups (MiniBatchKMeans on the dataset's distance-metric feature space) and keeps the point nearest each centroid. Coverage that, unlike pure farthest-point, does not over-weight sparse outliers.

MiniBatchKMeans always fits by minimizing squared Euclidean distance to the (real-valued) cluster centroids -- scikit-learn has no Hamming-native k-medoids implementation available here. For "euclidean" datasets that is exactly what's wanted. For "hamming" datasets (raw 0/1 features, no z-scoring -- see distance_features) it is a standard, widely-used approximation for clustering multi-hot data: every feature still carries equal, unscaled weight during clustering, which is what avoids the rare-category inflation Hamming distance is meant to avoid. The one step that matters most for the returned picks -- choosing which single member represents each cluster -- uses the dataset's real metric (Hamming/L1 for "hamming" datasets) rather than Euclidean distance to the centroid.

Args: dataset: Dataset whose majority rows to sub-select. budget: Number of majority examples to keep (= number of k-means clusters). seed: Random seed for k-means and the empty-cluster fill. **_kwargs: Ignored; accepted to match the strategy signature.

Returns: Sorted integer indices of the selected majority examples (one per cluster).

Source code in negative_ml/core/selection.py 
def density_aware_diversity(
    dataset: Dataset,
    budget: int,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
    **_kwargs,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Diversity selection that also respects local density / structure.

    Clusters the majority into budget groups (MiniBatchKMeans on the dataset's
    distance-metric feature space) and keeps the point nearest each centroid.
    Coverage that, unlike pure farthest-point, does not over-weight sparse
    outliers.

    MiniBatchKMeans always fits by minimizing squared Euclidean distance to the
    (real-valued) cluster centroids -- scikit-learn has no Hamming-native
    k-medoids implementation available here. For "euclidean" datasets that is
    exactly what's wanted. For "hamming" datasets (raw 0/1 features, no
    z-scoring -- see distance_features) it is a standard, widely-used
    approximation for clustering multi-hot data: every feature still carries
    equal, unscaled weight during clustering, which is what avoids the
    rare-category inflation Hamming distance is meant to avoid. The one step
    that matters most for the returned picks -- choosing which single member
    represents each cluster -- uses the dataset's real metric (Hamming/L1 for
    "hamming" datasets) rather than Euclidean distance to the centroid.

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset whose majority rows to sub-select.
        budget: Number of majority examples to keep (= number of k-means clusters).
        seed: Random seed for k-means and the empty-cluster fill.
        **_kwargs: Ignored; accepted to match the strategy signature.

    Returns:
        Sorted integer indices of the selected majority examples (one per cluster).
    """
    majority = majority_indices(dataset)
    k = clamp(budget, len(majority))
    if k == 0:
        return np.empty(0, dtype=int)
    if k >= len(majority):
        return np.sort(majority)

    Xz = distance_features(dataset)[majority]
    km = MiniBatchKMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=seed, n_init=KMEANS_N_INIT)
    labels = km.fit_predict(Xz)
    centers = km.cluster_centers_

    chosen: list[int] = []
    for c in range(k):
        members = np.where(labels == c)[0]
        if len(members) == 0:
            continue
        d = vector_distances(Xz[members], centers[c], dataset.distance_metric)
        chosen.append(int(members[np.argmin(d)]))
    chosen_arr = np.array(sorted(set(chosen)), dtype=int)

    # MiniBatchKMeans can produce empty clusters, leaving fewer than k centroid
    # representatives. Fill the shortfall with a random draw from unchosen majority
    # points so the returned set always has exactly k elements and n_train is
    # consistent across seeds at the same budget.
    if len(chosen_arr) < k:
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        remaining = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(majority)), chosen_arr)
        fill = rng.choice(remaining, size=k - len(chosen_arr), replace=False)
        chosen_arr = np.sort(np.concatenate([chosen_arr, fill]))

    return np.sort(majority[chosen_arr])

docs.text:
Feature matrix prepared for dataset.distance_metric.

"euclidean" datasets get z-scored features (standardized_features) so no raw-scale feature dominates. "hamming" datasets get the raw feature matrix, unscaled: Hamming distance is meant to count differing (typically one-hot) positions with every position weighted equally, and z-scoring would reintroduce a rarity-based weighting (rare categories get inflated) that Hamming distance is chosen specifically to avoid.

Args: dataset: Dataset whose distance_metric selects the treatment.

Returns: The feature matrix to run distance / clustering computations on.

Source code in negative_ml/core/selection.py 
def distance_features(dataset: Dataset) -> np.ndarray:
    """Feature matrix prepared for dataset.distance_metric.

    "euclidean" datasets get z-scored features (standardized_features) so no
    raw-scale feature dominates. "hamming" datasets get the raw feature matrix,
    unscaled: Hamming distance is meant to count differing (typically one-hot)
    positions with every position weighted equally, and z-scoring would
    reintroduce a rarity-based weighting (rare categories get inflated) that
    Hamming distance is chosen specifically to avoid.

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset whose distance_metric selects the treatment.

    Returns:
        The feature matrix to run distance / clustering computations on.
    """
    if dataset.distance_metric == "hamming":
        return np.asarray(dataset.X, dtype=float)
    return standardized_features(dataset)

docs.title: diversity_selection(dataset, budget, seed=RANDOM_SEED, **_kwargs)
docs.text:
Maximize feature-space coverage of the kept majority examples.

Greedy farthest-point (k-center) sampling on standardized features (H3). For very large majorities the candidate pool is randomly subsampled to DIVERSITY_POOL_CAP first to bound the O(n*budget) cost.

Args: dataset: Dataset whose majority rows to sub-select. budget: Number of majority examples to keep. seed: Random seed for the candidate-pool subsample and starting point. **_kwargs: Ignored; accepted to match the strategy signature.

Returns: Sorted integer indices of the selected majority examples.

Source code in negative_ml/core/selection.py 
def diversity_selection(
    dataset: Dataset,
    budget: int,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
    **_kwargs,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Maximize feature-space coverage of the kept majority examples.

    Greedy farthest-point (k-center) sampling on standardized features (H3). For
    very large majorities the candidate pool is randomly subsampled to
    DIVERSITY_POOL_CAP first to bound the O(n*budget) cost.

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset whose majority rows to sub-select.
        budget: Number of majority examples to keep.
        seed: Random seed for the candidate-pool subsample and starting point.
        **_kwargs: Ignored; accepted to match the strategy signature.

    Returns:
        Sorted integer indices of the selected majority examples.
    """
    majority = majority_indices(dataset)
    k = clamp(budget, len(majority))
    if k == 0:
        return np.empty(0, dtype=int)

    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    pool = majority
    if len(pool) > DIVERSITY_POOL_CAP and k < DIVERSITY_POOL_CAP:
        pool = np.sort(rng.choice(majority, size=DIVERSITY_POOL_CAP, replace=False))
        logger.info(
            f"  [diversity] majority {len(majority):,} > cap "
            f"{DIVERSITY_POOL_CAP:,}; sampling candidate pool to the cap."
        )
    if k >= len(pool):
        return np.sort(pool)

    Xz = distance_features(dataset)[pool]
    start = int(rng.integers(len(pool)))
    selected = greedy_k_center(Xz, k, start, metric=dataset.distance_metric)
    return np.sort(pool[selected])

docs.title: greedy_k_center(Xz, k, start, metric='euclidean')
docs.text:
Greedy k-center farthest-point selection on a feature matrix.

Starting from start, repeatedly adds the point farthest from the current selection using a vectorized min-distance update.

Args: Xz: Feature matrix (n_pool, n_features) already prepared for metric (z-scored for "euclidean", raw for "hamming"; see distance_features). k: Number of points to select. start: Index of the initial seed point in Xz. metric: "euclidean" or "hamming" (see vector_distances).

Returns: Integer array of k indices into Xz, in selection order.

Source code in negative_ml/core/selection.py 
def greedy_k_center(
    Xz: np.ndarray, k: int, start: int, metric: str = "euclidean"
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Greedy k-center farthest-point selection on a feature matrix.

    Starting from start, repeatedly adds the point farthest from the current
    selection using a vectorized min-distance update.

    Args:
        Xz: Feature matrix (n_pool, n_features) already prepared for metric
            (z-scored for "euclidean", raw for "hamming"; see distance_features).
        k: Number of points to select.
        start: Index of the initial seed point in Xz.
        metric: "euclidean" or "hamming" (see vector_distances).

    Returns:
        Integer array of k indices into Xz, in selection order.
    """
    selected = np.empty(k, dtype=int)
    selected[0] = start
    min_dist = vector_distances(Xz, Xz[start], metric)
    for i in range(1, k):
        nxt = int(np.argmax(min_dist))
        selected[i] = nxt
        d = vector_distances(Xz, Xz[nxt], metric)
        min_dist = np.minimum(min_dist, d)
    return selected

docs.title: hard_examples(dataset, budget, metric='nearest_minority', **_kwargs)
docs.text:
Keep majority examples closest to the minority class / decision boundary.

Tests H2: inactive molecules structurally similar to actives, near-miss home runs, one-ingredient-off sandwich variants.

Args: dataset: Dataset whose majority examples are being sub-selected. budget: Number of majority examples to keep. metric: How "hardness" is scored. Only "nearest_minority" (distance to the nearest minority example, in the feature space dataset. distance_metric selects) is currently implemented. **_kwargs: Ignored; accepted so all selection strategies share a signature.

Returns: Sorted integer indices of the kept majority examples.

Source code in negative_ml/core/selection.py 
def hard_examples(
    dataset: Dataset,
    budget: int,
    metric: str = "nearest_minority",
    **_kwargs,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Keep majority examples closest to the minority class / decision boundary.

    Tests H2: inactive molecules structurally similar to actives, near-miss
    home runs, one-ingredient-off sandwich variants.

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset whose majority examples are being sub-selected.
        budget: Number of majority examples to keep.
        metric: How "hardness" is scored. Only "nearest_minority" (distance to
            the nearest minority example, in the feature space dataset.
            distance_metric selects) is currently implemented.
        **_kwargs: Ignored; accepted so all selection strategies share a
            signature.

    Returns:
        Sorted integer indices of the kept majority examples.
    """
    if metric != "nearest_minority":
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unsupported hardness metric {metric!r}; only 'nearest_minority'."
        )
    majority = majority_indices(dataset)
    k = clamp(budget, len(majority))
    minority = np.where(dataset.minority_mask())[0]
    if len(minority) == 0:
        # No boundary to measure against; fall back to a deterministic head.
        return np.sort(majority[:k])

    Xz = distance_features(dataset)
    nn = NearestNeighbors(
        n_neighbors=HARDNESS_N_NEIGHBORS, metric=dataset.distance_metric
    ).fit(Xz[minority])
    dist, _ = nn.kneighbors(Xz[majority])
    dist = dist.ravel()
    # Smallest distances == hardest (closest to the minority class).
    order = np.argsort(dist, kind="stable")[:k]
    return np.sort(majority[order])

docs.text:
Z-score features so distances are not dominated by raw scale.

Zero-variance columns are left centered (their std is treated as 1).

Args: X: Feature matrix to standardize, shape (n_samples, n_features).

def standardize(X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Z-score features so distances are not dominated by raw scale.

    Zero-variance columns are left centered (their std is treated as 1).

    Args:
        X: Feature matrix to standardize, shape (n_samples, n_features).

    Returns:
        A standardized copy of X with zero mean and unit variance per column.
    """
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    mu = X.mean(axis=0)
    sd = X.std(axis=0)
    sd = np.where(sd == 0, 1.0, sd)
    return (X - mu) / sd

docs.title: standardized_features(dataset)
docs.text:
Z-scored feature matrix for a dataset, cached on the dataset instance.

Every distance-based selection strategy standardizes the same full feature matrix, and a single compare_strategies call runs several strategies across seeds and budgets on one fixed training pool. Caching the z-scores on the Dataset the first time avoids recomputing them on every strategy call; the cache is keyed to the exact array, so a fresh subset (which builds a new Dataset) recomputes its own.

Args: dataset: Dataset whose features to standardize.

Returns: The z-scored feature matrix (the same array is returned on repeat calls).

Source code in negative_ml/core/selection.py 
def standardized_features(dataset: Dataset) -> np.ndarray:
    """Z-scored feature matrix for a dataset, cached on the dataset instance.

    Every distance-based selection strategy standardizes the same full feature
    matrix, and a single compare_strategies call runs several strategies across
    seeds and budgets on one fixed training pool. Caching the z-scores on the
    Dataset the first time avoids recomputing them on every strategy call; the
    cache is keyed to the exact array, so a fresh subset (which builds a new
    Dataset) recomputes its own.

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset whose features to standardize.

    Returns:
        The z-scored feature matrix (the same array is returned on repeat calls).
    """
    cached = getattr(dataset, "_standardized_X", None)
    if cached is None or cached.shape != dataset.X.shape:
        cached = standardize(dataset.X)
        dataset._standardized_X = cached
    return cached

docs.title: vector_distances(Xz, point, metric)
docs.text:
Distance from every row of Xz to a single point, under the given metric.

Args: Xz: Feature matrix, shape (n, d). point: A single feature vector, shape (d,), e.g. Xz[i] or a centroid. metric: "euclidean" (L2 norm) or "hamming" (L1 / count of differing positions -- exact for 0/1 one-hot rows, and the natural continuous extension when point is a real-valued centroid rather than another 0/1 row).

Returns: Distance from every row of Xz to point, shape (n,).

Source code in negative_ml/core/selection.py 
def vector_distances(Xz: np.ndarray, point: np.ndarray, metric: str) -> np.ndarray:
    """Distance from every row of Xz to a single point, under the given metric.

    Args:
        Xz: Feature matrix, shape (n, d).
        point: A single feature vector, shape (d,), e.g. Xz[i] or a centroid.
        metric: "euclidean" (L2 norm) or "hamming" (L1 / count of differing
            positions -- exact for 0/1 one-hot rows, and the natural continuous
            extension when point is a real-valued centroid rather than another
            0/1 row).

    Returns:
        Distance from every row of Xz to point, shape (n,).
    """
    diff = Xz - point
    if metric == "hamming":
        return np.abs(diff).sum(axis=1)
    return np.linalg.norm(diff, axis=1)

Holds the budget constant and varies how the kept majority examples are chosen — using the strategies in negative_ml.core.selection — to isolate whether boundary proximity (H2) or coverage (H3) beats raw volume, and whether class weighting (H4) can stand in for data.

docs.title: budget_sweep(dataset, model_factory, budgets, strategies=BUDGET_VARYING, n_seeds=SWEEP_N_SEEDS, scaffold_split=False, include_weighted=True, split=None, seed=RANDOM_SEED, neg_to_pos_ratio=None)
docs.text:
Run compare_strategies across several budgets.

The budget-varying strategies are swept over budgets; the full-data references (as_is and, when requested, weighted) are evaluated once at the full majority size and appended. Produces the strategy-vs-budget curves that are the talk's main result.

Args: dataset: Dataset whose majority class is sub-selected. model_factory: Builds a fresh estimator for each fit. budgets: Majority-class budgets to sweep over. strategies: Budget-varying selection strategies to compare. n_seeds: Number of seeds averaged at each budget. scaffold_split: Whether to use a scaffold/grouped split when split is None. include_weighted: Whether to add the full-data weighted reference. split: Pre-built EvalSplit (e.g. cross-season) forwarded to every compare_strategies call so the test set is identical across budgets; when None a stratified split of dataset is used. seed: Base random seed for the splits and selection. neg_to_pos_ratio: Forwarded to every compare_strategies call (see there); None (default) keeps every minority example at every budget, otherwise the minority is subsampled to track this ratio.

Returns: Long-format DataFrame: [strategy, seed, budget, n_train, minority_size, ]. Source code in negative_ml/core/sweep.py 

def budget_sweep(
    dataset: Dataset,
    model_factory: ModelFactory,
    budgets: Sequence[int],
    strategies: Sequence[str] = BUDGET_VARYING,
    n_seeds: int = SWEEP_N_SEEDS,
    scaffold_split: bool = False,
    include_weighted: bool = True,
    split: EvalSplit | None = None,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
    neg_to_pos_ratio: float | None = None,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Run compare_strategies across several budgets.

    The budget-varying strategies are swept over budgets; the full-data
    references (as_is and, when requested, weighted) are evaluated once
    at the full majority size and appended. Produces the strategy-vs-budget
    curves that are the talk's main result.

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset whose majority class is sub-selected.
        model_factory: Builds a fresh estimator for each fit.
        budgets: Majority-class budgets to sweep over.
        strategies: Budget-varying selection strategies to compare.
        n_seeds: Number of seeds averaged at each budget.
        scaffold_split: Whether to use a scaffold/grouped split when split is
            None.
        include_weighted: Whether to add the full-data weighted reference.
        split: Pre-built EvalSplit (e.g. cross-season) forwarded to every
            compare_strategies call so the test set is identical across
            budgets; when None a stratified split of dataset is used.
        seed: Base random seed for the splits and selection.
        neg_to_pos_ratio: Forwarded to every compare_strategies call (see
            there); None (default) keeps every minority example at every
            budget, otherwise the minority is subsampled to track this ratio.

    Returns:
        Long-format DataFrame: [strategy, seed, budget, n_train, minority_size,
        <metrics>].
    """
    # Resolved once and reused across every budget: it does not depend on
    # budget, so re-resolving it per iteration would rebuild the same
    # train/test split (and copy the training Dataset) once per budget point.
    resolved_split = resolve_split(dataset, split, scaffold=scaffold_split, seed=seed)

    frames = []
    for budget in budgets:
        frames.append(
            compare_strategies(
                dataset,
                model_factory,
                budget=budget,
                strategies=strategies,
                n_seeds=n_seeds,
                scaffold_split=scaffold_split,
                include_weighted=False,
                split=resolved_split,
                seed=seed,
                neg_to_pos_ratio=neg_to_pos_ratio,
            )
        )

    # Full-data references: computed once (they ignore the budget).
    reference = compare_strategies(
        dataset,
        model_factory,
        budget=dataset.n_samples,  # clamped to the available majority internally
        strategies=("as_is",),
        n_seeds=n_seeds,
        neg_to_pos_ratio=neg_to_pos_ratio,
        scaffold_split=scaffold_split,
        include_weighted=include_weighted,
        split=resolved_split,
        seed=seed,
    )
    frames.append(reference)
    return pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)

docs.text:
Compare majority-selection strategies at a single budget.

Args: dataset: Full training domain (ignored when split is supplied). model_factory: Builds a fresh model for each fit (accepts kwargs such as class_weight). budget: Number of majority examples each strategy may keep. strategies: Names from negative_ml.core.selection.STRATEGIES. n_seeds: Repeats per strategy (drives error bars). scaffold_split: Use scaffold/grouped instead of random eval split. include_weighted: Also evaluate the class-weighting baseline (H4). The weighted reference always keeps every minority example (neg_to_pos_ratio is ignored for it): it tests weighting as a substitute for majority volume, not for a smaller minority. split: Pre-built EvalSplit (e.g. cross-season) to evaluate on; when None a stratified split of dataset is used. seed: Base seed for the (fixed) train/test split and per-repeat seeds. neg_to_pos_ratio: When set, each strategy's minority is subsampled to round(len(selected majority) / neg_to_pos_ratio) instead of keeping every minority example -- the "proportional" class-balance regime from core.saturation.fix_ratio_vary_majority, extended across selection strategies. None (default) keeps every minority example (the "disproportional" regime this function has always used).

Returns: Long-format DataFrame: [strategy, seed, budget, n_train, minority_size, ]. Source code in negative_ml/core/sweep.py 

def compare_strategies(
    dataset: Dataset,
    model_factory: ModelFactory,
    budget: int,
    strategies: Sequence[str] = tuple(STRATEGIES),
    n_seeds: int = SWEEP_N_SEEDS,
    scaffold_split: bool = False,
    include_weighted: bool = False,
    split: EvalSplit | None = None,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
    neg_to_pos_ratio: float | None = None,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Compare majority-selection strategies at a single budget.

    Args:
        dataset: Full training domain (ignored when split is supplied).
        model_factory: Builds a fresh model for each fit (accepts kwargs such as
            class_weight).
        budget: Number of majority examples each strategy may keep.
        strategies: Names from negative_ml.core.selection.STRATEGIES.
        n_seeds: Repeats per strategy (drives error bars).
        scaffold_split: Use scaffold/grouped instead of random eval split.
        include_weighted: Also evaluate the class-weighting baseline (H4).
            The weighted reference always keeps every minority example
            (neg_to_pos_ratio is ignored for it): it tests weighting as a
            substitute for majority volume, not for a smaller minority.
        split: Pre-built EvalSplit (e.g. cross-season) to evaluate on;
            when None a stratified split of dataset is used.
        seed: Base seed for the (fixed) train/test split and per-repeat seeds.
        neg_to_pos_ratio: When set, each strategy's minority is subsampled to
            round(len(selected majority) / neg_to_pos_ratio) instead of
            keeping every minority example -- the "proportional" class-balance
            regime from core.saturation.fix_ratio_vary_majority, extended
            across selection strategies. None (default) keeps every minority
            example (the "disproportional" regime this function has always
            used).

    Returns:
        Long-format DataFrame: [strategy, seed, budget, n_train, minority_size,
        <metrics>].
    """
    # One fixed split so the test set is identical across every strategy.
    sp = resolve_split(dataset, split, scaffold=scaffold_split, seed=seed)
    train_ds = sp.train_ds
    X_test, y_test = sp.X_test, sp.y_test

    minority_idx = np.where(train_ds.minority_mask())[0]
    n_majority = int(train_ds.majority_mask().sum())
    n_minority = len(minority_idx)

    rows = []
    for name in strategies:
        strategy = STRATEGIES[name]
        for s in range(n_seeds):
            selected = strategy(train_ds, budget, seed=seed + s)
            if neg_to_pos_ratio is None:
                minority_rows = minority_idx
            else:
                min_count = clamp(round(len(selected) / neg_to_pos_ratio), n_minority)
                rng = np.random.default_rng(seed + s)
                minority_rows = rng.choice(minority_idx, size=min_count, replace=False)
            train_rows = np.concatenate([minority_rows, selected])
            metrics = fit_score(train_ds, train_rows, X_test, y_test, model_factory)
            rows.append(
                {
                    "strategy": name,
                    "seed": s,
                    "budget": int(min(budget, n_majority)),
                    "n_train": int(len(train_rows)),
                    "minority_size": int(len(minority_rows)),
                    **metrics,
                }
            )

    if include_weighted:
        # Full majority, but up-weight the minority instead of deleting data.
        majority_idx = np.where(train_ds.majority_mask())[0]
        train_rows = np.concatenate([minority_idx, majority_idx])
        ratio = float(n_majority / max(len(minority_idx), 1))
        for s in range(n_seeds):
            metrics = fit_score(
                train_ds,
                train_rows,
                X_test,
                y_test,
                model_factory,
                class_weight=ratio,
            )
            rows.append(
                {
                    "strategy": WEIGHTED,
                    "seed": s,
                    "budget": n_majority,
                    "n_train": int(len(train_rows)),
                    **metrics,
                }
            )

    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

docs.title: Saturation experiments
docs.text:
Saturation experiments — how much majority-class data is enough? (4.1, H1).

Three complementary sweeps, all returning a tidy results frame (one row per budget x seed) ready for plotting a saturation curve:

A) fix_minority_vary_majority — keep all minority examples, grow the
   majority count; find where performance plateaus.
B) scale_total_proportional — subsample the whole dataset at a fixed
   class ratio; separates "more majority data" from "more data overall".
C) fix_ratio_vary_majority — grow the majority count like A, but hold the
   minority:majority ratio fixed at the training pool's natural balance
   (e.g. ~3% active in the antibacterial screen) instead of keeping every
   minority example; isolates the value of class balance itself from
   majority-class volume, on the same majority-size axis as A.

docs.text:
Hold the minority:majority ratio fixed while the majority count grows.

Complements fix_minority_vary_majority (A), which instead keeps every minority example fixed and lets the class ratio skew as the majority grows. Here the minority count is subsampled in step with the majority so the positive share stays anchored to the training pool's own class balance (e.g. ~3% active in the antibacterial screen) at every point on the same majority-size axis A sweeps, isolating the value of class balance itself from majority-class volume.

Draws majority examples via the same random_undersample(train_ds, size, seed=seed + s) call fix_minority_vary_majority uses, so at a matched (seed, majority_size) the two sweeps train on the identical negative examples and differ only in how many positives are included.

Args: dataset: Full training domain (ignored when split is supplied). model_factory: Builds a fresh model for each fit. majority_sizes: Majority-class counts to evaluate. n_seeds: Repeats per size for error bars. scaffold_split: Use scaffold/grouped instead of random eval split. split: Pre-built EvalSplit (e.g. cross-season) to evaluate on; when None a stratified split of dataset is used. seed: Base seed for the (fixed) split and per-repeat selection.

Returns: Long-format DataFrame with columns [majority_size, minority_size, seed, n_train, auroc, auprc, ...].

def fix_ratio_vary_majority(
    dataset: Dataset,
    model_factory: ModelFactory,
    majority_sizes: Sequence[int],
    n_seeds: int = SWEEP_N_SEEDS,
    scaffold_split: bool = False,
    split: EvalSplit | None = None,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Hold the minority:majority ratio fixed while the majority count grows.

    Complements fix_minority_vary_majority (A), which instead keeps every
    minority example fixed and lets the class ratio skew as the majority
    grows. Here the minority count is subsampled in step with the majority so
    the positive share stays anchored to the training pool's own class
    balance (e.g. ~3% active in the antibacterial screen) at every point on
    the same majority-size axis A sweeps, isolating the value of class
    balance itself from majority-class volume.

    Draws majority examples via the same random_undersample(train_ds, size,
    seed=seed + s) call fix_minority_vary_majority uses, so at a matched
    (seed, majority_size) the two sweeps train on the identical negative
    examples and differ only in how many positives are included.

    Args:
        dataset: Full training domain (ignored when split is supplied).
        model_factory: Builds a fresh model for each fit.
        majority_sizes: Majority-class counts to evaluate.
        n_seeds: Repeats per size for error bars.
        scaffold_split: Use scaffold/grouped instead of random eval split.
        split: Pre-built EvalSplit (e.g. cross-season) to evaluate on;
            when None a stratified split of dataset is used.
        seed: Base seed for the (fixed) split and per-repeat selection.

    Returns:
        Long-format DataFrame with columns
        [majority_size, minority_size, seed, n_train, auroc, auprc, ...].
    """
    sp = resolve_split(dataset, split, scaffold=scaffold_split, seed=seed)
    train_ds = sp.train_ds
    X_test, y_test = sp.X_test, sp.y_test
    minority_idx = np.where(train_ds.minority_mask())[0]
    n_majority = int(train_ds.majority_mask().sum())
    n_minority = len(minority_idx)
    # Ratio anchored to the training pool's own class balance, not a
    # hardcoded target -- mirrors how the reference negative-dataset study
    # computes neg_to_pos_ratio from the source dataframe once and reuses it
    # for every size.
    neg_to_pos_ratio = max(n_majority, 1) / max(n_minority, 1)

    rows = []
    for size in majority_sizes:
        maj_count = min(size, n_majority)
        min_count = clamp(round(maj_count / neg_to_pos_ratio), n_minority)
        for s in range(n_seeds):
            selected_majority = random_undersample(train_ds, maj_count, seed=seed + s)
            rng = np.random.default_rng(seed + s)
            selected_minority = rng.choice(minority_idx, size=min_count, replace=False)
            train_rows = np.concatenate([selected_minority, selected_majority])
            metrics = fit_score(train_ds, train_rows, X_test, y_test, model_factory)
            rows.append(
                {
                    "majority_size": int(maj_count),
                    "minority_size": int(min_count),
                    "seed": s,
                    "n_train": int(len(train_rows)),
                    **metrics,
                }
            )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

docs.text:
Subsample the whole training set at a fixed class ratio.

Isolates the gain from more data overall vs. more majority data: both classes shrink together, so the imbalance ratio is held roughly constant.

Args: dataset: Dataset to subsample. model_factory: Builds a fresh estimator for each fit. fractions: Fractions of the full training set to subsample. n_seeds: Number of subsampling seeds averaged at each fraction. scaffold_split: Whether to use a scaffold/grouped split when split is None. split: Pre-built EvalSplit (e.g. cross-season) to evaluate on; when None a stratified split of dataset is used. seed: Base random seed for the splits and subsampling.

Returns: Long-format DataFrame with columns [fraction, seed, n_train, auroc, auprc, ...].

Source code in negative_ml/core/saturation.py 
def scale_total_proportional(
    dataset: Dataset,
    model_factory: ModelFactory,
    fractions: Sequence[float],
    n_seeds: int = SWEEP_N_SEEDS,
    scaffold_split: bool = False,
    split: EvalSplit | None = None,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Subsample the whole training set at a fixed class ratio.

    Isolates the gain from more data overall vs. more majority data: both
    classes shrink together, so the imbalance ratio is held roughly constant.

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset to subsample.
        model_factory: Builds a fresh estimator for each fit.
        fractions: Fractions of the full training set to subsample.
        n_seeds: Number of subsampling seeds averaged at each fraction.
        scaffold_split: Whether to use a scaffold/grouped split when split is
            None.
        split: Pre-built EvalSplit (e.g. cross-season) to evaluate on;
            when None a stratified split of dataset is used.
        seed: Base random seed for the splits and subsampling.

    Returns:
        Long-format DataFrame with columns
        [fraction, seed, n_train, auroc, auprc, ...].
    """
    sp = resolve_split(dataset, split, scaffold=scaffold_split, seed=seed)
    train_ds = sp.train_ds
    X_test, y_test = sp.X_test, sp.y_test
    minority_idx = np.where(train_ds.minority_mask())[0]
    majority_idx = np.where(train_ds.majority_mask())[0]

    rows = []
    for frac in fractions:
        for s in range(n_seeds):
            rng = np.random.default_rng(seed + s)
            n_min = max(1, int(round(len(minority_idx) * frac)))
            n_maj = max(1, int(round(len(majority_idx) * frac)))
            keep_min = rng.choice(minority_idx, size=n_min, replace=False)
            keep_maj = rng.choice(majority_idx, size=n_maj, replace=False)
            train_rows = np.concatenate([keep_min, keep_maj])
            metrics = fit_score(train_ds, train_rows, X_test, y_test, model_factory)
            rows.append(
                {
                    "fraction": float(frac),
                    "seed": s,
                    "n_train": int(len(train_rows)),
                    **metrics,
                }
            )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

docs.title: Active learning
docs.text:
Pool-based active learning simulation over the three study domains.

Labels are known in advance (the full training pool is observable); the simulation queries one batch at a time and tracks how quickly each acquisition strategy recovers positive examples and how model performance evolves, while the negative data composition (the strategy used to sub-select labeled negatives before each model fit) is varied independently.

Two acquisition strategies and a random baseline are implemented. Each is crossed with the existing majority-class selection strategies applied to the labeled negatives at every round, so the design isolates whether composition of the negative training data matters inside an active-learning loop.

docs.title: gp_ei_acquisition(model, X_pool, batch_size, seed, X_labeled, y_labeled)
docs.text:
Bayesian optimization acquisition: Gaussian Process + Expected Improvement.

Fits a GaussianProcessRegressor on the labeled data and uses Expected Improvement (EI) to select the next batch. EI scores each unlabeled example as:

EI(x) = (μ(x) − f*) · Φ(Z) + σ(x) · φ(Z),  Z = (μ(x) − f*) / σ(x)

where f* = 1.0 (the best achievable label), μ and σ are the GP posterior mean and standard deviation, and Φ/φ are the standard normal CDF/PDF. Examples with high predicted probability AND high GP uncertainty score highest, naturally balancing exploitation and exploration without manual heuristics.

When the labeled set exceeds _GP_MAX_LABELED examples, a random subsample is drawn to keep GP training tractable (O(n³) cost). Features are standardized before fitting.

Args: model: Ignored; accepted to match AcquisitionFn signature. X_pool: Feature matrix for the unlabeled pool. batch_size: Number of examples to select. seed: Random seed for GP subsample and reproducibility. X_labeled: Feature matrix for all currently labeled examples. y_labeled: Labels for all currently labeled examples.

Returns: Sorted pool indices of the batch_size examples with highest EI.

Source code in negative_ml/core/active_learning.py 
def gp_ei_acquisition(
    model: object,
    X_pool: np.ndarray,
    batch_size: int,
    seed: int,
    X_labeled: np.ndarray,
    y_labeled: np.ndarray,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Bayesian optimization acquisition: Gaussian Process + Expected Improvement.

    Fits a GaussianProcessRegressor on the labeled data and uses Expected
    Improvement (EI) to select the next batch. EI scores each unlabeled
    example as:

        EI(x) = (μ(x) − f*) · Φ(Z) + σ(x) · φ(Z),  Z = (μ(x) − f*) / σ(x)

    where f* = 1.0 (the best achievable label), μ and σ are the GP posterior
    mean and standard deviation, and Φ/φ are the standard normal CDF/PDF.
    Examples with high predicted probability AND high GP uncertainty score
    highest, naturally balancing exploitation and exploration without manual
    heuristics.

    When the labeled set exceeds _GP_MAX_LABELED examples, a random subsample
    is drawn to keep GP training tractable (O(n³) cost). Features are
    standardized before fitting.

    Args:
        model: Ignored; accepted to match AcquisitionFn signature.
        X_pool: Feature matrix for the unlabeled pool.
        batch_size: Number of examples to select.
        seed: Random seed for GP subsample and reproducibility.
        X_labeled: Feature matrix for all currently labeled examples.
        y_labeled: Labels for all currently labeled examples.

    Returns:
        Sorted pool indices of the batch_size examples with highest EI.
    """
    k = clamp(batch_size, len(X_pool))
    if k == 0:
        return np.empty(0, dtype=int)
    if k >= len(X_pool):
        return np.arange(len(X_pool))

    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X_train, y_train = X_labeled, y_labeled
    if len(X_train) > _GP_MAX_LABELED:
        idx = rng.choice(len(X_train), size=_GP_MAX_LABELED, replace=False)
        X_train, y_train = X_train[idx], y_train[idx]

    X_train_z = standardize(X_train)
    gp = GaussianProcessRegressor(
        kernel=Matern(nu=2.5),
        normalize_y=True,
        n_restarts_optimizer=2,
        random_state=int(rng.integers(2**31)),
    )
    gp.fit(X_train_z, y_train.astype(float))

    # Standardize pool using same scale as training (reuse standardize per-matrix)
    X_pool_z = standardize(X_pool)
    mu, sigma = gp.predict(X_pool_z, return_std=True)

    f_best = 1.0
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore"):
        Z = (mu - f_best) / sigma
    ei = (mu - f_best) * norm.cdf(Z) + sigma * norm.pdf(Z)
    ei = np.where(sigma > 0, ei, 0.0)

    chosen = np.argpartition(-ei, k)[:k]
    return np.sort(chosen)

docs.title: make_cold_start_labeled(train_pool_ds, n_pos, n_neg, neg_pool_size, neg_strategy, seed=RANDOM_SEED)
docs.text:
Initial labeled bolus whose negatives are drawn from a capped candidate pool.

Seeds n_pos positives directly, then draws a neg_pool_size-example candidate pool of negatives at random and sub-selects n_neg of them with a selection.STRATEGIES entry (neg_strategy). This isolates the cold-start question -- does the negative selection strategy used to seed a study matter -- from ongoing active-learning acquisition, which is unaffected by neg_pool_size. The candidate pool passed to the strategy includes the seeded positives alongside the pool negatives, so strategies that need a minority reference (e.g. "hard"/decoys, scored by distance to the nearest positive) see one.

Args: train_pool_ds: The full training pool Dataset. n_pos: Number of positive (minority) examples to seed. n_neg: Number of negative (majority) examples to keep after neg_strategy sub-selects from the candidate pool. neg_pool_size: Size of the random candidate pool of negatives that neg_strategy chooses n_neg from. neg_strategy: Name in selection.STRATEGIES used to sub-select the negatives. seed: Random seed for reproducibility.

Returns: Sorted integer indices into train_pool_ds for the initial labeled bolus.

Source code in negative_ml/core/active_learning.py 
def make_cold_start_labeled(
    train_pool_ds: Dataset,
    n_pos: int,
    n_neg: int,
    neg_pool_size: int,
    neg_strategy: str,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Initial labeled bolus whose negatives are drawn from a capped candidate pool.

    Seeds n_pos positives directly, then draws a neg_pool_size-example candidate
    pool of negatives at random and sub-selects n_neg of them with a
    selection.STRATEGIES entry (neg_strategy). This isolates the cold-start
    question -- does the negative selection strategy used to seed a study
    matter -- from ongoing active-learning acquisition, which is unaffected by
    neg_pool_size. The candidate pool passed to the strategy includes the
    seeded positives alongside the pool negatives, so strategies that need a
    minority reference (e.g. "hard"/decoys, scored by distance to the nearest
    positive) see one.

    Args:
        train_pool_ds: The full training pool Dataset.
        n_pos: Number of positive (minority) examples to seed.
        n_neg: Number of negative (majority) examples to keep after
            neg_strategy sub-selects from the candidate pool.
        neg_pool_size: Size of the random candidate pool of negatives that
            neg_strategy chooses n_neg from.
        neg_strategy: Name in selection.STRATEGIES used to sub-select the
            negatives.
        seed: Random seed for reproducibility.

    Returns:
        Sorted integer indices into train_pool_ds for the initial labeled bolus.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    pos_all = np.where(train_pool_ds.minority_mask())[0]
    neg_all = np.where(train_pool_ds.majority_mask())[0]

    k_pos = clamp(n_pos, len(pos_all))
    chosen_pos = rng.choice(pos_all, size=k_pos, replace=False)

    k_pool = clamp(neg_pool_size, len(neg_all))
    neg_pool = rng.choice(neg_all, size=k_pool, replace=False)

    candidate_idx = np.sort(np.concatenate([chosen_pos, neg_pool]))
    candidate_ds = train_pool_ds.subset(candidate_idx)
    strategy_fn = STRATEGIES[neg_strategy]
    local_neg_idx = strategy_fn(candidate_ds, n_neg, seed=seed)
    chosen_neg = candidate_idx[local_neg_idx]

    return np.sort(np.concatenate([chosen_pos, chosen_neg]))

Samples exactly n_pos minority examples and n_neg majority examples from the training pool. If fewer than n_pos positives or n_neg negatives exist, all available examples of that class are returned instead.

def make_init_labeled(
    train_pool_ds: Dataset,
    n_pos: int,
    n_neg: int,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Stratified initial labeled set with n_pos positives and n_neg negatives.

    Samples exactly n_pos minority examples and n_neg majority examples from
    the training pool. If fewer than n_pos positives or n_neg negatives exist,
    all available examples of that class are returned instead.

    Args:
        train_pool_ds: The full training pool Dataset.
        n_pos: Number of positive (minority) examples to seed.
        n_neg: Number of negative (majority) examples to seed.
        seed: Random seed for reproducibility.

    Returns:
        Sorted integer indices into train_pool_ds for the initial labeled set.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    pos_all = np.where(train_pool_ds.minority_mask())[0]
    neg_all = np.where(train_pool_ds.majority_mask())[0]
    k_pos = clamp(n_pos, len(pos_all))
    k_neg = clamp(n_neg, len(neg_all))
    chosen_pos = rng.choice(pos_all, size=k_pos, replace=False)
    chosen_neg = rng.choice(neg_all, size=k_neg, replace=False)
    return np.sort(np.concatenate([chosen_pos, chosen_neg]))

docs.text:
Simulate pool-based active learning over n_batches query rounds.

At each round the labeled set is sub-selected for training (all labeled positives plus negatives chosen by neg_composition), a fresh model is fit, scored on the test set, and then used to score the unlabeled pool for the next acquisition step. Round 0 records the state after seeding the initial labeled set (before any queries), so the returned frame has n_batches + 1 rows.

Args: train_pool_ds: Full training pool; all labels are visible (simulation). X_test: Held-out evaluation features. y_test: Held-out evaluation labels. model_factory: Builds a fresh classifier for each fit. batch_size: Number of examples queried per active-learning round. n_batches: Number of query rounds after the initial seed. acquisition_fn: AcquisitionFn selecting pool indices to label next. neg_composition: Name in selection.STRATEGIES for negative sub-selection. neg_budget: Cap on the number of labeled negatives used to train. init_labeled_idx: Indices into train_pool_ds for the initial labeled set. seed: Base random seed; per-round seeds are derived by incrementing.

Returns: Long-format DataFrame with one row per round (including round 0): [batch, n_labeled, n_positives_labeled, positives_in_batch, auroc, auprc, f1].

Source code in negative_ml/core/active_learning.py 
def run_active_learning(
    train_pool_ds: Dataset,
    X_test: np.ndarray,
    y_test: np.ndarray,
    model_factory: ModelFactory,
    batch_size: int,
    n_batches: int,
    acquisition_fn: AcquisitionFn,
    neg_composition: str,
    neg_budget: int,
    init_labeled_idx: np.ndarray,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Simulate pool-based active learning over n_batches query rounds.

    At each round the labeled set is sub-selected for training (all labeled
    positives plus negatives chosen by neg_composition), a fresh model is fit,
    scored on the test set, and then used to score the unlabeled pool for the
    next acquisition step. Round 0 records the state after seeding the initial
    labeled set (before any queries), so the returned frame has n_batches + 1
    rows.

    Args:
        train_pool_ds: Full training pool; all labels are visible (simulation).
        X_test: Held-out evaluation features.
        y_test: Held-out evaluation labels.
        model_factory: Builds a fresh classifier for each fit.
        batch_size: Number of examples queried per active-learning round.
        n_batches: Number of query rounds after the initial seed.
        acquisition_fn: AcquisitionFn selecting pool indices to label next.
        neg_composition: Name in selection.STRATEGIES for negative sub-selection.
        neg_budget: Cap on the number of labeled negatives used to train.
        init_labeled_idx: Indices into train_pool_ds for the initial labeled set.
        seed: Base random seed; per-round seeds are derived by incrementing.

    Returns:
        Long-format DataFrame with one row per round (including round 0):
        [batch, n_labeled, n_positives_labeled, positives_in_batch,
         auroc, auprc, f1].
    """
    composition = STRATEGIES[neg_composition]
    labeled_idx = np.array(init_labeled_idx, dtype=int)
    pool_mask = np.ones(train_pool_ds.n_samples, dtype=bool)
    pool_mask[labeled_idx] = False

    rows: list[dict] = []
    prev_n_pos = 0

    for batch_idx in range(n_batches + 1):
        labeled_ds = train_pool_ds.subset(labeled_idx)
        pos_rows = np.where(labeled_ds.minority_mask())[0]
        neg_rows = composition(labeled_ds, neg_budget, seed=seed + batch_idx)
        train_rows = np.concatenate([pos_rows, neg_rows])

        model = model_factory()
        model.fit(labeled_ds.X[train_rows], labeled_ds.y[train_rows])
        metrics = compute_metrics(y_test, positive_scores(model, X_test))

        n_pos_now = int(labeled_ds.minority_mask().sum())
        rows.append(
            {
                "batch": batch_idx,
                "n_labeled": len(labeled_idx),
                "n_positives_labeled": n_pos_now,
                "positives_in_batch": n_pos_now - prev_n_pos,
                **metrics,
            }
        )
        prev_n_pos = n_pos_now

        if batch_idx < n_batches:
            pool_idx = np.where(pool_mask)[0]
            X_pool = train_pool_ds.X[pool_idx]
            pool_chosen = acquisition_fn(
                model, X_pool, batch_size, seed + batch_idx, labeled_ds.X, labeled_ds.y
            )
            new_idx = pool_idx[pool_chosen]
            labeled_idx = np.sort(np.concatenate([labeled_idx, new_idx]))
            pool_mask[new_idx] = False

    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

docs.title: ucb_acquisition(model, X_pool, batch_size, seed, X_labeled, y_labeled)
docs.text:
Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) acquisition using the existing fitted model.

Scores each unlabeled example as UCB = μ + κ·σ, where μ is the model's positive-class probability (exploitation) and σ = 1 − |2μ − 1| is a margin-based uncertainty proxy (exploration). κ = 1.0 balances the two terms. Examples with high predicted probability AND high uncertainty score highest, unlike pure uncertainty sampling which ignores the exploitation signal entirely.

Args: model: Fitted classifier exposing predict_proba or decision_function. X_pool: Feature matrix for the unlabeled pool. batch_size: Number of examples to select. seed: Ignored (deterministic); accepted to match AcquisitionFn signature. X_labeled: Ignored; accepted to match AcquisitionFn signature. y_labeled: Ignored; accepted to match AcquisitionFn signature.

Returns: Sorted pool indices of the batch_size examples with highest UCB score.

Source code in negative_ml/core/active_learning.py 
def ucb_acquisition(
    model: object,
    X_pool: np.ndarray,
    batch_size: int,
    seed: int,
    X_labeled: np.ndarray,
    y_labeled: np.ndarray,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) acquisition using the existing fitted model.

    Scores each unlabeled example as UCB = μ + κ·σ, where μ is the model's
    positive-class probability (exploitation) and σ = 1 − |2μ − 1| is a
    margin-based uncertainty proxy (exploration). κ = 1.0 balances the two
    terms. Examples with high predicted probability AND high uncertainty score
    highest, unlike pure uncertainty sampling which ignores the exploitation
    signal entirely.

    Args:
        model: Fitted classifier exposing predict_proba or decision_function.
        X_pool: Feature matrix for the unlabeled pool.
        batch_size: Number of examples to select.
        seed: Ignored (deterministic); accepted to match AcquisitionFn signature.
        X_labeled: Ignored; accepted to match AcquisitionFn signature.
        y_labeled: Ignored; accepted to match AcquisitionFn signature.

    Returns:
        Sorted pool indices of the batch_size examples with highest UCB score.
    """
    k = clamp(batch_size, len(X_pool))
    if k == 0:
        return np.empty(0, dtype=int)
    if k >= len(X_pool):
        return np.arange(len(X_pool))

    kappa = 1.0
    p = positive_scores(model, X_pool)
    uncertainty = 1.0 - np.abs(2.0 * p - 1.0)
    ucb = p + kappa * uncertainty
    chosen = np.argpartition(-ucb, k)[:k]
    return np.sort(chosen)

docs.title: Matched-pair evaluation
docs.text:
Matched-pair discovery and pairwise evaluation utilities.

A matched pair is one positive (minority) example and one negative (majority) example that are close in standardized feature space but carry opposite labels. Evaluating trained models on such pairs tests whether a selection strategy teaches fine-grained decision-boundary discrimination rather than broad class separation.

The headline metric is pair_auroc: AUROC computed over the pooled positive and negative scores from the matched pairs. A random classifier scores ~0.5; a perfect boundary learner scores 1.0. Because the pairs are the hardest, closest cross-label examples, pair_auroc is normally lower than the model's global test-set AUROC -- that gap is the signal.

docs.title: find_matched_pairs(X, y, *, max_pairs=500, metric='euclidean')
docs.text:
Find cross-label pairs sorted by proximity in the chosen distance metric.

For each positive example, finds its nearest negative in feature space. Deduplicates so each negative is used at most once. Returns the top max_pairs pairs sorted by distance (closest first).

Args: X: Feature matrix (n_samples, n_features). y: Binary labels (1 = positive / minority, 0 = negative / majority). max_pairs: Maximum number of pairs to return. metric: "euclidean" (default) z-scores X first, matching every other distance-based strategy in negative_ml.core.selection. "hamming" leaves X unscaled and counts differing positions -- for domains built from multi-hot / one-hot features (e.g. sandwich ingredients), where z-scoring would weight rare categories far more heavily than common ones.

Returns: DataFrame with columns [idx_pos, idx_neg, dist]. Indices reference rows in the original X / y arrays.

Source code in negative_ml/core/mmp.py 
def find_matched_pairs(
    X: np.ndarray,
    y: np.ndarray,
    *,
    max_pairs: int = 500,
    metric: str = "euclidean",
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Find cross-label pairs sorted by proximity in the chosen distance metric.

    For each positive example, finds its nearest negative in feature space.
    Deduplicates so each negative is used at most once. Returns the top
    max_pairs pairs sorted by distance (closest first).

    Args:
        X: Feature matrix (n_samples, n_features).
        y: Binary labels (1 = positive / minority, 0 = negative / majority).
        max_pairs: Maximum number of pairs to return.
        metric: "euclidean" (default) z-scores X first, matching every other
            distance-based strategy in negative_ml.core.selection. "hamming"
            leaves X unscaled and counts differing positions -- for domains
            built from multi-hot / one-hot features (e.g. sandwich
            ingredients), where z-scoring would weight rare categories far more
            heavily than common ones.

    Returns:
        DataFrame with columns [idx_pos, idx_neg, dist]. Indices reference
        rows in the original X / y arrays.
    """
    X_std = (
        np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        if metric == "hamming"
        else standardize(np.asarray(X, dtype=float))
    )
    y = np.asarray(y)
    pos_idx = np.where(y == 1)[0]
    neg_idx = np.where(y == 0)[0]

    if len(pos_idx) == 0 or len(neg_idx) == 0:
        return pd.DataFrame(columns=["idx_pos", "idx_neg", "dist"])

    # For each positive, find its single nearest negative (ball_tree is fast).
    nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1, algorithm="ball_tree", metric=metric)
    nn.fit(X_std[neg_idx])
    dist_arr, local_neg_arr = nn.kneighbors(X_std[pos_idx])
    dist_arr = dist_arr.ravel()
    local_neg_arr = local_neg_arr.ravel()

    # Greedy deduplication: iterate positives from closest to farthest;
    # skip when the nearest negative has already been claimed.
    order = np.argsort(dist_arr, kind="stable")
    seen_neg: set[int] = set()
    pairs: list[dict] = []
    for i in order:
        neg_global = int(neg_idx[local_neg_arr[i]])
        if neg_global in seen_neg:
            continue
        seen_neg.add(neg_global)
        pairs.append(
            {
                "idx_pos": int(pos_idx[i]),
                "idx_neg": neg_global,
                "dist": float(dist_arr[i]),
            }
        )
        if len(pairs) >= max_pairs:
            break

    return pd.DataFrame(pairs)

docs.title: mmp_metrics(scored_pairs)
docs.text:
Pairwise performance metrics over a set of scored matched pairs.

Args: scored_pairs: Output of score_pairs with score_pos, score_neg, and margin columns.

Returns: Dict with pair_auroc (AUROC over the pooled positive/negative scores from the matched pairs) and mean_margin (mean score_pos - score_neg).

Source code in negative_ml/core/mmp.py 
def mmp_metrics(scored_pairs: pd.DataFrame) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Pairwise performance metrics over a set of scored matched pairs.

    Args:
        scored_pairs: Output of score_pairs with score_pos, score_neg, and
            margin columns.

    Returns:
        Dict with pair_auroc (AUROC over the pooled positive/negative scores
        from the matched pairs) and mean_margin (mean score_pos - score_neg).
    """
    if scored_pairs.empty:
        return {"pair_auroc": float("nan"), "mean_margin": float("nan")}
    n = len(scored_pairs)
    y_true = np.concatenate([np.ones(n), np.zeros(n)])
    y_score = np.concatenate(
        [scored_pairs["score_pos"].to_numpy(), scored_pairs["score_neg"].to_numpy()]
    )
    return {
        "pair_auroc": auroc(y_true, y_score),
        "mean_margin": float(scored_pairs["margin"].mean()),
    }
