docs.text:
Fit one model per strategy at a fixed seed and score matched-pair examples.

Used in the plot phase to attach per-strategy model scores to the saved example pairs DataFrame without repeating the full n-seed evaluation sweep.

Args: train_ds: Dataset to train each strategy model on. score_X: Feature matrix the pairs index into (may differ from train_ds.X when the model is trained on the full dataset but scored on a subset, or vice versa). pairs: Matched-pairs DataFrame (from find_matched_pairs) whose idx_pos / idx_neg reference rows in score_X. model_factory: Returns a fresh unfitted estimator. budget: Majority-class budget passed to each selection strategy. strategies: Which strategies to score (default: all budget-varying ones). seed: Random seed for strategy selection.

Returns: Dict mapping strategy name to the scored pairs DataFrame (output of score_pairs for that strategy).

Source code in negative_ml/core/mmp.py 
def rescore_examples(
    train_ds: Dataset,
    score_X: np.ndarray,
    pairs: pd.DataFrame,
    model_factory: ModelFactory,
    budget: int,
    *,
    strategies: tuple[str, ...] = BUDGET_VARYING,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> dict[str, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Fit one model per strategy at a fixed seed and score matched-pair examples.

    Used in the plot phase to attach per-strategy model scores to the saved
    example pairs DataFrame without repeating the full n-seed evaluation sweep.

    Args:
        train_ds: Dataset to train each strategy model on.
        score_X: Feature matrix the pairs index into (may differ from train_ds.X
            when the model is trained on the full dataset but scored on a subset,
            or vice versa).
        pairs: Matched-pairs DataFrame (from find_matched_pairs) whose idx_pos /
            idx_neg reference rows in score_X.
        model_factory: Returns a fresh unfitted estimator.
        budget: Majority-class budget passed to each selection strategy.
        strategies: Which strategies to score (default: all budget-varying ones).
        seed: Random seed for strategy selection.

    Returns:
        Dict mapping strategy name to the scored pairs DataFrame
        (output of score_pairs for that strategy).
    """
    minority_idx = np.where(train_ds.minority_mask())[0]
    scored: dict[str, pd.DataFrame] = {}
    for strat_name in strategies:
        majority_idx = STRATEGIES[strat_name](train_ds, budget, seed=seed)
        train_rows = np.sort(np.concatenate([minority_idx, majority_idx]))
        model = model_factory()
        model.fit(train_ds.X[train_rows], train_ds.y[train_rows])
        scored[strat_name] = score_pairs(model, score_X, pairs)
    return scored

docs.title: run_mmp_evaluation(split, test_pairs, model_factory, budget, *, strategies=BUDGET_VARYING, n_seeds=SWEEP_N_SEEDS)
docs.text:
Evaluate models trained with different selection strategies on matched pairs.

For each (strategy, seed) combination, applies the strategy at the given budget to split.train_ds, fits a fresh model, and scores both the overall test set and the pre-computed matched pairs. Returns a long-format DataFrame covering every (strategy, seed).

Args: split: EvalSplit whose train_ds is the training pool and X_test/y_test is the held-out evaluation set (pairs must index into X_test/y_test). test_pairs: Pre-computed cross-label pairs from find_matched_pairs called on split.X_test / split.y_test. model_factory: Callable returning a fresh unfitted estimator. budget: Number of majority examples each strategy selects. strategies: Which selection strategies to evaluate (must be keys of negative_ml.core.selection.STRATEGIES). n_seeds: Number of random seeds per strategy (for stochastic strategies; hard selection is deterministic but repeating gives the same result).

Returns: Long-format DataFrame with one row per (strategy, seed) and columns: [strategy, seed, budget, n_train, pair_auroc, mean_margin, n_pairs, auroc, auprc, f1]. auroc is the model's global test-set AUROC; pair_auroc is AUROC restricted to the matched hard pairs.

Source code in negative_ml/core/mmp.py 
def run_mmp_evaluation(
    split: EvalSplit,
    test_pairs: pd.DataFrame,
    model_factory: ModelFactory,
    budget: int,
    *,
    strategies: tuple[str, ...] = BUDGET_VARYING,
    n_seeds: int = SWEEP_N_SEEDS,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Evaluate models trained with different selection strategies on matched pairs.

    For each (strategy, seed) combination, applies the strategy at the given
    budget to split.train_ds, fits a fresh model, and scores both the overall
    test set and the pre-computed matched pairs. Returns a long-format DataFrame
    covering every (strategy, seed).

    Args:
        split: EvalSplit whose train_ds is the training pool and X_test/y_test
            is the held-out evaluation set (pairs must index into X_test/y_test).
        test_pairs: Pre-computed cross-label pairs from find_matched_pairs
            called on split.X_test / split.y_test.
        model_factory: Callable returning a fresh unfitted estimator.
        budget: Number of majority examples each strategy selects.
        strategies: Which selection strategies to evaluate (must be keys of
            negative_ml.core.selection.STRATEGIES).
        n_seeds: Number of random seeds per strategy (for stochastic strategies;
            hard selection is deterministic but repeating gives the same result).

    Returns:
        Long-format DataFrame with one row per (strategy, seed) and columns:
        [strategy, seed, budget, n_train, pair_auroc, mean_margin, n_pairs,
         auroc, auprc, f1]. auroc is the model's global test-set AUROC;
         pair_auroc is AUROC restricted to the matched hard pairs.
    """
    n_pairs = len(test_pairs)
    minority_idx = np.where(split.train_ds.minority_mask())[0]
    rows: list[dict] = []

    for strat_name in strategies:
        strategy_fn = STRATEGIES[strat_name]
        for seed in range(n_seeds):
            majority_idx = strategy_fn(split.train_ds, budget, seed=seed)
            train_rows = np.sort(np.concatenate([minority_idx, majority_idx]))

            model = model_factory()
            model.fit(split.train_ds.X[train_rows], split.train_ds.y[train_rows])

            y_score = positive_scores(model, split.X_test)
            global_m = compute_metrics(split.y_test, y_score)

            if n_pairs > 0:
                scored = score_pairs(model, split.X_test, test_pairs)
                pair_m = mmp_metrics(scored)
            else:
                pair_m = {"pair_auroc": float("nan"), "mean_margin": float("nan")}

            rows.append(
                {
                    "strategy": strat_name,
                    "seed": seed,
                    "budget": budget,
                    "n_train": len(train_rows),
                    "pair_auroc": pair_m["pair_auroc"],
                    "mean_margin": pair_m["mean_margin"],
                    "n_pairs": n_pairs,
                    **{k: global_m[k] for k in ("auroc", "auprc", "f1")},
                }
            )
            logger.info(
                f"  [{strat_name} seed={seed}] "
                f"pair_auroc={pair_m['pair_auroc']:.3f} "
                f"auroc={global_m['auroc']:.3f} "
                f"n_train={len(train_rows):,}"
            )

    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

docs.title: score_pairs(model, X, pairs)
docs.text:
Attach positive-class scores to a matched-pairs DataFrame.

Adds score_pos, score_neg, correct (bool: positive scored higher), and margin (score_pos - score_neg) columns.

Args: model: A fitted classifier exposing predict_proba or decision_function. X: Feature matrix aligned with the indices in pairs. pairs: DataFrame with idx_pos and idx_neg columns (from find_matched_pairs).

Returns: A copy of pairs with the four score columns appended.

Source code in negative_ml/core/mmp.py 
def score_pairs(
    model: object,
    X: np.ndarray,
    pairs: pd.DataFrame,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Attach positive-class scores to a matched-pairs DataFrame.

    Adds score_pos, score_neg, correct (bool: positive scored higher), and
    margin (score_pos - score_neg) columns.

    Args:
        model: A fitted classifier exposing predict_proba or decision_function.
        X: Feature matrix aligned with the indices in pairs.
        pairs: DataFrame with idx_pos and idx_neg columns (from find_matched_pairs).

    Returns:
        A copy of pairs with the four score columns appended.
    """
    scores = positive_scores(model, X)
    result = pairs.copy()
    result["score_pos"] = scores[pairs["idx_pos"].to_numpy()]
    result["score_neg"] = scores[pairs["idx_neg"].to_numpy()]
    result["correct"] = result["score_pos"] > result["score_neg"]
    result["margin"] = result["score_pos"] - result["score_neg"]
    return result

docs.title: Negative control
docs.text:
Negative-control experiment: single-feature baselines vs. the full model.

For a fixed train/test split, score the test set two ways and report the same metric panel for each:

- one CorrelationModel per feature — the
  single-feature negative control (rank by that feature, oriented by its
  correlation sign);
- the full model trained on every feature.

If the full model barely beats the best single-feature control, the features carry the signal individually and the model adds little; if every control sits near chance while the model does not (the triples case, where no single feature separates the classes), the model is capturing genuine multivariate structure. The control rides the exact same fit_score path as the real models, so the two are measured identically.

Score each single-feature control and the full model on one split.

Args: dataset: Full training domain (ignored when split is supplied). full_model_factory: Builds the full (all-feature) model to compare against. control_factory: Builds a fresh single-feature control estimator for a given feature index (e.g. a CorrelationModel). split: Pre-built EvalSplit (e.g. cross-season) to evaluate on; when None a stratified split of dataset is used. scaffold_split: Use scaffold/grouped instead of random eval split. seed: Base seed for the (fixed) split.

Returns: Long-format DataFrame with one row per feature plus one full-model row: [model, feature, corr, n_train, auroc, auprc, f1, precision_at_k, enrichment_factor]. model is "correlation" for the per-feature controls and "full_model" for the trained model (whose feature is "all" and corr is NaN).

Source code in negative_ml/core/negative_control.py 
def run_negative_control(
    dataset: Dataset,
    full_model_factory: ModelFactory,
    control_factory: ControlFactory,
    split: EvalSplit | None = None,
    scaffold_split: bool = False,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Score each single-feature control and the full model on one split.

    Args:
        dataset: Full training domain (ignored when split is supplied).
        full_model_factory: Builds the full (all-feature) model to compare against.
        control_factory: Builds a fresh single-feature control estimator for a
            given feature index (e.g. a CorrelationModel).
        split: Pre-built EvalSplit (e.g. cross-season) to evaluate on;
            when None a stratified split of dataset is used.
        scaffold_split: Use scaffold/grouped instead of random eval split.
        seed: Base seed for the (fixed) split.

    Returns:
        Long-format DataFrame with one row per feature plus one full-model row:
        [model, feature, corr, n_train, auroc, auprc, f1, precision_at_k,
        enrichment_factor]. model is "correlation" for the per-feature
        controls and "full_model" for the trained model (whose feature is
        "all" and corr is NaN).
    """
    sp = resolve_split(dataset, split, scaffold=scaffold_split, seed=seed)
    train_ds = sp.train_ds
    # No downselection: the control and the full model both see the whole pool.
    train_rows = np.arange(train_ds.n_samples)

    feature_names = train_ds.feature_names or [
        f"x{j}" for j in range(train_ds.X.shape[1])
    ]
    y_train = train_ds.y.astype(float)

    rows = []
    for j, fname in enumerate(feature_names):
        col = train_ds.X[:, j].astype(float)
        corr = (
            float(np.corrcoef(col, y_train)[0, 1])
            if col.std() and y_train.std()
            else 0.0
        )
        metrics = fit_score(
            train_ds,
            train_rows,
            sp.X_test,
            sp.y_test,
            correlation_factory(control_factory, j),
        )
        rows.append(
            {
                "model": "correlation",
                "feature": fname,
                "corr": 0.0 if np.isnan(corr) else corr,
                "n_train": int(len(train_rows)),
                **metrics,
            }
        )

    full_metrics = fit_score(
        train_ds, train_rows, sp.X_test, sp.y_test, full_model_factory
    )
    rows.append(
        {
            "model": "full_model",
            "feature": "all",
            "corr": np.nan,
            "n_train": int(len(train_rows)),
            **full_metrics,
        }
    )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

docs.title: Evaluation metrics
docs.text:
Evaluation metrics for the imbalance study (plan.md 4.3).

Two families of metrics for classification models, all collected by compute_metrics:

A) Global discrimination - AUROC, AUPRC, F1 at a threshold.
B) Early retrieval / top-k - precision@k, enrichment factor (the practical
   "we only act on the top predictions" scenario).

Regression models (currently only the sandwich domain) are scored by compute_regression_metrics instead: AUROC/AUPRC require binary ground truth, so they are not meaningful once the target is a continuous rating. Spearman rank correlation is the regression analog of AUROC/AUPRC - both ask whether the model ranks examples correctly, without needing a threshold to binarize the target.

    threshold: float = DEFAULT_THRESHOLD,
) -> dict[str, float]:

    Args:

docs.title: enrichment_factor(y_true, y_score, k)
docs.text:
Top-k hit rate relative to the dataset-wide positive rate.

Args: y_true: Ground-truth binary labels. y_score: Model scores for the positive class. k: Number of top-scored items to consider.

Returns: Enrichment factor (precision@k / base rate); 0.0 when base rate is zero.

Source code in negative_ml/core/eval.py 
def enrichment_factor(y_true: np.ndarray, y_score: np.ndarray, k: int) -> float:
    """Top-k hit rate relative to the dataset-wide positive rate.

    Args:
        y_true: Ground-truth binary labels.
        y_score: Model scores for the positive class.
        k: Number of top-scored items to consider.

    Returns:
        Enrichment factor (precision@k / base rate); 0.0 when base rate is zero.
    """
    y_true = np.asarray(y_true)
    base_rate = float(np.mean(y_true))
    if base_rate == 0.0:
        return 0.0
    return precision_at_k(y_true, y_score, k) / base_rate

docs.text:
F1 score after thresholding scores into hard labels.

Args: y_true: Ground-truth binary labels. y_score: Model scores for the positive class. threshold: Score cutoff above which a prediction is treated as positive.

Returns: F1 score in [0, 1].

def f1_at_threshold(
    y_true: np.ndarray, y_score: np.ndarray, threshold: float = DEFAULT_THRESHOLD
) -> float:
    """F1 score after thresholding scores into hard labels.

    Args:
        y_true: Ground-truth binary labels.
        y_score: Model scores for the positive class.
        threshold: Score cutoff above which a prediction is treated as positive.

    Returns:
        F1 score in [0, 1].
    """
    y_pred = (np.asarray(y_score) >= threshold).astype(int)
    return float(f1_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0))

docs.title: precision_at_k(y_true, y_score, k)
docs.text:
Fraction of the top-k highest-scored items that are true positives.

Args: y_true: Ground-truth binary labels. y_score: Model scores for the positive class. k: Number of top-scored items to consider.

Returns: Precision@k value in [0, 1].

Source code in negative_ml/core/eval.py 
def precision_at_k(y_true: np.ndarray, y_score: np.ndarray, k: int) -> float:
    """Fraction of the top-k highest-scored items that are true positives.

    Args:
        y_true: Ground-truth binary labels.
        y_score: Model scores for the positive class.
        k: Number of top-scored items to consider.

    Returns:
        Precision@k value in [0, 1].
    """
    y_true = np.asarray(y_true)
    k = min(k, len(y_true))
    if k <= 0:
        return 0.0
    top_k = np.argsort(y_score)[::-1][:k]
    return float(np.mean(y_true[top_k]))

docs.title: spearman(y_true, y_score)
docs.text:
Spearman rank correlation between the true values and model scores.

The regression analog of AUROC/AUPRC: it asks whether the model ranks examples in the same order as the ground truth, without requiring a threshold to binarize the (continuous) target.

Args: y_true: Ground-truth continuous target values. y_score: Model scores (predictions).

Returns: Spearman correlation in [-1, 1]; 0.0 when either side is constant (correlation is undefined).

Source code in negative_ml/core/eval.py 
def spearman(y_true: np.ndarray, y_score: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Spearman rank correlation between the true values and model scores.

    The regression analog of AUROC/AUPRC: it asks whether the model ranks
    examples in the same order as the ground truth, without requiring a
    threshold to binarize the (continuous) target.

    Args:
        y_true: Ground-truth continuous target values.
        y_score: Model scores (predictions).

    Returns:
        Spearman correlation in [-1, 1]; 0.0 when either side is constant
        (correlation is undefined).
    """
    y_true = np.asarray(y_true, dtype=float)
    y_score = np.asarray(y_score, dtype=float)
    if y_true.std() == 0 or y_score.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(spearmanr(y_true, y_score).statistic)

docs.title: Experiment plumbing
docs.text:
Shared plumbing for the experiment runners.

Both the saturation (4.1) and selection (4.2) experiments follow the same recipe: hold one train/test split fixed, fit a fresh model on some subset of the training rows, and score it on the held-out test set with the standard metric panel. Centralizing that here keeps the two runners focused on which rows they select rather than on plumbing.

The split itself is an injectable EvalSplit so the same runners serve two regimes: an in-dataset random/scaffold split (the default), and a cross-dataset split that trains on one dataset and tests on another (e.g. train on 2023, test on 2024 - the "hard" distribution-shift split). Runners that take split=None build the default split, preserving their original behavior.

docs.title: EvalSplit dataclass
docs.text:
A fixed train pool + held-out test set fed to the experiment runners.

Attributes: train_ds: The training-pool Dataset; selection strategies index rows into this (its minority is always kept, its majority sub-selected). X_test: The held-out evaluation features. y_test: The held-out evaluation labels. name: Label for the split regime, carried into result frames as the split column by the scripts (e.g. "random" or "hard"). test_idx: Row indices into the source dataset that produced X_test/ y_test, when the split was drawn from a single dataset (None for cross-dataset splits, where the test set is a whole separate Dataset with no shared row indexing). Lets callers that need dataset-aligned columns not carried on Dataset itself (e.g. groups, meta) slice them consistently with X_test/y_test instead of re-deriving the split.

@dataclass
class EvalSplit:
    """A fixed train pool + held-out test set fed to the experiment runners.

    Attributes:
        train_ds: The training-pool Dataset; selection strategies index rows
            into this (its minority is always kept, its majority sub-selected).
        X_test: The held-out evaluation features.
        y_test: The held-out evaluation labels.
        name: Label for the split regime, carried into result frames as the
            split column by the scripts (e.g. "random" or "hard").
        test_idx: Row indices into the source dataset that produced X_test/
            y_test, when the split was drawn from a single dataset (None for
            cross-dataset splits, where the test set is a whole separate
            Dataset with no shared row indexing). Lets callers that need

docs.text:
Fit a fresh model on train_ds rows and score it on the test set.

Dispatches on train_ds.task: a regression model (currently only the sandwich domain) is scored by compute_regression_metrics (Spearman correlation against the continuous target) since AUROC/AUPRC require binary ground truth; every other task is scored by the classification compute_metrics panel.

Args: train_ds: The training-split Dataset rows are indexed into. train_rows: Row indices (into train_ds) to train on. X_test: Held-out evaluation features. y_test: Held-out evaluation labels. model_factory: Builds a fresh estimator; forwarded model_kwargs. **model_kwargs: Hyper-parameters forwarded to model_factory.

Returns: The negative_ml.core.eval.compute_regression_metrics panel when train_ds.task is "regression", otherwise the compute_metrics panel.

def fit_score(
    train_ds: Dataset,
    train_rows: np.ndarray,
    X_test: np.ndarray,
    y_test: np.ndarray,
    model_factory: ModelFactory,
    **model_kwargs,
) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Fit a fresh model on train_ds rows and score it on the test set.

    Dispatches on train_ds.task: a regression model (currently only the
    sandwich domain) is scored by compute_regression_metrics (Spearman
    correlation against the continuous target) since AUROC/AUPRC require
    binary ground truth; every other task is scored by the classification
    compute_metrics panel.

    Args:
        train_ds: The training-split Dataset rows are indexed into.
        train_rows: Row indices (into train_ds) to train on.
        X_test: Held-out evaluation features.
        y_test: Held-out evaluation labels.
        model_factory: Builds a fresh estimator; forwarded model_kwargs.
        **model_kwargs: Hyper-parameters forwarded to model_factory.

    Returns:
        The negative_ml.core.eval.compute_regression_metrics panel when
        train_ds.task is "regression", otherwise the compute_metrics panel.
    """
    rows = np.asarray(train_rows)
    model = model_factory(**model_kwargs)
    model.fit(train_ds.X[rows], train_ds.y[rows])
    y_score = positive_scores(model, X_test)
    if train_ds.task == "regression":
        return ev.compute_regression_metrics(y_test, y_score)
    return ev.compute_metrics(y_test, y_score)

docs.title: positive_scores(model, X)
docs.text:
Positive-class scores from a fitted estimator.

Returns predict_proba for the positive class when the estimator exposes it. Otherwise the decision_function margin is squashed through a logistic sigmoid, which is strictly monotonic (so the rank-based AUROC and AUPRC are unchanged) and maps the classifier's own boundary at margin 0 to a score of 0.5. This lets estimators without calibrated probabilities (e.g. a RidgeClassifier pipeline) flow through the same experiment plumbing as the XGBoost models, including the F1 metric: compute_metrics binarizes at DEFAULT_THRESHOLD (0.5), which now matches the estimator's hard predictions instead of thresholding an unbounded margin at an arbitrary cutoff. When neither predict_proba nor decision_function is available (e.g. a plain XGBRegressor), predict() is used directly; its raw continuous output serves as a ranking score for AUROC / AUPRC (classification) or is compared to the continuous target via Spearman correlation (regression; see fit_score).

Args: model: A fitted estimator exposing predict_proba, decision_function, or predict. X: Features to score.

Returns: A 1-D array of scores aligned with X.

Source code in negative_ml/core/experiment.py 
def positive_scores(model: object, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Positive-class scores from a fitted estimator.

    Returns predict_proba for the positive class when the estimator exposes it.
    Otherwise the decision_function margin is squashed through a logistic sigmoid,
    which is strictly monotonic (so the rank-based AUROC and AUPRC are unchanged)
    and maps the classifier's own boundary at margin 0 to a score of 0.5. This lets
    estimators without calibrated probabilities (e.g. a RidgeClassifier pipeline)
    flow through the same experiment plumbing as the XGBoost models, including the
    F1 metric: compute_metrics binarizes at DEFAULT_THRESHOLD (0.5), which now
    matches the estimator's hard predictions instead of thresholding an unbounded
    margin at an arbitrary cutoff. When neither predict_proba nor decision_function
    is available (e.g. a plain XGBRegressor), predict() is used directly; its raw
    continuous output serves as a ranking score for AUROC / AUPRC (classification)
    or is compared to the continuous target via Spearman correlation (regression;
    see fit_score).

    Args:
        model: A fitted estimator exposing predict_proba, decision_function, or
            predict.
        X: Features to score.

    Returns:
        A 1-D array of scores aligned with X.
    """
    if hasattr(model, "predict_proba"):
        return model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
    if hasattr(model, "decision_function"):
        return expit(np.asarray(model.decision_function(X), dtype=float))
    return np.asarray(model.predict(X), dtype=float)

def split_from_dataset(
    dataset: Dataset,
    scaffold: bool = False,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
    name: str = "random",
) -> EvalSplit:
    """Build an EvalSplit from one dataset via make_split.

    This is the default regime: a stratified random (or scaffold) split where the
    train pool and test set come from the same dataset.

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset to split.
        scaffold: Use a scaffold/grouped split when True.
        seed: Random seed for the split.
        name: Split-regime label carried into result frames.

    Returns:
        An EvalSplit built from train and test halves of dataset.
    """
    train_idx, test_idx = make_split(dataset, scaffold=scaffold, seed=seed)
    return EvalSplit(
        train_ds=dataset.subset(train_idx),
        X_test=dataset.X[test_idx],
        y_test=dataset.y[test_idx],
        name=name,
        test_idx=test_idx,
    )

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Model wrappers and the factory used to request a model by task without importing a specific estimator.

Common model interface and factory.

Experiments should depend on this thin surface (make_model returning an sklearn-compatible estimator) rather than on a concrete library, so that the saturation / selection runners never change when the underlying model does.

Negative-control baselines: how far does a single feature get you?

A CorrelationModel is a deliberately under-powered estimator that scores examples with one feature, oriented by the sign of that feature's correlation with the label. It captures no interactions and no non-monotonic structure, so its AUROC/AUPRC answer the question "how much signal is in this feature alone" — the natural negative control for the trained model. Comparing each single-feature control against the full model shows whether the model is doing real work (e.g. for triples, no single feature separates the classes, so every control sits near chance while the model does not).

The estimator follows the minimal sklearn surface the experiments rely on (fit / predict_proba) so it drops straight into negative_ml.core.experiment.fit_score like any other model.

Regularized linear model builders for the sandwich classifier.

Thin builders returning configured scikit-learn estimators, parallel to the xgboost builders. The sandwich ingredient encoding is wide and sparse (one indicator per ingredient value) with very few rows, the regime where an L2-regularized linear model generalizes better than deep gradient-boosted trees:

- ridge_classifier: the ridge classifier behind the good-vs-bad sandwich
  model; it fits a regularized linear decision boundary to the binary label.
- feature_selected_ridge_classifier: the full good-vs-bad sandwich model, a
  pipeline that keeps the top-k features by F-test before the ridge classifier.
- logistic_classifier: a logistic-regression classifier (an alternative linear
  classifier exposing calibrated probabilities).
- ridge_regressor: a ridge regression on the continuous 0-10 rating.

XGBoost classifier / regressor wrappers.

Thin builders returning configured XGBClassifier / XGBRegressor instances. Supports the class-weighting / scale_pos_weight and focal-loss style knobs needed to test whether weighting can stand in for majority-class volume (H4).

Forwarded to scikit-learn directly for the logistic classifier (including the string "balanced"); a numeric value becomes XGBoost's scale_pos_weight. **params: Extra hyper-parameters forwarded to the estimator.

def make_model(
    task: str,
    kind: str = "xgboost",
    class_weight: str | dict | None = None,
    **params: Any,
) -> Estimator:
    """Construct an estimator for the given task.

    Args:
        task: "classification" or "regression".
        kind: Model family — "xgboost" (default), "ridge" (the L2-regularized
            linear model behind the good-vs-bad sandwich classifier; a
            RidgeClassifier for classification and a Ridge regressor for
            regression), "logistic" (an alternative linear classifier exposing
            probabilities), or "correlation" (the single-feature negative control,
            which requires a feature_index).
        class_weight: Optional class weighting to test the "weighting can
            substitute for data" hypothesis (H4) without deleting examples.
            Forwarded to scikit-learn directly for the logistic classifier
            (including the string "balanced"); a numeric value becomes XGBoost's
            scale_pos_weight.
        **params: Extra hyper-parameters forwarded to the estimator.

    Returns:
        An unfitted sklearn-compatible estimator.
    """
    if kind == "correlation":
        return CorrelationModel(feature_index=params["feature_index"])
    if kind == "logistic":
        if task != "classification":
            raise ValueError(
                f"kind='logistic' is a classifier; task must be 'classification', "
                f"got {task!r}."
            )
        return logistic_classifier(class_weight=class_weight, **params)
    if kind == "ridge":
        if task == "classification":
            return ridge_classifier(class_weight=class_weight, **params)
        if task == "regression":
            return ridge_regressor(**params)
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unknown task {task!r}; expected 'classification' or 'regression'."
        )
    if kind != "xgboost":
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unsupported model kind {kind!r}; expected 'xgboost', 'logistic', "
            "'ridge', or 'correlation'."
        )

    if task == "classification":
        # "balanced" weighting is resolved against the data later (it needs the
        # class ratio); accept it here as an explicit scale_pos_weight instead.
        scale_pos_weight = (
            class_weight if isinstance(class_weight, (int, float)) else None
        )
        return xgb_classifier(scale_pos_weight=scale_pos_weight, **params)
    if task == "regression":
        return xgb_regressor(**params)
    raise ValueError(
        f"Unknown task {task!r}; expected 'classification' or 'regression'."
    )

def model_factory(task: str) -> Callable[..., Estimator]:
    """Return a factory that builds a fresh model for task on each call.

    The experiment runners expect a callable that accepts keyword overrides
    (e.g. class_weight) and returns an unfitted estimator; this binds the task
    so callers do not repeat the make_model wiring.

    Args:
        task: "classification" or "regression" — forwarded to make_model.

    Returns:
        A callable (**kwargs) -> Estimator that builds a fresh model on each call.

Single-feature negative control with a minimal sklearn surface.

Scores examples by one feature, oriented by the sign of that feature's correlation with the label, so its discrimination measures the signal in that feature alone.

Source code in negative_ml/models/baseline.py 
class CorrelationModel:
    """Single-feature negative control with a minimal sklearn surface.

    Scores examples by one feature, oriented by the sign of that feature's
    correlation with the label, so its discrimination measures the signal in
    that feature alone.
    """

    def __init__(self, feature_index: int) -> None:
        """Bind the control to one column of the feature matrix.

        Args:
            feature_index: Column of X this control scores on.
        """
        self.feature_index = int(feature_index)

    def fit(self, X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> "CorrelationModel":
        """Store the feature's correlation sign and its signed training moments.

        Args:
            X: Feature matrix; only the column at feature_index is used.
            y: Binary label aligned with X rows.

        Returns:
            Self (fitted in place).
        """
        col = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)[:, self.feature_index]
        y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
        if col.std() == 0 or y.std() == 0:
            corr = 0.0
        else:
            corr = float(np.corrcoef(col, y)[0, 1])
        self.corr_ = 0.0 if np.isnan(corr) else corr
        self.sign_ = 1.0 if self.corr_ >= 0 else -1.0
        signed = self.sign_ * col
        self.mean_ = float(signed.mean())
        std = float(signed.std())
        self.scale_ = std if std > 0 else 1.0
        return self

    def predict_proba(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Return (n, 2) pseudo-probabilities; column 1 is the squashed feature.

        The oriented feature is z-scored by its training mean / std and passed
        through a logistic sigmoid. The sigmoid is strictly monotonic, so the
        ranking (and hence AUROC / AUPRC) is preserved even for test values beyond
        the training range -- unlike a linear clip, which would collapse all
        out-of-range values to a tied 0.0 or 1.0 and distort the ranking under
        distribution shift. A constant training feature (zero std) maps every row
        to 0.5.

        Args:
            X: Feature matrix to score; only the column at feature_index is used.

        Returns:
            Array of shape (n_samples, 2) with [P(negative), P(positive)] per row.
        """
        signed = self.sign_ * np.asarray(X, dtype=float)[:, self.feature_index]
        p1 = expit((signed - self.mean_) / self.scale_)
        return np.column_stack([1.0 - p1, p1])

    def predict(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Return the hard 0/1 classification decision for each row.

        Thresholds the positive-class probability from predict_proba at 0.5,
        matching the sklearn classifier convention of a discrete class label so
        CorrelationModel satisfies the same Estimator surface as every other
        model make_model can return.

        Args:
            X: Feature matrix to predict on; only the column at feature_index
                is used.

        Returns:
            Array of shape (n_samples,) with 0/1 class predictions.
        """
        return (self.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] >= 0.5).astype(int)

docs.title: feature_selected_ridge_classifier(k, alpha, class_weight=None)
docs.text:
Build the good-vs-bad sandwich model: top-k F-test selection then ridge.

A two-step scikit-learn Pipeline. The first step keeps the k features with the strongest univariate F-test (ANOVA) association with the label -- the importance measure that matches a linear model, since gradient-boosted "gain" importance ranks split usefulness and does not transfer to a linear boundary. The second step is a ridge classifier on that reduced space. Refit fresh on each call so a cross-validation or selection loop can refit the selection inside every fold.

Args: k: Number of top features to keep (SelectKBest k). alpha: L2 penalty for the ridge classifier. class_weight: Class weighting forwarded to the ridge classifier (e.g. "balanced" or a {label: weight} dict); None leaves it unweighted.

Returns: An unfitted Pipeline with named steps "select" and "ridge". The ridge classifier exposes decision_function (not predict_proba), so score it with the decision function for ranking metrics.

Source code in negative_ml/models/linear.py 
def feature_selected_ridge_classifier(
    k: int,
    alpha: float,
    class_weight: str | dict | float | None = None,
) -> Pipeline:
    """Build the good-vs-bad sandwich model: top-k F-test selection then ridge.

    A two-step scikit-learn Pipeline. The first step keeps the k features with the
    strongest univariate F-test (ANOVA) association with the label -- the
    importance measure that matches a linear model, since gradient-boosted "gain"
    importance ranks split usefulness and does not transfer to a linear boundary.
    The second step is a ridge classifier on that reduced space. Refit fresh on
    each call so a cross-validation or selection loop can refit the selection
    inside every fold.

    Args:
        k: Number of top features to keep (SelectKBest k).
        alpha: L2 penalty for the ridge classifier.
        class_weight: Class weighting forwarded to the ridge classifier (e.g.
            "balanced" or a {label: weight} dict); None leaves it unweighted.

    Returns:
        An unfitted Pipeline with named steps "select" and "ridge". The ridge
        classifier exposes decision_function (not predict_proba), so score it with
        the decision function for ranking metrics.
    """
    return Pipeline(
        [
            ("select", SelectKBest(f_classif, k=k)),
            ("ridge", ridge_classifier(class_weight=class_weight, alpha=alpha)),
        ]
    )

docs.title: resolve_class_weight(class_weight)
docs.text:
Translate a numeric minority up-weight into an sklearn class_weight.

The experiment runners express the H4 weighting baseline as a single numeric ratio (majority / minority) so it reads the same across model families. The XGBoost path turns that number into scale_pos_weight; scikit-learn's linear classifiers instead take a {label: weight} dict (or "balanced"), so a numeric ratio is mapped to {0: 1.0, 1: ratio}, up-weighting the positive minority class. Non-numeric values (None, a dict, or "balanced") pass through unchanged, keeping the weighting concept owned by the model builder rather than each calling domain.

Args: class_weight: A numeric up-weight ratio, an sklearn class_weight value, or None.

Returns: An sklearn-ready class_weight (dict, "balanced", or None).

Source code in negative_ml/models/linear.py 
def resolve_class_weight(
    class_weight: str | dict | float | None,
) -> str | dict | None:
    """Translate a numeric minority up-weight into an sklearn class_weight.

    The experiment runners express the H4 weighting baseline as a single numeric
    ratio (majority / minority) so it reads the same across model families. The
    XGBoost path turns that number into scale_pos_weight; scikit-learn's linear
    classifiers instead take a {label: weight} dict (or "balanced"), so a numeric
    ratio is mapped to {0: 1.0, 1: ratio}, up-weighting the positive minority
    class. Non-numeric values (None, a dict, or "balanced") pass through unchanged,
    keeping the weighting concept owned by the model builder rather than each
    calling domain.

    Args:
        class_weight: A numeric up-weight ratio, an sklearn class_weight value, or
            None.

    Returns:
        An sklearn-ready class_weight (dict, "balanced", or None).
    """
    if isinstance(class_weight, bool):
        # bool is an int subclass, so this must be checked before the
        # numeric branch below; a bool is neither a valid up-weight ratio nor
        # a valid sklearn class_weight, so fail loudly here instead of
        # silently forwarding True/False and deferring an sklearn error to a
        # confusing point at .fit() time.
        raise TypeError(
            f"class_weight must not be a bool; got {class_weight!r}. Pass a "
            "numeric up-weight ratio, an sklearn class_weight dict, "
            "'balanced', or None."
        )
    if isinstance(class_weight, (int, float)):
        return {0: 1.0, 1: float(class_weight)}
    return class_weight

def bemis_murcko_scaffolds(smiles: list[str]) -> np.ndarray:
    """Return a scaffold id per molecule for grouped / scaffold splitting.

    Molecules sharing a Bemis-Murcko scaffold get the same scaffold SMILES id so
    that whole structural families can be held out together. Molecules that
    RDKit cannot parse (or that have no ring system) get an empty-string id.

    Args:
        smiles: SMILES strings.

    Returns:
        Array of scaffold-id strings, shape (len(smiles),).
    """
    scaffolds = []
    for smi in smiles:
        mol = Chem.MolFromSmiles(smi)
        scaffolds.append(
            "" if mol is None else MurckoScaffold.MurckoScaffoldSmiles(mol=mol)
        )
    return np.asarray(scaffolds, dtype=object)

docs.title: compute_fingerprints(smiles, radius=MORGAN_RADIUS, n_bits=MORGAN_N_BITS, *, cache_path=None)
docs.text:
Compute Morgan (ECFP-like) fingerprints for a list of SMILES.

A single Morgan generator folds each molecule into an n_bits bit vector. SMILES that RDKit cannot parse are emitted as an all-zero row so the output stays row-aligned with the input (and with the precomputed descriptor matrix, which is indexed the same way).

Results are written to cache_path on first call and loaded from it on subsequent calls, avoiding repeated SMILES parsing when the same screen is featurized more than once (e.g. when morgan and both featurizations are both enabled).

Args: smiles: SMILES strings. radius: Morgan radius (2 is ECFP4). n_bits: Length of the folded bit vector. cache_path: Optional path to a .npy cache file. If the file exists its contents are returned directly; on a cache miss the fingerprints are computed and saved there before returning.

Returns: Binary fingerprint matrix, shape (len(smiles), n_bits), dtype uint8.

Source code in negative_ml/molecules/io.py 
def compute_fingerprints(
    smiles: list[str],
    radius: int = MORGAN_RADIUS,
    n_bits: int = MORGAN_N_BITS,
    *,
    cache_path: Path | None = None,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Compute Morgan (ECFP-like) fingerprints for a list of SMILES.

    A single Morgan generator folds each molecule into an n_bits bit vector.
    SMILES that RDKit cannot parse are emitted as an all-zero row so the output
    stays row-aligned with the input (and with the precomputed descriptor
    matrix, which is indexed the same way).

    Results are written to cache_path on first call and loaded from it on
    subsequent calls, avoiding repeated SMILES parsing when the same screen is
    featurized more than once (e.g. when morgan and both featurizations are both
    enabled).

    Args:
        smiles: SMILES strings.
        radius: Morgan radius (2 is ECFP4).
        n_bits: Length of the folded bit vector.
        cache_path: Optional path to a .npy cache file.  If the file exists its
            contents are returned directly; on a cache miss the fingerprints are
            computed and saved there before returning.

    Returns:
        Binary fingerprint matrix, shape (len(smiles), n_bits), dtype uint8.
    """
    if cache_path is not None and cache_path.exists():
        return np.load(cache_path)
    generator = rdFingerprintGenerator.GetMorganGenerator(radius=radius, fpSize=n_bits)
    fingerprints = np.zeros((len(smiles), n_bits), dtype=np.uint8)
    for i, smi in enumerate(smiles):
        mol = Chem.MolFromSmiles(smi)
        if mol is not None:
            fingerprints[i] = generator.GetFingerprintAsNumPy(mol)
    if cache_path is not None:
        np.save(cache_path, fingerprints)
    return fingerprints

docs.text:
Build the feature matrix + names for one of the three featurizations.

Args: smiles: SMILES strings, row-aligned with the descriptor .npz. npz_path: Path to the precomputed RDKit descriptor .npz. featurization: One of MOLECULE_FEATURIZATIONS. "rdkit" uses the precomputed descriptors, "morgan" the Morgan fingerprints, and "both" concatenates the descriptors with the fingerprints. fp_cache: Optional cache path forwarded to compute_fingerprints when morgan fingerprints are needed (ignored for "rdkit" featurization).

Returns: A tuple (X, feature_names) with X of shape (len(smiles), n_features).

Raises: ValueError: If featurization is not one of MOLECULE_FEATURIZATIONS or the descriptor matrix is not row-aligned with smiles.

Source code in negative_ml/molecules/io.py 
def featurize(
    smiles: list[str],
    npz_path: str | Path,
    featurization: str = "both",
    *,
    fp_cache: Path | None = None,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, list[str]]:
    """Build the feature matrix + names for one of the three featurizations.

    Args:
        smiles: SMILES strings, row-aligned with the descriptor .npz.
        npz_path: Path to the precomputed RDKit descriptor .npz.
        featurization: One of MOLECULE_FEATURIZATIONS. "rdkit" uses the
            precomputed descriptors, "morgan" the Morgan fingerprints, and
            "both" concatenates the descriptors with the fingerprints.
        fp_cache: Optional cache path forwarded to compute_fingerprints when
            morgan fingerprints are needed (ignored for "rdkit" featurization).

    Returns:
        A tuple (X, feature_names) with X of shape (len(smiles), n_features).

    Raises:
        ValueError: If featurization is not one of MOLECULE_FEATURIZATIONS or the
            descriptor matrix is not row-aligned with smiles.
    """
    if featurization not in MOLECULE_FEATURIZATIONS:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unknown featurization {featurization!r}; "
            f"choose from {list(MOLECULE_FEATURIZATIONS)}."
        )
    blocks: list[np.ndarray] = []
    names: list[str] = []
    if featurization in ("rdkit", "both"):
        descriptors = load_rdkit_descriptors(npz_path)
        if len(descriptors) != len(smiles):
            raise ValueError(
                f"Descriptor matrix ({len(descriptors)} rows) is not aligned with "
                f"the {len(smiles)} SMILES; check the paired csv/npz files."
            )
        blocks.append(descriptors)
        names.extend(get_rdkit_feature_names())
    if featurization in ("morgan", "both"):
        fingerprints = compute_fingerprints(smiles, cache_path=fp_cache).astype(float)
        blocks.append(fingerprints)
        names.extend(f"morgan_{i}" for i in range(fingerprints.shape[1]))
    X = blocks[0] if len(blocks) == 1 else np.hstack(blocks)
    return X, names

def load_gnn_saturation_results(
    processed_dir: str | Path | None = None,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Load and combine the precomputed GNN saturation results for both regimes.

    Reads each file in MOLECULE_GNN_RESULT_FILES, tidies it with tidy_gnn_results,
    and concatenates the two regimes into one long-format frame tagged with a
    class_balance column.

    Args:
        processed_dir: Directory holding the raw GNN result CSVs. Defaults to
            PROCESSED_DATA_DIR (data/processed).

    Returns:
        The combined tidy frame (see tidy_gnn_results for the columns), covering
        both the proportional and disproportional regimes.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: If a configured result file is missing, with a message
            pointing at where the files are expected.
    """
    root = Path(processed_dir) if processed_dir is not None else PROCESSED_DATA_DIR
    frames = []
    for class_balance, filename in MOLECULE_GNN_RESULT_FILES.items():
        path = root / filename
        if not path.exists():
            raise FileNotFoundError(
                f"Missing GNN result file {path}; place the gonorrhea GNN "
                f"result CSVs under {root} (see data/README.md)."
            )
        frames.append(tidy_gnn_results(pd.read_csv(path), class_balance))
    return pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)

def load_rdkit_descriptors(npz_path: str | Path) -> np.ndarray:
    """Load the precomputed RDKit descriptor matrix, imputing non-finite values.

    The .npz files store the descriptors under the "features" key, row-aligned
    with their paired CSV. A handful of descriptor cells are NaN (RDKit emits
    them for a few molecules); they are zero-filled so the distance-based
    selection strategies, which standardize the features, stay finite. XGBoost
    itself tolerates NaN, but the shared strategies do not.

    Args:
        npz_path: Path to the descriptor .npz file.

    Returns:
        Float descriptor matrix, shape (n_samples, n_descriptors).
    """
    with np.load(npz_path) as data:
        features = np.asarray(data["features"], dtype=float)
    return np.nan_to_num(features)

Load one gonorrhea screening file as a classification Dataset.

Reads the paired .csv (SMILES + hit label) and .npz (precomputed RDKit descriptors) and featurizes the molecules per featurization. The result is memoized per (stem, featurization, raw_dir): a single script run asks for the same screen file several times (across EDA, performance, and downselection figures), and each call would otherwise re-read the CSV and re-run RDKit scaffold/descriptor extraction from scratch.

Args: stem: File stem shared by the .csv and .npz (e.g. MOLECULE_TRAIN_STEM). featurization: One of MOLECULE_FEATURIZATIONS (see featurize). raw_dir: Directory holding the files; defaults to GONORRHEA_RAW_DIR.

Returns: A Dataset with the chosen features in X, binary activity labels in y (1 == active/hit), Bemis-Murcko scaffold ids in groups, and the raw rows (Name/SMILES/hit) in meta.

Raises: FileNotFoundError: If either paired file is missing.

Source code in negative_ml/molecules/io.py 
@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def load_screen(
    stem: str,
    featurization: str = "both",
    raw_dir: str | Path | None = None,
) -> Dataset:
    """Load one gonorrhea screening file as a classification Dataset.

    Reads the paired <stem>.csv (SMILES + hit label) and <stem>.npz (precomputed
    RDKit descriptors) and featurizes the molecules per featurization. The
    result is memoized per (stem, featurization, raw_dir): a single script run
    asks for the same screen file several times (across EDA, performance, and
    downselection figures), and each call would otherwise re-read the CSV and
    re-run RDKit scaffold/descriptor extraction from scratch.

    Args:
        stem: File stem shared by the .csv and .npz (e.g. MOLECULE_TRAIN_STEM).
        featurization: One of MOLECULE_FEATURIZATIONS (see featurize).
        raw_dir: Directory holding the files; defaults to GONORRHEA_RAW_DIR.

    Returns:
        A Dataset with the chosen features in X, binary activity labels in y
        (1 == active/hit), Bemis-Murcko scaffold ids in groups, and the raw
        rows (Name/SMILES/hit) in meta.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: If either paired file is missing.
    """
    root = Path(raw_dir) if raw_dir is not None else GONORRHEA_RAW_DIR
    csv_path = root / f"{stem}.csv"
    npz_path = root / f"{stem}.npz"
    for path in (csv_path, npz_path):
        if not path.exists():
            raise FileNotFoundError(
                f"Missing gonorrhea screen file {path}; expected the paired "
                f"{stem}.csv and {stem}.npz under {root}."
            )
    frame = pd.read_csv(csv_path)
    smiles = frame["SMILES"].astype(str).tolist()
    y = frame["hit"].to_numpy().astype(int)
    fp_cache = fp_cache_path(stem, MORGAN_RADIUS, MORGAN_N_BITS)
    X, feature_names = featurize(smiles, npz_path, featurization, fp_cache=fp_cache)
    groups = bemis_murcko_scaffolds(smiles)
    return Dataset(
        X=X,
        y=y,
        task="classification",
        feature_names=feature_names,
        groups=groups,
        meta=frame,
    )

docs.title: tidy_gnn_results(raw, class_balance)
docs.text:
Reshape one raw GNN result file into the study's tidy long format.

The source files store one row per (seed, negative budget, selection strategy, test set, metric) with the score in a single Value column. This pivots the two metrics (auROC, auPR) into their own auroc / auprc columns, normalizes the strategy / test-set vocabulary, and recovers the total training size.

The proportional file records the Total Dataset Size directly (positives are held to ~3% as negatives grow); the disproportional file records only the negative count, so the total is negatives + the full active pool (MOLECULE_GNN_N_POSITIVES), which are always kept.

Args: raw: A raw GNN result frame as read from PROCESSED_DATA_DIR, with the columns Seed, N (negatives), Data Selection, Test Set, Metric, Value (and Total Dataset Size for the proportional regime). class_balance: Which regime this frame is, one of MOLECULE_GNN_RESULT_FILES ("proportional" or "disproportional"); recorded in a class_balance column so both regimes can share one combined frame.

Returns: A long-format frame with one row per (strategy, test_set, seed, n_negatives) and columns [class_balance, strategy, test_set, seed, n_negatives, n_train, auroc, auprc].

Raises: ValueError: If a strategy, test set, or metric label is not one the study recognizes, so a schema drift in the source is caught early.

Source code in negative_ml/molecules/io.py 
def tidy_gnn_results(raw: pd.DataFrame, class_balance: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Reshape one raw GNN result file into the study's tidy long format.

    The source files store one row per (seed, negative budget, selection strategy,
    test set, metric) with the score in a single Value column. This pivots the two
    metrics (auROC, auPR) into their own auroc / auprc columns, normalizes the
    strategy / test-set vocabulary, and recovers the total training size.

    The proportional file records the Total Dataset Size directly (positives are
    held to ~3% as negatives grow); the disproportional file records only the
    negative count, so the total is negatives + the full active pool
    (MOLECULE_GNN_N_POSITIVES), which are always kept.

    Args:
        raw: A raw GNN result frame as read from PROCESSED_DATA_DIR, with the
            columns Seed, N (negatives), Data Selection, Test Set, Metric, Value
            (and Total Dataset Size for the proportional regime).
        class_balance: Which regime this frame is, one of MOLECULE_GNN_RESULT_FILES
            ("proportional" or "disproportional"); recorded in a class_balance
            column so both regimes can share one combined frame.

    Returns:
        A long-format frame with one row per (strategy, test_set, seed,
        n_negatives) and columns [class_balance, strategy, test_set, seed,
        n_negatives, n_train, auroc, auprc].

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a strategy, test set, or metric label is not one the study
            recognizes, so a schema drift in the source is caught early.
    """
    df = raw.rename(
        columns={
            "Seed": "seed",
            "N (negatives)": "n_negatives",
            "Data Selection": "strategy",
            "Test Set": "test_set",
            "Metric": "metric",
            "Value": "value",
        }
    )
    for column, mapping, what in (
        ("strategy", GNN_STRATEGIES, "selection strategy"),
        ("test_set", GNN_TEST_SETS, "test set"),
        ("metric", GNN_METRICS, "metric"),
    ):
        unknown = set(df[column]) - set(mapping)
        if unknown:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Unrecognized {what}(s) in GNN results: {sorted(unknown)}"
            )
        df[column] = df[column].map(mapping)

    keys = ["strategy", "test_set", "seed", "n_negatives"]
    wide = (
        df.pivot_table(index=keys, columns="metric", values="value")
        .reset_index()
        .rename_axis(columns=None)
    )

    if "Total Dataset Size" in raw.columns:
        totals = raw.rename(columns={"N (negatives)": "n_negatives"})[
            ["n_negatives", "Total Dataset Size"]
        ].drop_duplicates()
        wide = wide.merge(totals, on="n_negatives", how="left")
        wide["n_train"] = wide.pop("Total Dataset Size").astype(int)
    else:
        wide["n_train"] = wide["n_negatives"] + MOLECULE_GNN_N_POSITIVES

    wide.insert(0, "class_balance", class_balance)
    ordered = [
        "class_balance",
        "strategy",
        "test_set",
        "seed",
        "n_negatives",
        "n_train",
        "auroc",
        "auprc",
    ]
    return wide[ordered].sort_values(keys).reset_index(drop=True)

def build_splits(
    train_ds: Dataset,
    featurization: str = "both",
) -> dict[str, EvalSplit]:
    """Pair the training screen with its two held-out test files.

    Both test files are featurized the same way as train_ds and wrapped as
    cross-dataset EvalSplits: "random" is the random 20% holdout
    (MOLECULE_TEST_RANDOM_STEM) and "time" is the easy/medium/hard time-split
    validation set (MOLECULE_TEST_TIME_STEM). Training uses all of train_ds; the
    selection and saturation runners sub-select its majority against these fixed
    test sets.

    Args:
        train_ds: The training-screen Dataset (its featurization must match).
        featurization: One of MOLECULE_FEATURIZATIONS (see featurize).

    Returns:
        Mapping of split name to EvalSplit, keyed "random" and "time".

    Raises:
        ValueError: If featurization does not produce the same feature space
            as train_ds, e.g. train_ds was loaded with a different
            featurization than the one requested here.
    """
    test_random = load_screen(MOLECULE_TEST_RANDOM_STEM, featurization)
    test_time = load_screen(MOLECULE_TEST_TIME_STEM, featurization)
    if train_ds.X.shape[1] != test_random.X.shape[1]:
        raise ValueError(
            f"train_ds has {train_ds.X.shape[1]} features but featurization "
            f"{featurization!r} produces {test_random.X.shape[1]}; train_ds "
            "must be loaded with the same featurization passed here."
        )
    return {
        "random": cross_dataset_split(train_ds, test_random, name="random"),
        "time": cross_dataset_split(train_ds, test_time, name="time"),
    }

docs.title: adjusted_spray_angle(hc_x, hc_y, stand)
docs.text:
Pull-positive spray angle (degrees) from Statcast hit coordinates.

The angle is measured from the line straight up the middle: raw is positive toward the first-base / right-field side. It is adjusted by batter hand so that, for every batter, positive means pulled and negative means opposite field — right-handers pull to left field (raw < 0) and left-handers pull to right field (raw > 0), so the sign is flipped only for right-handers.

Args: hc_x: Statcast hit-coordinate x values (home-plate origin). hc_y: Statcast hit-coordinate y values (home-plate origin). stand: Batter handedness per row ("L" or "R").

Returns: Pull-positive spray angle in degrees, shape (n,).

Source code in negative_ml/baseball/io.py 
def adjusted_spray_angle(
    hc_x: np.ndarray, hc_y: np.ndarray, stand: np.ndarray
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Pull-positive spray angle (degrees) from Statcast hit coordinates.

    The angle is measured from the line straight up the middle: raw is
    positive toward the first-base / right-field side. It is adjusted by batter
    hand so that, for every batter, positive means pulled and negative means
    opposite field — right-handers pull to left field (raw < 0) and left-handers
    pull to right field (raw > 0), so the sign is flipped only for right-handers.

    Args:
        hc_x: Statcast hit-coordinate x values (home-plate origin).
        hc_y: Statcast hit-coordinate y values (home-plate origin).
        stand: Batter handedness per row ("L" or "R").

    Returns:
        Pull-positive spray angle in degrees, shape (n,).
    """
    raw = np.degrees(np.arctan2(hc_x - _HC_X_ORIGIN, _HC_Y_ORIGIN - hc_y))
    handed = np.where(np.asarray(stand) == "L", 1.0, -1.0)
    return raw * handed

def featurize(
    events: pd.DataFrame, binary: bool = True, target: str = "home_run"
) -> Dataset:
    """Turn a raw Statcast events frame into a featurized Dataset.

    Pure and offline-testable: keeps only batted balls with valid kinematics and
    hit coordinates, builds the (exit velocity, launch angle, spray angle) feature
    matrix, and labels each row. See load for the public entry point.

    Args:
        events: Raw Statcast events frame (e.g. from fetch_statcast).
        binary: target-vs-rest label if True, else 5-class integer target.
        target: Positive/minority hit type for the binary framing — one of
            _HIT_EVENTS.

    Returns:
        A classification Dataset.
    """
    if binary and target not in _HIT_EVENTS:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unknown target {target!r}; choose from {sorted(_HIT_EVENTS)}."
        )
    df = events.loc[:, _NEEDED_COLUMNS].copy()
    # Keep batted balls only: valid kinematics and a landing location.
    df = df.dropna(subset=["launch_speed", "launch_angle", "hc_x", "hc_y"])
    df = df.reset_index(drop=True)

    spray = adjusted_spray_angle(
        df["hc_x"].to_numpy(float),
        df["hc_y"].to_numpy(float),
        df["stand"].to_numpy(),
    )
    # Continuous block (order matches CONTINUOUS_FEATURES), median-imputed so the
    # downstream distance / clustering selection code stays NaN-free.
    continuous = np.column_stack(
        [
            df["launch_speed"].to_numpy(float),
            df["launch_angle"].to_numpy(float),
            spray,
            df["plate_x"].to_numpy(float),
            df["plate_z"].to_numpy(float),
            df["release_speed"].to_numpy(float),
            df["release_spin_rate"].to_numpy(float),
        ]
    )
    continuous = impute_column_medians(continuous)
    indicators = pitch_class_indicators(df["pitch_type"])
    X = np.column_stack([continuous, indicators])

    outcome = outcome_label(df["events"])
    if binary:
        y = (df["events"] == target).astype(int).to_numpy()
    else:
        classes = ["out", "single", "double", "triple", "home_run"]
        codes = pd.Categorical(outcome, categories=classes).codes
        y = np.asarray(codes, dtype=int)

    meta = df.assign(outcome=outcome.to_numpy(), spray_angle=spray)
    return Dataset(
        X=X,
        y=y,
        # A 5-class integer-coded y (binary=False) is neither the binary
        # {0, 1} minority label "classification" implies nor a continuous
        # "regression" target; labeling it "multiclass" keeps minority_mask /
        # majority_mask from silently mistaking one outcome class for the
        # minority instead of failing loudly.
        task="classification" if binary else "multiclass",
        feature_names=list(_FEATURE_NAMES),
        groups=df["home_team"].to_numpy(),
        meta=meta,
    )

Fetch and cache Statcast batted-ball events for a date range.

Thin wrapper over pybaseball.statcast. The raw events frame is cached as parquet under data/raw so repeated experiment runs are cheap; the first full-season pull takes several minutes.

def fetch_statcast(start: str, end: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Fetch and cache Statcast batted-ball events for a date range.

    Thin wrapper over pybaseball.statcast. The raw events frame is cached as
    parquet under data/raw so repeated experiment runs are cheap; the first
    full-season pull takes several minutes.

    Args:
        start: Start date, YYYY-MM-DD.
        end: End date, YYYY-MM-DD.

    Returns:
        The raw Statcast events DataFrame.
    """
    cache_path = RAW_DATA_DIR / f"statcast_{start}_{end}.parquet"
    if cache_path.exists():
        return pd.read_parquet(cache_path)

    events = statcast(start_dt=start, end_dt=end)
    RAW_DATA_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    events.to_parquet(cache_path)
    return events

docs.title: impute_column_medians(X)
docs.text:
Fill NaNs in each column with that column's median.

The selection strategies standardize and run nearest-neighbor and k-means on the feature matrix, none of which tolerate NaNs. Pitch-context columns carry a small residual missing fraction (e.g. release_spin_rate ~0.6%), so they are median-imputed here once at featurization time.

Args: X: Float feature matrix that may contain NaNs.

Returns: A copy of X with each column's NaNs replaced by that column's median.

Source code in negative_ml/baseball/io.py 
def impute_column_medians(X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Fill NaNs in each column with that column's median.

    The selection strategies standardize and run nearest-neighbor and k-means on
    the feature matrix, none of which tolerate NaNs. Pitch-context columns carry a
    small residual missing fraction (e.g. release_spin_rate ~0.6%), so they are
    median-imputed here once at featurization time.

    Args:
        X: Float feature matrix that may contain NaNs.

    Returns:
        A copy of X with each column's NaNs replaced by that column's median.
    """
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float).copy()
    medians = np.nanmedian(X, axis=0)
    rows, cols = np.where(np.isnan(X))
    X[rows, cols] = np.take(medians, cols)
    return X

Convenience wrapper over load that resolves a season's date range, so callers say load_season(2023, target="triple") rather than repeating the Statcast start/end dates. The result is memoized per (year, target, binary): a single script run asks for the same season several times (across EDA, performance, leakage, and downselection figures), and each call would otherwise re-read the season parquet and re-featurize it from scratch.

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def load_season(year: int, target: str = "home_run", binary: bool = True) -> Dataset:
    """Load a full MLB season by year (see SEASONS).

    Convenience wrapper over load that resolves a season's date range, so
    callers say load_season(2023, target="triple") rather than repeating the
    Statcast start/end dates. The result is memoized per (year, target, binary):
    a single script run asks for the same season several times (across EDA,
    performance, leakage, and downselection figures), and each call would
    otherwise re-read the season parquet and re-featurize it from scratch.

    Args:
        year: Season year present in SEASONS (2023 or 2024).
        target: Positive/minority hit type (see load).
        binary: Binary target-vs-rest framing if True, else 5-class.

    Returns:
        The featurized Dataset for that season (shared across repeat calls).
    """
    if year not in SEASONS:
        raise ValueError(
            f"No date range for season {year!r}; known: {sorted(SEASONS)}."
        )
    start, end = SEASONS[year]
    return load(binary=binary, start=start, end=end, target=target)

def pitch_class_indicators(pitch_type: pd.Series) -> np.ndarray:
    """Coarse pitch-class indicators (fastball / breaking / offspeed).

    Groups the many raw Statcast pitch_type codes into three classes so the pitch
    mix enters the model as three indicator columns rather than a wide one-hot.
    Unknown or missing codes map to all-zero (an implicit "other" class).

    Args:
        pitch_type: Raw Statcast pitch_type codes, one per batted ball.

    Returns:
        Float array of shape (n, 3): the fastball, breaking, and offspeed columns.
    """
    codes = pitch_type.fillna("").to_numpy()
    is_fastball = np.isin(codes, list(_FASTBALL_CODES)).astype(float)
    is_breaking = np.isin(codes, list(_BREAKING_CODES)).astype(float)
    is_offspeed = np.isin(codes, list(_OFFSPEED_CODES)).astype(float)
    return np.column_stack([is_fastball, is_breaking, is_offspeed])

docs.title: ballpark_split(dataset, test_parks=OUTLIER_BALLPARKS)
docs.text:
Hold entire ballparks out of training (a park-factor distribution shift).

Every row whose group (the batter's home team / ballpark) is in test_parks goes to the test set; the rest are training. Unlike a random or scaffold split, the held-out parks are fixed and chosen for their quirky dimensions (see OUTLIER_BALLPARKS), so the model is scored on parks it never trained on. This is a harder, deterministic alternative to the chronological cross-season split. Requires dataset.groups to be set (mirrors scaffold_split).

Args: dataset: Dataset whose groups hold the per-row ballpark identifier. test_parks: Ballpark identifiers (Statcast home_team codes) to hold out.

Returns: (train_idx, test_idx) integer index arrays.

Raises: ValueError: If dataset.groups is None, or no row matches test_parks.

Source code in negative_ml/baseball/split.py 
def ballpark_split(
    dataset: Dataset,
    test_parks: Sequence[str] = OUTLIER_BALLPARKS,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Hold entire ballparks out of training (a park-factor distribution shift).

    Every row whose group (the batter's home team / ballpark) is in test_parks
    goes to the test set; the rest are training. Unlike a random or scaffold
    split, the held-out parks are fixed and chosen for their quirky dimensions
    (see OUTLIER_BALLPARKS), so the model is scored on parks it never trained on.
    This is a harder, deterministic alternative to the chronological cross-season
    split. Requires dataset.groups to be set (mirrors scaffold_split).

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset whose groups hold the per-row ballpark identifier.
        test_parks: Ballpark identifiers (Statcast home_team codes) to hold out.

    Returns:
        (train_idx, test_idx) integer index arrays.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If dataset.groups is None, or no row matches test_parks.
    """
    if dataset.groups is None:
        raise ValueError("ballpark_split requires dataset.groups to be set.")
    groups = np.asarray(dataset.groups)
    is_test = np.isin(groups, list(test_parks))
    if not is_test.any():
        raise ValueError(
            f"None of the test_parks {list(test_parks)!r} appear in dataset.groups."
        )
    indices = np.arange(dataset.n_samples)
    return indices[~is_test], indices[is_test]

def build_splits(ds_train: Dataset, ds_test: Dataset) -> dict[str, EvalSplit]:
    """The three baseball evaluation regimes keyed by name.

    random is a stratified holdout within the training season; hard trains on the
    full training season and tests on the full held-out season (a chronological
    cross-season shift); park holds the quirky outlier ballparks (carried in
    ds_train.groups) entirely out of training (a park-factor shift). Shared by
    every baseball script so the regimes are defined once.

        ds_train: The training-season Dataset (its groups hold the ballpark).

Build an EvalSplit that holds entire ballparks out of training.

Wraps ballpark_split into an EvalSplit (parallel to split_from_dataset). The train pool and test set come from the same season, so this isolates a park-factor distribution shift from the season shift of cross_dataset_split.

Args: dataset: Dataset whose groups hold the per-row ballpark identifier. test_parks: Ballpark identifiers (home_team codes) to hold out for test. name: Split-regime label carried into result frames.

Returns: An EvalSplit whose train pool excludes the held-out parks.

def park_split_from_dataset(
    dataset: Dataset,
    test_parks: Sequence[str] = OUTLIER_BALLPARKS,
    name: str = "park",
) -> EvalSplit:
    """Build an EvalSplit that holds entire ballparks out of training.

    Wraps ballpark_split into an EvalSplit (parallel to split_from_dataset). The
    train pool and test set come from the same season, so this isolates a
    park-factor distribution shift from the season shift of cross_dataset_split.

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset whose groups hold the per-row ballpark identifier.
        test_parks: Ballpark identifiers (home_team codes) to hold out for test.
        name: Split-regime label carried into result frames.

    Returns:
        An EvalSplit whose train pool excludes the held-out parks.
    """
    train_idx, test_idx = ballpark_split(dataset, test_parks=test_parks)
    return EvalSplit(
        train_ds=dataset.subset(train_idx),
        X_test=dataset.X[test_idx],
        y_test=dataset.y[test_idx],
        name=name,
    )

def clean_ratings(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Clean the long ratings frame and add the numeric Clean_Rating column.

    Drops rows with any null field (which also removes the off-season melt copies
    whose Episode is null), repairs and validates the Rating, standardizes
    unrecorded-data ingredient placeholders onto their column's explicit "No X"
    label (see standardize_null_ingredients), then parses the "X.X/10" string
    into a float 0-10 rating.

    Args:
        frame: The long frame from read_ratings.

    Returns:
        A cleaned frame with a Clean_Rating float column added.
    """
    cleaned = frame.dropna(how="any")
    cleaned = normalize_ratings(cleaned)
    cleaned = validate_ratings(cleaned)
    cleaned = standardize_null_ingredients(cleaned)
    cleaned = cleaned.reset_index(drop=True)
    rating = cleaned[RATING_COL].str.split("/").str[0].astype(float)
    return cleaned.assign(**{CLEAN_RATING_COL: rating})

Multi-hot encode the six ingredient columns.

Each ingredient value becomes its own indicator column named "Column=Value", so a sandwich row has exactly six ones (one per ingredient column). Passing feature_names reindexes the output to that fixed column order, filling unseen values with zeros; this lets candidate sandwiches built for the deli search be encoded into a trained model's exact feature space.

Args: frame: A frame containing the six INGREDIENT_COLS. feature_names: Optional fixed column order to reindex onto. When None, the columns observed in frame are used (sorted by pandas get_dummies).

Returns: (X, feature_names): the float multi-hot matrix and its column names.

def encode_ingredients(
    frame: pd.DataFrame, feature_names: list[str] | None = None
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, list[str]]:
    """Multi-hot encode the six ingredient columns.

    Each ingredient value becomes its own indicator column named "Column=Value",
    so a sandwich row has exactly six ones (one per ingredient column). Passing
    feature_names reindexes the output to that fixed column order, filling unseen
    values with zeros; this lets candidate sandwiches built for the deli search be
    encoded into a trained model's exact feature space.

    Args:
        frame: A frame containing the six INGREDIENT_COLS.
        feature_names: Optional fixed column order to reindex onto. When None, the
            columns observed in frame are used (sorted by pandas get_dummies).

    Returns:
        (X, feature_names): the float multi-hot matrix and its column names.
    """
    dummies = pd.get_dummies(frame[INGREDIENT_COLS], prefix_sep="=")
    if feature_names is not None:
        dummies = dummies.reindex(columns=feature_names, fill_value=0)
    # get_dummies returns booleans on modern pandas; the models and the distance /
    # clustering selection code expect floats.
    return dummies.to_numpy(dtype=float), list(dummies.columns)

docs.title: featurize(frame)
docs.text:
Turn a raw long ratings frame into a featurized regression Dataset.

Pure and offline-testable (parallel to baseball.featurize): cleans the frame, multi-hot encodes the ingredients, prunes ingredient-value columns seen in fewer than SANDWICH_MIN_INGREDIENT_COUNT sandwiches (see prune_rare_features), and packages the 0-10 rating as the regression target. The raw ingredient columns plus Season / Episode / Rating / Clean_Rating are retained in meta for the EDA and matched-pair construction.

Args: frame: The long frame from read_ratings.

Returns: A regression Dataset whose y holds the 0-10 rating; the high-rated good sandwiches (y >= SANDWICH_GOOD_RATING_THRESHOLD) are the minority of interest.

Source code in negative_ml/sandwich/io.py 
def featurize(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> Dataset:
    """Turn a raw long ratings frame into a featurized regression Dataset.

    Pure and offline-testable (parallel to baseball.featurize): cleans the frame,
    multi-hot encodes the ingredients, prunes ingredient-value columns seen in
    fewer than SANDWICH_MIN_INGREDIENT_COUNT sandwiches (see prune_rare_features),
    and packages the 0-10 rating as the regression target. The raw ingredient
    columns plus Season / Episode / Rating / Clean_Rating are retained in meta for
    the EDA and matched-pair construction.

    Args:
        frame: The long frame from read_ratings.

    Returns:
        A regression Dataset whose y holds the 0-10 rating; the high-rated good
        sandwiches (y >= SANDWICH_GOOD_RATING_THRESHOLD) are the minority of
        interest.
    """
    cleaned = clean_ratings(frame)
    X, feature_names = encode_ingredients(cleaned)
    keep = prune_rare_features(X, min_count=SANDWICH_MIN_INGREDIENT_COUNT)
    X = X[:, keep]
    feature_names = [name for name, k in zip(feature_names, keep) if k]
    meta = cleaned[
        INGREDIENT_COLS + [RATING_COL, "Season", "Episode", CLEAN_RATING_COL]
    ].reset_index(drop=True)
    return Dataset(
        X=X,
        y=cleaned[CLEAN_RATING_COL].to_numpy(dtype=float),
        task="regression",
        feature_names=feature_names,
        groups=cleaned[GROUP_COLUMN].to_numpy(),
        meta=meta,
        # Multi-hot ingredient encoding: every column is a nominal category
        # indicator, so distance should count differing ingredients equally
        # rather than z-score-weighting rare ones. See core.selection.
        distance_metric="hamming",
    )

The reference notebook's "interesting_items": restricts each ingredient column to its well-sampled values so the EDA panels and the deli search are not dominated by one-off ingredients. Assumes frame has already been through standardize_null_ingredients (see clean_ratings), so a well-sampled "No X" value here already folds in sandwiches that recorded that ingredient as unrecorded data rather than an explicit choice.

def ingredient_value_counts(
    frame: pd.DataFrame, threshold: int
) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    """Per-column ingredient values that occur at least threshold times.

    The reference notebook's "interesting_items": restricts each ingredient
    column to its well-sampled values so the EDA panels and the deli search are
    not dominated by one-off ingredients. Assumes frame has already been
    through standardize_null_ingredients (see clean_ratings), so a well-sampled
    "No X" value here already folds in sandwiches that recorded that
    ingredient as unrecorded data rather than an explicit choice.

    Args:
        frame: A cleaned frame with the six INGREDIENT_COLS.
        threshold: Minimum number of occurrences for a value to be kept.

    Returns:
        Mapping of ingredient column to the list of values meeting the
        threshold.
    """
    frequent: dict[str, list[str]] = {}
    for col in INGREDIENT_COLS:
        counts = frame[col].value_counts()
        frequent[col] = counts[counts >= threshold].index.tolist()
    return frequent
