docs.title: normalize_ratings(frame)
docs.text:
Repair obviously typo'd rating strings so their rows can be kept.

A handful of ratings carry harmless formatting slips: stray spaces (" 4.2/10", "4.9/ 10") or a missing denominator ("4.6"). These are clearly recoverable, so rather than drop the rows in validate_ratings, repair the Rating in place: remove all whitespace, and append "/10" when only a bare number is left. Ratings still malformed after this fall to validate_ratings.

Args: frame: A frame with a Rating column (see read_ratings).

Returns: A copy of frame with the Rating column repaired.

Source code in negative_ml/sandwich/io.py 
def normalize_ratings(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Repair obviously typo'd rating strings so their rows can be kept.

    A handful of ratings carry harmless formatting slips: stray spaces
    ("  4.2/10", "4.9/ 10") or a missing denominator ("4.6"). These are clearly
    recoverable, so rather than drop the rows in validate_ratings, repair the
    Rating in place: remove all whitespace, and append "/10" when only a bare
    number is left. Ratings still malformed after this fall to validate_ratings.

    Args:
        frame: A frame with a Rating column (see read_ratings).

    Returns:
        A copy of frame with the Rating column repaired.
    """
    bare_number = re.compile(r"^\d+(\.\d+)?$")

    def repair(value: object) -> object:
        """Strip whitespace and append /10 to a bare numeric rating.

        Args:
            value: Raw rating cell value (may be str, float, or other).

        Returns:
            The repaired string, or the original value stringified if not repairable.
        """
        text = str(value).replace(" ", "")
        if bare_number.match(text):
            text = f"{text}/10"
        return text

    out = frame.copy()
    out[RATING_COL] = out[RATING_COL].map(repair)
    return out

docs.title: prune_rare_features(X, min_count)
docs.text:
Boolean mask keeping only multi-hot columns seen in enough sandwiches.

The multi-hot ingredient encoding is very wide (one indicator per ingredient value), and with only a few hundred sandwiches most columns are near-singleton ingredient values that a model can only memorize. Dropping the columns whose count (their column sum, since the matrix is 0/1) falls below min_count trims that noise before the linear classifier without touching the well-sampled ingredients. Apply the returned mask to both the matrix and feature_names to keep them aligned.

Args: X: A 0/1 multi-hot feature matrix, shape (n_samples, n_features). min_count: Minimum number of sandwiches a column must appear in to be kept (columns with a smaller column sum are dropped).

Returns: Boolean array of length n_features; True for columns to keep.

def prune_rare_features(X: np.ndarray, min_count: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Boolean mask keeping only multi-hot columns seen in enough sandwiches.

    The multi-hot ingredient encoding is very wide (one indicator per ingredient
    value), and with only a few hundred sandwiches most columns are near-singleton
    ingredient values that a model can only memorize. Dropping the columns whose
    count (their column sum, since the matrix is 0/1) falls below min_count trims
    that noise before the linear classifier without touching the well-sampled
    ingredients. Apply the returned mask to both the matrix and feature_names to
    keep them aligned.

    Args:
        X: A 0/1 multi-hot feature matrix, shape (n_samples, n_features).
        min_count: Minimum number of sandwiches a column must appear in to be
            kept (columns with a smaller column sum are dropped).

    Returns:
        Boolean array of length n_features; True for columns to keep.
    """
    return np.asarray(X).sum(axis=0) >= min_count

Read and reshape the raw ratings workbook into a long frame.

The I/O half of the loader (parallel to baseball.read_cached): reads the first NUM_SEASONS season sheets, harmonizes the Season 1 "Other / Wild Magic" header to "Wild Magic", concatenates them, drops the dice / date / name columns by keeping only the ingredient, rating, and season columns, and melts the per-season episode columns into a single (Season, Episode) pair. The result is memoized per path: a single script run asks for the ratings several times (across EDA, classifier, and downselection figures), and each call would otherwise re-read all five workbook sheets from scratch.

Args: path: Path to the workbook. Defaults to RAW_DATA_DIR / SANDWICH_FILENAME.

Returns: A long DataFrame with the six ingredient columns, Rating, Season, and Episode. Rows whose Episode is null (a season column that does not match the sandwich's own season) are left for clean_ratings to drop.

Source code in negative_ml/sandwich/io.py 
@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def read_ratings(path: str | Path | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read and reshape the raw ratings workbook into a long frame.

    The I/O half of the loader (parallel to baseball.read_cached): reads the
    first NUM_SEASONS season sheets, harmonizes the Season 1 "Other / Wild Magic"
    header to "Wild Magic", concatenates them, drops the dice / date / name
    columns by keeping only the ingredient, rating, and season columns, and melts
    the per-season episode columns into a single (Season, Episode) pair. The
    result is memoized per path: a single script run asks for the ratings
    several times (across EDA, classifier, and downselection figures), and each
    call would otherwise re-read all five workbook sheets from scratch.

    Args:
        path: Path to the workbook. Defaults to RAW_DATA_DIR / SANDWICH_FILENAME.

    Returns:
        A long DataFrame with the six ingredient columns, Rating, Season, and
        Episode. Rows whose Episode is null (a season column that does not match
        the sandwich's own season) are left for clean_ratings to drop.
    """
    if path is None:
        path = RAW_DATA_DIR / SANDWICH_FILENAME

    sheets = []
    for season in range(NUM_SEASONS):
        sheet = pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name=f"Season {season + 1}")
        # Season 1 labels the column "Other / Wild Magic"; later seasons use the
        # shorter "Wild Magic". Harmonize before concatenating so the column lines
        # up across sheets.
        if "Wild Magic" not in sheet.columns:
            sheet = sheet.rename(columns={"Other / Wild Magic": "Wild Magic"})
        sheets.append(sheet)
    frame = pd.concat(sheets, ignore_index=True)

    keep = INGREDIENT_COLS + [RATING_COL] + SEASON_COLS
    return frame[keep].melt(
        id_vars=INGREDIENT_COLS + [RATING_COL],
        value_vars=SEASON_COLS,
        var_name="Season",
        value_name="Episode",
    )

docs.text:
Rewrite unrecorded-data placeholders onto each column's "No X" label.

A sandwich with no cheese was sometimes recorded as an explicit choice ("No cheese") and sometimes as unrecorded data (a dash placeholder, e.g. "--"; see PLACEHOLDER_VALUE_RE). Left alone, encode_ingredients one-hots those as two different features even though both sandwiches have no cheese. This maps every placeholder value in the six INGREDIENT_COLS onto "No " (the spelling already used for Cheese and Bread), so the multi-hot encoding, the EDA value counts, and the deli-search candidate menu all treat a blank cell the same as the equivalent explicit choice.

Args: frame: A frame containing the six INGREDIENT_COLS.

Returns: A copy of frame with placeholder ingredient values replaced.

Source code in negative_ml/sandwich/io.py 
def standardize_null_ingredients(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Rewrite unrecorded-data placeholders onto each column's "No X" label.

    A sandwich with no cheese was sometimes recorded as an explicit choice
    ("No cheese") and sometimes as unrecorded data (a dash placeholder, e.g.
    "--"; see PLACEHOLDER_VALUE_RE). Left alone, encode_ingredients one-hots
    those as two different features even though both sandwiches have no
    cheese. This maps every placeholder value in the six INGREDIENT_COLS onto
    "No <column>" (the spelling already used for Cheese and Bread), so the
    multi-hot encoding, the EDA value counts, and the deli-search candidate
    menu all treat a blank cell the same as the equivalent explicit choice.

    Args:
        frame: A frame containing the six INGREDIENT_COLS.

    Returns:
        A copy of frame with placeholder ingredient values replaced.
    """
    out = frame.copy()
    for col in INGREDIENT_COLS:
        is_placeholder = out[col].str.match(PLACEHOLDER_VALUE_RE)
        out.loc[is_placeholder, col] = f"No {col.lower()}"
    return out

docs.title: to_classification(dataset, threshold=SANDWICH_GOOD_RATING_THRESHOLD)
docs.text:
Recast the regression sandwich Dataset as good-vs-bad classification.

The shared selection and saturation experiments score a positive (minority) class with classification metrics, so they need a binary label rather than the 0-10 rating. This relabels each sandwich as positive when its rating reaches the rare high-value "good" tier (rating >= threshold) and negative otherwise, leaving the features, groups, and meta untouched. The result drops straight into the same majority-class downselection pipeline used by the molecule and baseball classification domains.

Args: dataset: A regression sandwich Dataset (see load / featurize). threshold: Rating at or above which a sandwich is the good minority.

Returns: A classification Dataset whose y is 1 for the good (high-rated) minority and 0 for every other sandwich.

Source code in negative_ml/sandwich/io.py 
def to_classification(
    dataset: Dataset, threshold: float = SANDWICH_GOOD_RATING_THRESHOLD
) -> Dataset:
    """Recast the regression sandwich Dataset as good-vs-bad classification.

    The shared selection and saturation experiments score a positive (minority)
    class with classification metrics, so they need a binary label rather than the
    0-10 rating. This relabels each sandwich as positive when its rating reaches
    the rare high-value "good" tier (rating >= threshold) and negative otherwise,
    leaving the features, groups, and meta untouched. The result drops straight
    into the same majority-class downselection pipeline used by the molecule and
    baseball classification domains.

    Args:
        dataset: A regression sandwich Dataset (see load / featurize).
        threshold: Rating at or above which a sandwich is the good minority.

    Returns:
        A classification Dataset whose y is 1 for the good (high-rated) minority
        and 0 for every other sandwich.
    """
    return Dataset(
        X=dataset.X,
        y=(dataset.y >= threshold).astype(int),
        task="classification",
        feature_names=dataset.feature_names,
        groups=dataset.groups,
        meta=dataset.meta,
        distance_metric=dataset.distance_metric,
    )

Replaces the reference notebook's Pandera schema (kept dependency-light): every ingredient must be a non-null string, the Rating must match RATING_REGEX, and the Season must be one of S1..S5. Invalid rows are dropped rather than raised on, matching the notebook's drop_invalid_rows behavior; run normalize_ratings first so recoverable rating typos survive.

def validate_ratings(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Drop rows that do not match the expected ingredient / rating / season shape.

    Replaces the reference notebook's Pandera schema (kept dependency-light): every
    ingredient must be a non-null string, the Rating must match RATING_REGEX, and
    the Season must be one of S1..S5. Invalid rows are dropped rather than raised
    on, matching the notebook's drop_invalid_rows behavior; run normalize_ratings
    first so recoverable rating typos survive.

    Args:
        frame: A frame with the ingredient, Rating, and Season columns.

    Returns:
        The subset of rows that satisfy every check.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a required column is missing entirely.
    """
    required = INGREDIENT_COLS + [RATING_COL, "Season"]
    missing = [col for col in required if col not in frame.columns]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"Ratings frame is missing columns: {missing}.")

    valid = pd.Series(True, index=frame.index)
    for col in INGREDIENT_COLS:
        valid &= frame[col].apply(lambda v: isinstance(v, str))
    valid &= frame[RATING_COL].astype(str).str.match(RATING_REGEX)
    valid &= frame["Season"].isin(SEASON_COLS)
    return frame[valid]

docs.title: build_regression_splits(reg_ds, threshold=SANDWICH_GOOD_RATING_THRESHOLD)
docs.text:
The three sandwich evaluation regimes for a regression model.

Produces EvalSplits where both the training Dataset and the held-out test labels carry the continuous 0-10 rating: the model (an XGBRegressor) trains on and is scored against the real rating signal, via Spearman rank correlation (see negative_ml.core.eval.spearman) rather than binarizing at threshold for AUROC/AUPRC. The label_y attribute on each train_ds is set to the threshold-derived binary labels so that minority_mask / majority_mask (used by the majority-class selection strategies, which still operate on a good/bad split of the training pool) work correctly without needing a threshold argument.

Split indices are derived from the classification version of reg_ds so the stratified random split and the grouped scaffold split are seeded with the same binary label information as build_splits.

Args: reg_ds: The sandwich regression Dataset (see load), whose y holds continuous 0-10 ratings and whose meta carries season information. threshold: Rating at or above which a sandwich is the good (positive) minority class, used only to derive the training pool's label_y. Defaults to SANDWICH_GOOD_RATING_THRESHOLD.

Returns: Mapping of split name to an EvalSplit whose train_ds.y and y_test are both the continuous 0-10 rating.

Source code in negative_ml/sandwich/split.py 
def build_regression_splits(
    reg_ds: Dataset,
    threshold: float = SANDWICH_GOOD_RATING_THRESHOLD,
) -> dict[str, EvalSplit]:
    """The three sandwich evaluation regimes for a regression model.

    Produces EvalSplits where both the training Dataset and the held-out test
    labels carry the continuous 0-10 rating: the model (an XGBRegressor) trains
    on and is scored against the real rating signal, via Spearman rank
    correlation (see negative_ml.core.eval.spearman) rather than binarizing at
    threshold for AUROC/AUPRC. The label_y attribute on each train_ds is set to
    the threshold-derived binary labels so that minority_mask / majority_mask
    (used by the majority-class selection strategies, which still operate on a
    good/bad split of the training pool) work correctly without needing a
    threshold argument.

    Split indices are derived from the classification version of reg_ds so the
    stratified random split and the grouped scaffold split are seeded with the
    same binary label information as build_splits.

    Args:
        reg_ds: The sandwich regression Dataset (see load), whose y holds
            continuous 0-10 ratings and whose meta carries season information.
        threshold: Rating at or above which a sandwich is the good (positive)
            minority class, used only to derive the training pool's label_y.
            Defaults to SANDWICH_GOOD_RATING_THRESHOLD.

    Returns:
        Mapping of split name to an EvalSplit whose train_ds.y and y_test are
        both the continuous 0-10 rating.
    """
    cds = to_classification(reg_ds, threshold)
    binary_y = cds.y

    rand_train, rand_test = random_split(cds)
    scaf_train, scaf_test = scaffold_split(cds)
    seas_train, seas_test = season_split(cds, SANDWICH_TEST_SEASON)

    def make(train_idx: np.ndarray, test_idx: np.ndarray, name: str) -> EvalSplit:
        """Build one EvalSplit from raw index arrays.

        Args:
            train_idx: Row indices into reg_ds for the training pool.
            test_idx: Row indices into reg_ds for the test set.
            name: Split-regime label carried into result frames.

        Returns:
            EvalSplit whose train_ds.y and y_test are both the continuous
            0-10 rating.
        """
        reg_train_ds = reg_ds.subset(train_idx)
        reg_train_ds = Dataset(
            X=reg_train_ds.X,
            y=reg_train_ds.y,
            task="regression",
            feature_names=reg_train_ds.feature_names,
            groups=reg_train_ds.groups,
            meta=reg_train_ds.meta,
            label_y=binary_y[train_idx],
            distance_metric=reg_train_ds.distance_metric,
        )
        return EvalSplit(
            train_ds=reg_train_ds,
            X_test=reg_ds.X[test_idx],
            y_test=reg_ds.y[test_idx],
            name=name,
        )

    return {
        "random": make(rand_train, rand_test, "random"),
        "scaffold": make(scaf_train, scaf_test, "scaffold"),
        "season": make(seas_train, seas_test, "season"),
    }

docs.title: season_split(dataset, test_season, season_col='Season')
docs.text:
Hold one entire season out of training (a chronological-style shift).

Every row whose season equals test_season goes to the test set and the rest are training. Like baseball's ballpark_split this is a deterministic held-out-group split, but grouped by the show's season rather than a structural family, so the model is scored on a season it never trained on -- the sandwich analog of the baseball chronological cross-season split. The per-row season labels are read from dataset.meta (they live there rather than in groups, which carries the Main filling family used by the scaffold split), so the split is always aligned with the dataset it is drawn from and needs no separate season array.

Args: dataset: Dataset to split; its meta must carry the season_col column. test_season: The season value to hold out entirely for testing. season_col: Name of the meta column holding each row's season.

Returns: (train_idx, test_idx) integer index arrays.

Raises: ValueError: If dataset.meta lacks season_col, or no row matches test_season.

Source code in negative_ml/sandwich/split.py 
def season_split(
    dataset: Dataset,
    test_season: str,
    season_col: str = "Season",
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Hold one entire season out of training (a chronological-style shift).

    Every row whose season equals test_season goes to the test set and the rest
    are training. Like baseball's ballpark_split this is a deterministic
    held-out-group split, but grouped by the show's season rather than a
    structural family, so the model is scored on a season it never trained on --
    the sandwich analog of the baseball chronological cross-season split. The
    per-row season labels are read from dataset.meta (they live there rather
    than in groups, which carries the Main filling family used by the scaffold
    split), so the split is always aligned with the dataset it is drawn from
    and needs no separate season array.

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset to split; its meta must carry the season_col column.
        test_season: The season value to hold out entirely for testing.
        season_col: Name of the meta column holding each row's season.

    Returns:
        (train_idx, test_idx) integer index arrays.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If dataset.meta lacks season_col, or no row matches
            test_season.
    """
    if dataset.meta is None or season_col not in dataset.meta.columns:
        raise ValueError(
            f"season_split requires dataset.meta with a {season_col!r} column."
        )
    seasons = np.asarray(dataset.meta[season_col])
    is_test = seasons == test_season
    if not is_test.any():
        raise ValueError(f"No row has season {test_season!r}.")
    indices = np.arange(dataset.n_samples)
    return indices[~is_test], indices[is_test]

Build an EvalSplit that holds one entire season out of training.

Wraps season_split into an EvalSplit (mirrors baseball's park_split_from_dataset): the train pool is every other season and the test set is the held-out season, so this isolates a season distribution shift the way the scaffold split isolates a held-out filling family. The per-row season labels are read from the dataset's own meta (they live there rather than in groups, which carries the scaffold family), so the split stays aligned with the dataset and needs no side array.

Args: dataset: Dataset whose meta carries the per-row season column. test_season: The season value to hold out for testing. season_col: Name of the meta column holding each row's season. name: Split-regime label carried into result frames.

Returns: An EvalSplit whose train pool excludes the held-out season.

def season_split_from_dataset(
    dataset: Dataset,
    test_season: str,
    season_col: str = "Season",
    name: str = "season",
) -> EvalSplit:
    """Build an EvalSplit that holds one entire season out of training.

    Wraps season_split into an EvalSplit (mirrors baseball's
    park_split_from_dataset): the train pool is every other season and the test
    set is the held-out season, so this isolates a season distribution shift the
    way the scaffold split isolates a held-out filling family. The per-row
    season labels are read from the dataset's own meta (they live there rather
    than in groups, which carries the scaffold family), so the split stays
    aligned with the dataset and needs no side array.

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset whose meta carries the per-row season column.
        test_season: The season value to hold out for testing.
        season_col: Name of the meta column holding each row's season.
        name: Split-regime label carried into result frames.

    Returns:
        An EvalSplit whose train pool excludes the held-out season.
    """
    train_idx, test_idx = season_split(dataset, test_season, season_col)
    return EvalSplit(
        train_ds=dataset.subset(train_idx),
        X_test=dataset.X[test_idx],
        y_test=dataset.y[test_idx],
        name=name,
    )

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
Plotting helpers that draw onto a caller-supplied matplotlib Axes, so the same code backs both the reproducible scripts under scripts/ and the notebooks under notebooks/.

Shared visual style for every figure in the study.

Centralizes the things that must look the same across all plots: the categorical palette, the sequential colormaps used for density / probability surfaces, the save resolution, and the axis cleanup (no top/right spines, no gridlines). Importing this module applies the style (see apply_style) so the scripts, the EDA helpers, the results helpers, and the notebooks all share one look.

The categorical palette is Matplotlib's Dark2 (the ColorBrewer qualitative set). Use the colors in order for categorical series — DARK2 is the canonical ordering and is installed as the default axes.prop_cycle, so any plot that does not pass an explicit color= cycles through Dark2 for free. Reference the named constants / PALETTE entries rather than hard-coding hex values so a single edit re-themes every figure.

Data-leakage and feature-relationship diagnostics, shared across all domains.

These are the critical-review figures a machine-learning scientist or statistician would ask for before trusting the models: do the train and test sets come from the same distribution (covariate shift), is any single feature suspiciously predictive of the label (leakage smell-test), how do the features relate to each other (correlation and pairwise structure), and how does the positive rate vary across categorical groups such as ballparks, protein choices, or molecular scaffolds.

Following the rest of negative_ml.viz, the compute functions return tidy frames so a generation step can persist them and a plotting step can redraw without recomputation; the single-axes plotters draw onto a caller-supplied Axes while the grid plotters (distributions, pair matrix) build and return their own Figure.

Plotting helpers for the downselection results frames (plan.md 4.1/4.2).

Domain-agnostic: anything that returns the long-format frames produced by negative_ml.core.sweep / .saturation can be plotted here. The headline figure realizes the talk's main result axes:

y = model performance metric, x = dataset size, color/marker = selection method.

As with the rest of negative_ml.viz, every function draws onto a caller-supplied Axes so the same code backs both scripts and notebooks. Colors and axis styling come from negative_ml.viz.style.

def apply_style() -> None:
    """Install the style into Matplotlib's global rcParams.

    Sets the default color cycle to DARK2 (so unstyled plots use the
    palette in order) and the saved-figure resolution to FIGURE_DPI.
    Idempotent and safe to call repeatedly; it is invoked once on import so
    simply importing negative_ml.viz is enough to pick up the look.
    """
    plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"] = cycler(color=DARK2)
    plt.rcParams["savefig.dpi"] = FIGURE_DPI
    plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 12
    plt.rcParams["axes.titlesize"] = 13
    plt.rcParams["axes.labelsize"] = 12
    plt.rcParams["xtick.labelsize"] = 11
    plt.rcParams["ytick.labelsize"] = 11
    plt.rcParams["legend.fontsize"] = 10
    plt.rcParams["legend.title_fontsize"] = 11

def save_fig(fig: plt.Figure, path: Path, dpi: int = FIGURE_DPI) -> Path:
    """Save a figure to path (creating parents) and close it.

    The one place every script writes a PNG, so resolution and the
    bbox_inches="tight" crop stay consistent. Closes the figure to bound
    memory when a script emits many panels.

    Args:
        fig: The figure to write.
        path: Destination path; parent directories are created as needed.
        dpi: Output resolution.

    Returns:
        The path written, for logging.
    """
    path = Path(path)
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    fig.savefig(path, dpi=dpi, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)
    return path

    """Randomly subsample an index array down to at most cap entries.

    Shared by every figure that draws a dense point cloud for legibility
    (baseball's exit-velocity scatter, the feature-pair matrix, the selection
    examples background): each caps a different array to a different budget
    but needs the same "subsample when over cap" logic.

    Args:
        idx: Integer index array to subsample.
        cap: Maximum number of indices to keep; idx is returned unchanged when
            it already has cap or fewer entries.
        seed: Random seed for the subsample.

    Returns:
        idx unchanged, or a random subset of size cap (order not preserved).
    """
    if len(idx) <= cap:
        return idx
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    return rng.choice(idx, cap, replace=False)

def covariate_shift_table(
    train_X: np.ndarray, test_X: np.ndarray, feature_names: Sequence[str]
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Per-feature train-vs-test KS statistic, sorted from most to least shifted.

    Quantifies covariate shift so a hard or park split's difficulty can be
    attributed to specific features rather than eyeballed from histograms.

    Args:
        train_X: Training feature matrix.
        test_X: Test feature matrix (same column order as train_X).
        feature_names: Column names aligned with the matrices.

    Returns:
        Frame with columns [feature, ks], sorted by descending ks.
    """
    train_X = np.asarray(train_X, dtype=float)
    test_X = np.asarray(test_X, dtype=float)
    rows = [
        {"feature": name, "ks": ks_statistic(train_X[:, i], test_X[:, i])}
        for i, name in enumerate(feature_names)
    ]
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("ks", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

docs.title: ks_statistic(a, b)
docs.text:
Two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic between two 1-D samples.

The KS statistic is the maximum absolute gap between the two empirical CDFs, a scale-free measure of distribution shift in [0, 1] (0 = identical, 1 = disjoint). Computed with numpy so no SciPy dependency is needed; only the statistic (not the p-value) is returned, which is what the shift chart shows.

Args: a: First sample (e.g. a training feature column). b: Second sample (e.g. the same feature in the test set).

Returns: The KS statistic; 0.0 if either sample is empty.

Source code in negative_ml/viz/diagnostics.py 
def ks_statistic(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic between two 1-D samples.

    The KS statistic is the maximum absolute gap between the two empirical CDFs,
    a scale-free measure of distribution shift in [0, 1] (0 = identical, 1 =
    disjoint). Computed with numpy so no SciPy dependency is needed; only the
    statistic (not the p-value) is returned, which is what the shift chart shows.

    Args:
        a: First sample (e.g. a training feature column).
        b: Second sample (e.g. the same feature in the test set).

    Returns:
        The KS statistic; 0.0 if either sample is empty.
    """
    a = np.sort(np.asarray(a, dtype=float))
    b = np.sort(np.asarray(b, dtype=float))
    if a.size == 0 or b.size == 0:
        return 0.0
    grid = np.concatenate([a, b])
    cdf_a = np.searchsorted(a, grid, side="right") / a.size
    cdf_b = np.searchsorted(b, grid, side="right") / b.size
    return float(np.max(np.abs(cdf_a - cdf_b)))

docs.title: label_correlation_table(X, y, feature_names)
docs.text:
Per-feature correlation with the label (a leakage smell-test).

Reports both Pearson (linear / point-biserial against the binary label) and Spearman (monotonic). A feature with a near-perfect correlation would signal leakage; moderate correlations are the expected healthy range.

Args: X: Feature matrix. y: Binary label aligned with X rows. feature_names: Column names aligned with X.

Returns: Frame with columns [feature, pearson, spearman], sorted by descending absolute Pearson correlation.

Source code in negative_ml/viz/diagnostics.py 
def label_correlation_table(
    X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, feature_names: Sequence[str]
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Per-feature correlation with the label (a leakage smell-test).

    Reports both Pearson (linear / point-biserial against the binary label) and
    Spearman (monotonic). A feature with a near-perfect correlation would signal
    leakage; moderate correlations are the expected healthy range.

    Args:
        X: Feature matrix.
        y: Binary label aligned with X rows.
        feature_names: Column names aligned with X.

    Returns:
        Frame with columns [feature, pearson, spearman], sorted by descending
        absolute Pearson correlation.
    """
    df = pd.DataFrame(np.asarray(X, dtype=float), columns=list(feature_names))
    label = pd.Series(np.asarray(y, dtype=float))
    # corrwith computes only the feature-vs-label correlations (O(F)), unlike
    # corr() which would build the full feature-by-feature matrix (O(F^2))
    # just to slice one column back out of it.
    pearson = df.corrwith(label, method="pearson")
    spearman = df.corrwith(label, method="spearman")
    out = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "feature": pearson.index,
            "pearson": pearson.values,
            "spearman": spearman.values,
        }
    )
    return out.reindex(
        out["pearson"].abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index
    ).reset_index(drop=True)

docs.text:
Grid of overlaid normalized histograms, one panel per feature.

Shared scaffold for plot_train_test_distributions and plot_class_stratified_distributions: both compare two groups' distributions feature by feature in a fixed 3-column grid, differing only in which two groups are compared and their labels/colors. Densities are normalized so differently sized groups are comparable.

Args: feature_names: Column names, one panel per name. group_a: Per-feature 1-D arrays for the first group (e.g. train, or majority), aligned with feature_names. group_b: Per-feature 1-D arrays for the second group (e.g. test, or minority), aligned with feature_names. label_a: Legend label for group_a. label_b: Legend label for group_b. color_a: Histogram outline color for group_a. color_b: Histogram outline color for group_b. bins: Histogram bin count per panel. suptitle: Figure-level title.

Returns: The created Figure (caller saves / displays it).

Source code in negative_ml/viz/diagnostics.py 
def overlaid_feature_histogram_grid(
    feature_names: Sequence[str],
    group_a: Sequence[np.ndarray],
    group_b: Sequence[np.ndarray],
    label_a: str,
    label_b: str,
    color_a: str,
    color_b: str,
    bins: int,
    suptitle: str,
) -> plt.Figure:
    """Grid of overlaid normalized histograms, one panel per feature.

    Shared scaffold for plot_train_test_distributions and
    plot_class_stratified_distributions: both compare two groups' distributions
    feature by feature in a fixed 3-column grid, differing only in which two
    groups are compared and their labels/colors. Densities are normalized so
    differently sized groups are comparable.

    Args:
        feature_names: Column names, one panel per name.
        group_a: Per-feature 1-D arrays for the first group (e.g. train, or
            majority), aligned with feature_names.
        group_b: Per-feature 1-D arrays for the second group (e.g. test, or
            minority), aligned with feature_names.
        label_a: Legend label for group_a.
        label_b: Legend label for group_b.
        color_a: Histogram outline color for group_a.
        color_b: Histogram outline color for group_b.
        bins: Histogram bin count per panel.
        suptitle: Figure-level title.

    Returns:
        The created Figure (caller saves / displays it).
    """
    n = len(feature_names)
    ncols = 3
    nrows = (n + ncols - 1) // ncols
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(
        nrows, ncols, figsize=(5 * ncols, 3.2 * nrows), squeeze=False
    )
    flat = axes.ravel()
    for i, name in enumerate(feature_names):
        ax = flat[i]
        col_a, col_b = group_a[i], group_b[i]
        lo = float(min(col_a.min(), col_b.min()))
        hi = float(max(col_a.max(), col_b.max()))
        edges = np.linspace(lo, hi, bins + 1)
        ax.hist(
            col_a,
            bins=edges,
            density=True,
            histtype="step",
            color=color_a,
            lw=1.6,
            label=label_a,
        )
        ax.hist(
            col_b,
            bins=edges,
            density=True,
            histtype="step",
            color=color_b,
            lw=1.6,
            label=label_b,
        )
        ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10)
        ax.set_yticks([])
        style_axes(ax)
    for ax in flat[n:]:
        ax.set_visible(False)
    flat[0].legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
    fig.suptitle(suptitle, fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.97))
    return fig

def per_group_positive_rate(groups: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Positive-class rate and sample count per categorical group.

    Groups can be any categorical grouping: ballparks, protein (Main) choices,
    molecular scaffolds, etc. The returned frame can be filtered and passed to
    plot_per_group_rate.

    Args:
        groups: Per-row group identifier (e.g. Statcast home_team code, scaffold
            SMILES, or sandwich Main ingredient).
        y: Binary label aligned with groups.

    Returns:
        Frame with columns [group, n, positive_rate], sorted by positive_rate.
    """
    df = pd.DataFrame({"group": np.asarray(groups), "y": np.asarray(y, dtype=float)})
    g = df.groupby("group")["y"].agg(["mean", "size"]).reset_index()
    g = g.rename(columns={"mean": "positive_rate", "size": "n"})
    return g.sort_values("positive_rate").reset_index(drop=True)

def plot_class_stratified_distributions(
    X: np.ndarray,
    y: np.ndarray,
    feature_names: Sequence[str],
    bins: int = 40,
    minority_label: str = "minority",
    majority_label: str = "majority",
) -> plt.Figure:
    """Overlaid normalized histograms per feature, stratified by class label.

    Shows which features separate the minority class from the majority: panels
    where the two outlines diverge identify the most discriminative features.
    Useful as a complement to label_correlation_table — correlation captures the
    linear signal while this view reveals the full distributional shape difference.

    Args:
        X: Feature matrix.
        y: Binary label aligned with X rows (1 == minority / positive class).
        feature_names: Column names aligned with X.
        bins: Histogram bin count per panel.
        minority_label: Legend label for the positive (minority) class.
        majority_label: Legend label for the negative (majority) class.

    Returns:
        The created Figure (caller saves / displays it).
    """
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=int)
    pos_mask = y == 1
    neg_mask = ~pos_mask
    group_a = [X[neg_mask, i] for i in range(len(feature_names))]
    group_b = [X[pos_mask, i] for i in range(len(feature_names))]
    return overlaid_feature_histogram_grid(
        feature_names,
        group_a,
        group_b,
        majority_label,
        minority_label,
        LIGHT_GRAY,
        PALETTE["magenta"],
        bins,
        f"Feature distributions by class ({minority_label} vs. {majority_label})",
    )

def plot_correlation_heatmap(

def plot_feature_pair_matrix(
    X: np.ndarray,
    feature_names: Sequence[str],
    minority_mask: np.ndarray,
    minority_label: str = "minority",
    max_points: int = VIZ_PAIRPLOT_POINTS,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> plt.Figure:
    """Scatter-matrix of continuous features, minority class drawn on top.

    The diagonal shows each feature's marginal histogram; the lower triangle
    shows pairwise scatters with the majority in gray and the minority class
    highlighted, exposing collinearity and where the class of interest sits in
    each plane. Points are subsampled for legibility.

    Args:
        X: Feature matrix restricted to the columns to show (continuous features).
        feature_names: Names aligned with the columns of X.
        minority_mask: Boolean mask (len == rows of X) flagging the minority rows.
        minority_label: Legend label for the highlighted class.
        max_points: Approximate cap on majority points drawn per panel.
        seed: Seed for the majority subsample.

    Returns:
        The created Figure.
    """
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    minority_mask = np.asarray(minority_mask, dtype=bool)
    maj_idx = subsample_indices(np.flatnonzero(~minority_mask), max_points, seed)
    min_idx = np.flatnonzero(minority_mask)

    n = len(feature_names)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(n, n, figsize=(2.2 * n, 2.2 * n), squeeze=False)
    for r in range(n):
        for c in range(n):
            ax = axes[r, c]
            if r == c:
                ax.hist(X[:, r], bins=40, color=PALETTE["teal"])
            elif r > c:
                ax.scatter(
                    X[maj_idx, c],
                    X[maj_idx, r],
                    s=4,
                    alpha=0.2,
                    color=LIGHT_GRAY,
                    edgecolors="none",
                )
                ax.scatter(
                    X[min_idx, c],
                    X[min_idx, r],
                    s=5,
                    alpha=0.5,
                    color=PALETTE["magenta"],
                    edgecolors="none",
                    label=minority_label,
                )
            else:
                ax.set_visible(False)
            if c == 0 and r != 0:
                ax.set_ylabel(feature_names[r], fontsize=8)
            if r == n - 1:
                ax.set_xlabel(feature_names[c], fontsize=8)
            ax.tick_params(labelsize=6)
            style_axes(ax)
    axes[1, 0].legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, markerscale=2)
    fig.suptitle("Feature pair matrix (minority class highlighted)", fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.98))
    return fig

def plot_label_correlations(
    df: pd.DataFrame, ax: plt.Axes, leakage_threshold: float = 0.95
) -> plt.Axes:
    """Grouped bars of each feature's Pearson and Spearman correlation with y.

    The leakage smell-test: bars that approach +/-1 would flag a feature that
    nearly determines the label. The dashed guides mark the leakage threshold.

    Args:
        df: Frame with [feature, pearson, spearman] (see label_correlation_table).
        ax: Target matplotlib axes.
        leakage_threshold: Absolute correlation above which a feature is flagged.

    Returns:
        The styled ax.
    """
    feats = df["feature"].tolist()
    x = np.arange(len(feats))
    width = 0.4
    ax.bar(
        x - width / 2,
        df["pearson"],
        width=width,
        color=PALETTE["teal"],
        label="Pearson",
    )
    ax.bar(
        x + width / 2,
        df["spearman"],
        width=width,
        color=PALETTE["orange"],
        label="Spearman",
    )
    ax.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=0.8)
    ax.axhline(
        leakage_threshold,
        color=PALETTE["magenta"],
        ls="--",
        lw=1,
        label=f"leakage flag (|r|>{leakage_threshold:g})",
    )
    ax.axhline(-leakage_threshold, color=PALETTE["magenta"], ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.set_ylim(-1, 1)
    ax.set_xticks(x)
    ax.set_xticklabels(feats, rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_ylabel("correlation with label")
    ax.set_title("Feature-label correlation (leakage smell-test)")
    ax.legend(loc="best", fontsize=8)
    return style_axes(ax)

def plot_per_group_rate(
    rate_df: pd.DataFrame,
    ax: plt.Axes,
    highlight: Sequence[str] = (),
    label: str = "positive",
) -> plt.Axes:
    """Bar chart of per-group positive rate, optionally highlighting held-out groups.

    Justifies group-based splits: highlighted groups should sit toward the
    extremes of the positive-rate distribution, so training without them and
    testing on them is a genuine distribution shift.

    Args:
        rate_df: Frame with [group, n, positive_rate] (see per_group_positive_rate).
        ax: Target matplotlib axes.
        highlight: Group identifiers drawn in the highlight color (e.g. held-out
            groups such as outlier ballparks or held-out protein families).
        label: Name of the positive class for the y-axis label.

    Returns:
        The styled ax.
    """
    d = rate_df.sort_values("positive_rate")
    highlight_set = set(highlight)
    colors = [
        PALETTE["orange"] if g in highlight_set else LIGHT_GRAY for g in d["group"]
    ]
    ax.bar(d["group"], d["positive_rate"], color=colors)
    ax.axhline(
        float(np.average(d["positive_rate"], weights=d["n"])),
        color=INK,
        ls="--",
        lw=1,
        label="overall rate",
    )
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(d["group"])))
    ax.set_xticklabels(d["group"], rotation=90, fontsize=7)
    ax.set_ylabel(f"{label} rate")
    ax.set_ylim(0, None)

    Args:
        train_X: Training feature matrix.
        test_X: Test feature matrix (same column order).
        feature_names: Column names aligned with the matrices.
        bins: Histogram bin count per panel.
        train_label: Legend label for the training distribution.
        test_label: Legend label for the test distribution.

    Returns:
        The created Figure (caller saves / displays it).
    """
    train_X = np.asarray(train_X, dtype=float)
    test_X = np.asarray(test_X, dtype=float)
    group_a = [train_X[:, i] for i in range(len(feature_names))]
    group_b = [test_X[:, i] for i in range(len(feature_names))]
    return overlaid_feature_histogram_grid(
        feature_names,
        group_a,
        group_b,
        train_label,
        test_label,
        PALETTE["teal"],
        PALETTE["orange"],
        bins,
        "Train vs. test feature distributions (covariate shift)",
    )

Mean + std of metric over seeds, grouped by x, sorted by x.

def aggregate(df: pd.DataFrame, x: str, metric: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Mean + std of metric over seeds, grouped by x, sorted by x.

    Args:
        df: Long-format results frame.
        x: Column to group by (the x-axis quantity).
        metric: Column to aggregate.

    Returns:
        Frame with one row per x value and mean / std columns.
    """
    g = df.groupby(x)[metric].agg(["mean", "std"]).reset_index()
    g["std"] = g["std"].fillna(0.0)
    return g.sort_values(x)

docs.text:
Set ax's y-limits, the single place every AUPRC (and other metric) plot in downselection/saturation/performance figures should route through.

Precedence: an explicit ylim wins outright; otherwise "auprc" checks AUPRC_YLIM_BY_DOMAIN[domain]; otherwise METRIC_YLIM[metric]. A no-op if none of those apply.

Args: ax: Axes whose y-limits to set. metric: Metric key into METRIC_YLIM / AUPRC_YLIM_BY_DOMAIN. domain: Domain name ("molecules" / "baseball" / "sandwiches"); for "auprc", overrides the generic [0, 1] bound with AUPRC_YLIM_BY_DOMAIN[domain] if present there. ylim: Explicit (lo, hi) override, bypassing both AUPRC_YLIM_BY_DOMAIN and METRIC_YLIM. For a one-off custom range (e.g. a study whose curves legitimately need the full axis regardless of domain).

Returns: The same ax, for chaining.

Source code in negative_ml/viz/selection_results.py 
def apply_metric_ylim(
    ax: plt.Axes,
    metric: str,
    domain: str | None = None,
    ylim: tuple[float | None, float | None] | None = None,
) -> plt.Axes:
    """Set ax's y-limits, the single place every AUPRC (and other metric) plot
    in downselection/saturation/performance figures should route through.

    Precedence: an explicit ylim wins outright; otherwise "auprc" checks
    AUPRC_YLIM_BY_DOMAIN[domain]; otherwise METRIC_YLIM[metric]. A no-op if
    none of those apply.

    Args:
        ax: Axes whose y-limits to set.
        metric: Metric key into METRIC_YLIM / AUPRC_YLIM_BY_DOMAIN.
        domain: Domain name ("molecules" / "baseball" / "sandwiches"); for
            "auprc", overrides the generic [0, 1] bound with
            AUPRC_YLIM_BY_DOMAIN[domain] if present there.
        ylim: Explicit (lo, hi) override, bypassing both AUPRC_YLIM_BY_DOMAIN
            and METRIC_YLIM. For a one-off custom range (e.g. a study whose
            curves legitimately need the full axis regardless of domain).

    Returns:
        The same ax, for chaining.
    """
    lim = ylim
    if lim is None:
        lim = AUPRC_YLIM_BY_DOMAIN.get(domain) if metric == "auprc" else None
    if lim is None:
        lim = METRIC_YLIM.get(metric)
    if lim is not None:
        ax.set_ylim(lim[0], lim[1])
    return ax

docs.title: freeze_best_legend(ax, legend)
docs.text:
Lock a loc="best" legend to its current spot; return its footprint.

A loc="best" legend recomputes its position on every draw. Left dynamic, a second such legend can't avoid the first (Legend artists aren't part of matplotlib's overlap-avoidance data, only lines/patches/text are) — and worse, on a later draw the first legend can drift to dodge its own reserved footprint, since it still sees itself as "best"-placed. Freezing each legend the moment it's placed keeps both stable and lets the next legend's own "best" pass treat this one's footprint as occupied.

Args: ax: Axes the legend belongs to. legend: A legend created with loc="best".

Returns: An invisible Rectangle patch (already added to ax) marking the legend's footprint in data coordinates, for the next legend to avoid; remove it once every legend on ax is frozen.

Source code in negative_ml/viz/selection_results.py 
def freeze_best_legend(ax: plt.Axes, legend: plt.Legend) -> Rectangle:
    """Lock a loc="best" legend to its current spot; return its footprint.

    A loc="best" legend recomputes its position on every draw. Left dynamic,
    a second such legend can't avoid the first (Legend artists aren't part of
    matplotlib's overlap-avoidance data, only lines/patches/text are) — and
    worse, on a later draw the first legend can drift to dodge its own
    reserved footprint, since it still sees itself as "best"-placed. Freezing
    each legend the moment it's placed keeps both stable and lets the next
    legend's own "best" pass treat this one's footprint as occupied.

    Args:
        ax: Axes the legend belongs to.
        legend: A legend created with loc="best".

    Returns:
        An invisible Rectangle patch (already added to ax) marking the
        legend's footprint in data coordinates, for the next legend to
        avoid; remove it once every legend on ax is frozen.
    """
    ax.figure.canvas.draw()
    axes_bbox = legend.get_window_extent().transformed(ax.transAxes.inverted())
    legend.set_bbox_to_anchor((axes_bbox.x0, axes_bbox.y0), transform=ax.transAxes)
    legend.set_loc("lower left")

    data_bbox = legend.get_window_extent().transformed(ax.transData.inverted())
    return ax.add_patch(
        Rectangle(
            (data_bbox.x0, data_bbox.y0),
            data_bbox.width,
            data_bbox.height,
            visible=False,
        )
    )

docs.text:
Grouped bars: each single-feature control + the full model, by split.

Shows how far a single feature alone (the correlation negative control) gets you versus the trained model, under each split. Each control bar is annotated with that feature's correlation with the label, so a near-zero bar is visibly explained (e.g. launch angle for triples, where the relationship is non-monotonic and the linear control is near chance).

Args: df: Long-format negative-control frame for one target with columns [model, feature, corr, split, ]. metric: Metric column to chart ("auprc" by default). ax: Target axes; created if None. annotate_corr: Annotate each control bar with its correlation coefficient.

Returns: The styled ax.

Source code in negative_ml/viz/selection_results.py 
def plot_negative_control(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    metric: str = "auprc",
    ax: plt.Axes | None = None,
    annotate_corr: bool = True,
) -> plt.Axes:
    """Grouped bars: each single-feature control + the full model, by split.

    Shows how far a single feature alone (the correlation negative control) gets
    you versus the trained model, under each split. Each control bar is annotated
    with that feature's correlation with the label, so a near-zero bar is visibly
    explained (e.g. launch angle for triples, where the relationship is
    non-monotonic and the linear control is near chance).

    Args:
        df: Long-format negative-control frame for one target with columns
            [model, feature, corr, split, <metric>].
        metric: Metric column to chart ("auprc" by default).
        ax: Target axes; created if None.
        annotate_corr: Annotate each control bar with its correlation coefficient.

    Returns:
        The styled ax.
    """
    if ax is None:
        _, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

    # Single-feature categories (in first-seen order) followed by the full model.
    corr_feats = list(dict.fromkeys(df.loc[df["model"] == "correlation", "feature"]))
    cats = corr_feats + ["all"]
    cat_labels = corr_feats + ["full model"]
    present_splits = [s for s in SPLIT_COLOR if s in df["split"].unique()]
    n = max(len(present_splits), 1)
    width = 0.8 / n
    xpos = np.arange(len(cats))

    for i, split_name in enumerate(present_splits):
        sub = df[df["split"] == split_name].set_index("feature")
        vals = [float(sub.loc[c, metric]) if c in sub.index else np.nan for c in cats]
        offsets = xpos + (i - (n - 1) / 2) * width
        ax.bar(
            offsets,
            vals,
            width=width,
            color=SPLIT_COLOR[split_name],
            label=SPLIT_LABEL[split_name],
        )
        if annotate_corr:
            for c, off, v in zip(cats, offsets, vals):
                if c == "all" or np.isnan(v):
                    continue
                r = float(sub.loc[c, "corr"])
                ax.text(
                    off,
                    v,
                    f"r={r:+.2f}",
                    ha="center",
                    va="bottom",
                    fontsize=9,
                    rotation=90,
                )

    if metric == "auroc":
        ax.axhline(0.5, color=INK, ls="--", lw=1, label="chance (0.5)")
    apply_metric_ylim(ax, metric)
    ax.set_xticks(xpos)
    ax.set_xticklabels(cat_labels, rotation=20, ha="right")
    ax.set_ylabel(METRIC_LABELS.get(metric, metric))
    ax.set_title(
        f"Negative control: single feature vs. full model "
        f"({METRIC_LABELS.get(metric, metric)})"
    )
    ax.legend(loc="best", fontsize=10)
    return style_axes(ax)

Human-readable inspection of what each downselection strategy actually keeps.

The selection strategies in negative_ml.core.selection are easy to describe but their behavior is worth checking concretely: at a tiny budget, which majority batted balls does each one retain? decoys should keep balls that just miss being home runs (high exit velocity, home-run-ish launch angle); diversity should reach for the extremes of the feature space (mishit grounders, weak pop-ups, bunts); density-diversity should keep typical cluster representatives; random should mirror the bulk (mostly ordinary outs). These helpers build a small table per strategy (so the rows can be read and sanity-checked) and a four-panel scatter that shows the picks against the full batted-ball cloud.

The table carries the full-dataset row index of every pick, so a generation step can persist it and the plotting step can highlight the same rows after reloading only the cached season — keeping with the decoupled generate/plot convention.

def plot_saturation_curve(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    metric: str,
    ax: plt.Axes,
    x: str = "n_train",
    label: str | None = None,
    color: str = PALETTE["gray"],
    domain: str | None = None,
) -> plt.Axes:
    """Single saturation curve (mean +/-1 std over seeds) for one frame.

    Args:
        df: Long-format results frame with seed, x, and metric.
        metric: Column to put on the y-axis.
        ax: Target matplotlib axes.
        x: Column for the x-axis (training set size by default).
        label: Legend label for the curve, if any.
        color: Line and band color for the curve.
        domain: Domain name, for the per-domain AUPRC y-limit override (see
            apply_metric_ylim).

    Returns:
        The styled ax.
    """
    g = aggregate(df, x, metric)
    ax.plot(
        g[x],
        g["mean"],
        marker="o",
        color=color,
        linewidth=1.8,
        label=label,
    )
    ax.fill_between(
        g[x], g["mean"] - g["std"], g["mean"] + g["std"], color=color, alpha=0.15
    )
    ax.set_xlabel(f"training set size ({x})")
    ax.set_ylabel(METRIC_LABELS.get(metric, metric))
    apply_metric_ylim(ax, metric, domain=domain)
    return style_axes(ax)

Defaults to AUROC, AUPRC, precision@k, and enrichment factor. x: Column for the shared x-axis. logx: Log-scale the x-axis on every panel. figsize: Figure size; defaults to a 2-column grid sized to the panels. domain: Domain name, for the per-domain AUPRC y-limit override (see apply_metric_ylim).

Returns: The created Figure (caller saves / displays it).

Source code in negative_ml/viz/selection_results.py 
def plot_selection_grid(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    metrics: list[str] | None = None,
    x: str = "n_train",
    logx: bool = True,
    figsize: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    domain: str | None = None,
) -> plt.Figure:
    """Multi-panel headline figure: one subplot per metric, shared legend.

    Args:
        df: Long-format results frame (see plot_strategy_curves).
        metrics: Metric columns to panel, one subplot each. Defaults to AUROC,
            AUPRC, precision@k, and enrichment factor.
        x: Column for the shared x-axis.
        logx: Log-scale the x-axis on every panel.
        figsize: Figure size; defaults to a 2-column grid sized to the panels.
        domain: Domain name, for the per-domain AUPRC y-limit override (see
            apply_metric_ylim).

    Returns:
        The created Figure (caller saves / displays it).
    """
    metrics = metrics or ["auroc", "auprc", "precision_at_k", "enrichment_factor"]
    n = len(metrics)
    ncols = 2
    nrows = (n + ncols - 1) // ncols
    figsize = figsize or (6.5 * ncols, 4.5 * nrows)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=figsize, squeeze=False)
    flat = axes.ravel()

    for ax, metric in zip(flat, metrics):
        plot_strategy_curves(df, metric, ax, x=x, logx=logx, domain=domain)
    for ax in flat[n:]:  # hide any unused panel
        ax.set_visible(False)

    handles, labels = flat[0].get_legend_handles_labels()
    fig.legend(
        handles,
        labels,
        loc="lower center",
        ncol=min(len(labels), 6),
        bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.02),
    )
    fig.suptitle("Majority-class selection: performance vs. dataset size", fontsize=16)
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.03, 1, 0.97))
    return fig

Overlay the same strategy curves across every evaluation split present.

Strategy is encoded by color (reusing STRATEGY_STYLE) and the split by linestyle (see SPLIT_LINESTYLE, e.g. solid = random, dashed = hard), so the two dimensions read independently. Answers "do selection strategies that look good in-distribution still help when generalizing to a harder split?". The title lists whichever splits actually appear in df, so it stays honest for the baseball (random/hard/park) and sandwich (random/scaffold/season) regimes alike.

Args: df: Long-format frame carrying a split column alongside strategy, seed, x, and metric (typically filtered to one target). metric: Column to put on the y-axis. ax: Target matplotlib axes. x: Column for the x-axis (total training size by default). logx: Log-scale the x-axis. domain: Domain name, for the per-domain AUPRC y-limit override (see apply_metric_ylim).

Returns: The styled ax.

Source code in negative_ml/viz/selection_results.py 
def plot_split_overlay(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    metric: str,
    ax: plt.Axes,
    x: str = "n_train",
    logx: bool = True,
    domain: str | None = None,
) -> plt.Axes:
    """Overlay the same strategy curves across every evaluation split present.

    Strategy is encoded by color (reusing STRATEGY_STYLE) and the split by
    linestyle (see SPLIT_LINESTYLE, e.g. solid = random, dashed = hard), so the
    two dimensions read independently. Answers "do selection strategies that look
    good in-distribution still help when generalizing to a harder split?". The
    title lists whichever splits actually appear in df, so it stays honest for the
    baseball (random/hard/park) and sandwich (random/scaffold/season) regimes
    alike.

    Args:
        df: Long-format frame carrying a split column alongside strategy,
            seed, x, and metric (typically filtered to one target).
        metric: Column to put on the y-axis.
        ax: Target matplotlib axes.
        x: Column for the x-axis (total training size by default).
        logx: Log-scale the x-axis.
        domain: Domain name, for the per-domain AUPRC y-limit override (see
            apply_metric_ylim).

    Returns:
        The styled ax.
    """
    present_splits = [s for s in SPLIT_LINESTYLE if s in df["split"].unique()]
    present_strats = [s for s in STRATEGY_STYLE if s in df["strategy"].unique()]

    for split_name in present_splits:
        ls = SPLIT_LINESTYLE[split_name]
        sub = df[df["split"] == split_name]
        for strat in present_strats:
            style = STRATEGY_STYLE[strat]
            g = aggregate(sub[sub["strategy"] == strat], x, metric)
            if g.empty:
                continue
            ax.plot(
                g[x],
                g["mean"],
                color=style["color"],
                linestyle=ls,
                marker=style["marker"],
                markersize=5,
                linewidth=1.6,
            )

    if logx:
        ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_xlabel(f"training set size ({x})")
    ax.set_ylabel(METRIC_LABELS.get(metric, metric))
    apply_metric_ylim(ax, metric, domain=domain)
    split_names = " vs. ".join(present_splits) if present_splits else "splits"
    ax.set_title(f"{METRIC_LABELS.get(metric, metric)}: {split_names} split")

    # Two independent legends: strategy (color) and split (linestyle).
    strat_handles = [
        Line2D(
            [],
            [],
            color=STRATEGY_STYLE[s]["color"],
            marker=STRATEGY_STYLE[s]["marker"],
            label=STRATEGY_STYLE[s]["label"],
        )
        for s in present_strats
    ]
    split_handles = [
        Line2D([], [], color=INK, linestyle=SPLIT_LINESTYLE[s], label=SPLIT_LABEL[s])
        for s in present_splits
    ]
    first = ax.legend(handles=strat_handles, loc="best", fontsize=10, title="strategy")
    ax.add_artist(first)
    first_footprint = freeze_best_legend(ax, first)

    second = ax.legend(handles=split_handles, loc="best", fontsize=10, title="split")
    second_footprint = freeze_best_legend(ax, second)

    first_footprint.remove()
    second_footprint.remove()
    return style_axes(ax)

docs.title: plot_strategy_curves(df, metric, ax, x='n_train', logx=False, domain=None)
docs.text:
One curve per selection strategy: metric vs. dataset size.

Each size-varying strategy in STRATEGY_STYLE is drawn as a line with markers and a +/-1 std band. The as-is-full and weighted-full baselines are not plotted, even if present in df.

Args: df: Long-format frame with strategy, seed, x, and metric. metric: Column to put on the y-axis. ax: Target matplotlib axes. x: Column for the x-axis ("n_train" total training size by default). logx: Log-scale the x-axis (recommended when budgets span orders of magnitude up to the full-data reference). domain: Domain name, for the per-domain AUPRC y-limit override (see apply_metric_ylim).

Returns: The styled ax.

Source code in negative_ml/viz/selection_results.py 
def plot_strategy_curves(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    metric: str,
    ax: plt.Axes,
    x: str = "n_train",
    logx: bool = False,
    domain: str | None = None,
) -> plt.Axes:
    """One curve per selection strategy: metric vs. dataset size.

    Each size-varying strategy in STRATEGY_STYLE is drawn as a line with
    markers and a +/-1 std band. The as-is-full and weighted-full baselines
    are not plotted, even if present in df.

    Args:
        df: Long-format frame with strategy, seed, x, and metric.
        metric: Column to put on the y-axis.
        ax: Target matplotlib axes.
        x: Column for the x-axis ("n_train" total training size by default).
        logx: Log-scale the x-axis (recommended when budgets span orders of
            magnitude up to the full-data reference).
        domain: Domain name, for the per-domain AUPRC y-limit override (see
            apply_metric_ylim).

    Returns:
        The styled ax.
    """
    present = list(df["strategy"].unique())
    varying = [s for s in STRATEGY_STYLE if s in present]

    # Snap n_train to the median per (strategy, budget) group so that seeds with
    # slightly different n_train (e.g. from density_diversity empty-cluster shortfalls)
    # collapse to one x-position rather than piling up side by side.
    if x == "n_train" and "budget" in df.columns:
        df = df.copy()
        df[x] = (
            df.groupby(["strategy", "budget"])[x]
            .transform("median")
            .round()
            .astype(int)
        )

    x_all = df[x].to_numpy()
    x_lo, x_hi = float(np.min(x_all)), float(np.max(x_all))
    # Cap the axis at the largest varying-strategy budget, not any unplotted
    # full-data baseline rows, which sit at the full dataset size.
    varying_x = df.loc[df["strategy"].isin(varying), x].to_numpy()
    x_hi_curve = float(np.max(varying_x)) if varying_x.size else x_hi

    for name in varying:
        style = STRATEGY_STYLE[name]
        g = aggregate(df[df["strategy"] == name], x, metric)
        ax.plot(
            g[x],
            g["mean"],
            marker=style["marker"],
            color=style["color"],
            label=style["label"],
            markersize=6,
            linewidth=1.8,
        )
        ax.fill_between(
            g[x],
            g["mean"] - g["std"],
            g["mean"] + g["std"],
            color=style["color"],
            alpha=0.15,
        )

    if logx:
        ax.set_xscale("log")
        ax.set_xlim(right=x_hi_curve * 1.05)  # tight margin past the largest budget
        # Restrict ticks to the plotted (varying-strategy) budgets rather than the
        # default log locator's per-decade minor ticks, which crowd and overlap at
        # this range -- and rather than x_all, which also holds unplotted full-data
        # baseline rows that would otherwise add a stray distant tick.
        ticks = sorted({int(v) for v in varying_x})
        ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(FixedLocator(ticks))
        ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(ScalarFormatter())
        ax.minorticks_off()
        ax.set_xticks(ticks)
        ax.set_xticklabels([str(t) for t in ticks], rotation=45, ha="right")
    else:
        ax.set_xlim(right=x_hi_curve + 0.02 * (x_hi_curve - x_lo))
    ax.set_xlabel(f"training set size ({x})")
    ax.set_ylabel(METRIC_LABELS.get(metric, metric))
    ax.set_title(METRIC_LABELS.get(metric, metric))
    apply_metric_ylim(ax, metric, domain=domain)
    return style_axes(ax)

def baseball_example_columns(dataset: Dataset, idx: np.ndarray) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Human-readable batted-ball descriptors for the picked rows.

    The default describe callback for selection_example_table: the three core
    kinematic features (exit velocity, launch angle, spray angle) and the
    multiclass outcome for each kept majority ball.

    Args:
        dataset: The dataset the rows index into; its meta supplies outcomes.
        idx: Full-dataset row indices of the picked majority balls.

    Returns:
        Frame with columns [exit_velocity, launch_angle, spray_angle, outcome].
    """
    outcome = (
        dataset.meta["outcome"].to_numpy()[idx]
        if dataset.meta is not None and "outcome" in dataset.meta
        else np.array([""] * len(idx))
    )
    return pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "exit_velocity": dataset.X[idx, 0].round(1),
            "launch_angle": dataset.X[idx, 1].round(1),
            "spray_angle": dataset.X[idx, 2].round(1),
            "outcome": outcome,

docs.title: nearest_minority_distance(dataset, rows, nn=None)
docs.text:
Distance from each given row to the nearest minority example.

The same notion of "hardness" the decoys strategy ranks on, reported here so a table reader can see how close each kept majority ball is to the minority class. Distance is computed in the feature space dataset.distance_metric selects (z-scored Euclidean, or raw Hamming for multi-hot domains).

Args: dataset: Dataset the rows index into. rows: Full-dataset row indices to score. nn: Optional NearestNeighbors already fit on the minority features (see selection_examples_frame, which fits this once and reuses it across strategies); fit fresh when not given.

Returns: Distance to the nearest minority example for each row (zeros if there are no minority examples).

Source code in negative_ml/viz/selection_examples.py 
def nearest_minority_distance(
    dataset: Dataset, rows: np.ndarray, nn: NearestNeighbors | None = None
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Distance from each given row to the nearest minority example.

    The same notion of "hardness" the decoys strategy ranks on, reported here so a
    table reader can see how close each kept majority ball is to the minority
    class. Distance is computed in the feature space dataset.distance_metric
    selects (z-scored Euclidean, or raw Hamming for multi-hot domains).

    Args:
        dataset: Dataset the rows index into.
        rows: Full-dataset row indices to score.
        nn: Optional NearestNeighbors already fit on the minority features (see
            selection_examples_frame, which fits this once and reuses it across
            strategies); fit fresh when not given.

    Returns:
        Distance to the nearest minority example for each row (zeros if there are
        no minority examples).
    """
    minority = np.where(dataset.minority_mask())[0]
    if len(minority) == 0:
        return np.zeros(len(rows))
    Xz = distance_features(dataset)
    if nn is None:
        nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1, metric=dataset.distance_metric).fit(
            Xz[minority]
        )
    dist, _ = nn.kneighbors(Xz[np.asarray(rows)])
    return dist.ravel()

def plot_selection_examples(
    dataset: Dataset,
    examples: pd.DataFrame,
    strategies: Sequence[str] = BUDGET_VARYING,
    label: str = "home run",
    budget: int | None = None,
    max_background: int = VIZ_MAX_POINTS,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> plt.Figure:
    """Four-panel scatter of each strategy's picks over the batted-ball cloud.

    Each panel shows the full cloud in gray, the minority class faintly, and the
    strategy's selected majority balls highlighted in that strategy's color, so it
    is visually obvious whether the picks cluster near the minority (decoys), spread
    to the extremes (diversity), represent dense regions (density-diversity), or
    look like a random draw.

    Args:
        dataset: The dataset the examples index into (for the background cloud).
        examples: Frame from selection_examples_frame carrying row_index/strategy.
        strategies: Strategies to panel (one each), in order.
        label: Minority-class display name.
        budget: Per-strategy budget shown in the figure title. Defaults to the
            largest per-strategy pick count in examples when not given.
        max_background: Cap on background points drawn per panel.
        seed: Seed for the background subsample.

    Returns:
        The created Figure.
    """
    if budget is None:
        budget = int(examples.groupby("strategy").size().max())
    ev_, la = dataset.X[:, 0], dataset.X[:, 1]
    minority = dataset.minority_mask()
    bg = subsample_indices(np.arange(dataset.n_samples), max_background, seed)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10), squeeze=False)
    for ax, strat in zip(axes.ravel(), strategies):
        ax.scatter(
            ev_[bg], la[bg], s=4, alpha=0.12, color=LIGHT_GRAY, edgecolors="none"
        )
        ax.scatter(
            ev_[minority],
            la[minority],
            s=6,
            alpha=0.25,
            color=PALETTE["magenta"],
            edgecolors="none",
            label=label,
        )
        picks = examples.loc[examples["strategy"] == strat, "row_index"].to_numpy()
        style = STRATEGY_STYLE.get(strat, {"color": PALETTE["teal"], "marker": "o"})
        ax.scatter(
            ev_[picks],
            la[picks],
            s=70,
            color=style["color"],
            marker=style["marker"],
            edgecolors="black",
            linewidths=0.6,
            label=f"{style.get('label', strat)} picks",
        )
        ax.set_xlabel("exit velocity (mph)")
        ax.set_ylabel("launch angle (deg)")
        ax.set_title(STRATEGY_STYLE.get(strat, {}).get("label", strat))
        ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8, markerscale=1)
        style_axes(ax)
    fig.suptitle(
        f"What each downselection strategy keeps (budget={budget}, {label}s)",
        fontsize=13,
    )
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.97))
    return fig

docs.title: selection_example_table(dataset, strategy, budget, describe=baseball_example_columns, seed=RANDOM_SEED, nn=None)
docs.text:
Tidy table of the majority examples one strategy keeps at a small budget.

The common columns (strategy, full-dataset row_index, standardized distance to the nearest minority example) are shared across domains; the domain-specific, human-readable descriptor columns are supplied by the describe callback, so one builder serves the baseball kinematics and the sandwich ingredients alike.

Args: dataset: The (full) dataset to select from. strategy: Strategy name in negative_ml.core.selection.STRATEGIES. budget: Number of majority examples to keep. describe: Callback mapping (dataset, picked indices) to a frame of readable descriptor columns for those rows (baseball kinematics by default). seed: Seed forwarded to the (stochastic) strategies. nn: Optional NearestNeighbors already fit on the standardized minority features, forwarded to nearest_minority_distance; fit fresh when not given.

Returns: Frame with columns [strategy, row_index, , dist_to_minority], sorted by dist_to_minority. Source code in negative_ml/viz/selection_examples.py 

def selection_example_table(
    dataset: Dataset,
    strategy: str,
    budget: int,
    describe: Callable[[Dataset, np.ndarray], pd.DataFrame] = baseball_example_columns,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
    nn: NearestNeighbors | None = None,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Tidy table of the majority examples one strategy keeps at a small budget.

    The common columns (strategy, full-dataset row_index, standardized distance to
    the nearest minority example) are shared across domains; the domain-specific,
    human-readable descriptor columns are supplied by the describe callback, so one
    builder serves the baseball kinematics and the sandwich ingredients alike.

    Args:
        dataset: The (full) dataset to select from.
        strategy: Strategy name in negative_ml.core.selection.STRATEGIES.
        budget: Number of majority examples to keep.
        describe: Callback mapping (dataset, picked indices) to a frame of
            readable descriptor columns for those rows (baseball kinematics by
            default).
        seed: Seed forwarded to the (stochastic) strategies.
        nn: Optional NearestNeighbors already fit on the standardized minority
            features, forwarded to nearest_minority_distance; fit fresh when
            not given.

    Returns:
        Frame with columns [strategy, row_index, <descriptor columns>,
        dist_to_minority], sorted by dist_to_minority.
    """
    idx = STRATEGIES[strategy](dataset, budget, seed=seed)
    table = pd.DataFrame({"strategy": strategy, "row_index": idx})
    descriptors = describe(dataset, idx).reset_index(drop=True)
    table = pd.concat([table, descriptors], axis=1)
    table["dist_to_minority"] = nearest_minority_distance(dataset, idx, nn=nn).round(2)
    return table.sort_values("dist_to_minority").reset_index(drop=True)

docs.text:
Concatenate selection_example_table across strategies into one frame.

Args: dataset: The dataset to select from. budget: Number of majority examples each strategy keeps. strategies: Strategy names to include (the budget-varying strategies). describe: Descriptor-column callback forwarded to selection_example_table. seed: Seed forwarded to the strategies.

Returns: The stacked per-strategy tables.

Source code in negative_ml/viz/selection_examples.py 
def selection_examples_frame(
    dataset: Dataset,
    budget: int,
    strategies: Sequence[str] = BUDGET_VARYING,
    describe: Callable[[Dataset, np.ndarray], pd.DataFrame] = baseball_example_columns,
    seed: int = RANDOM_SEED,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Concatenate selection_example_table across strategies into one frame.

    Args:
        dataset: The dataset to select from.
        budget: Number of majority examples each strategy keeps.
        strategies: Strategy names to include (the budget-varying strategies).
        describe: Descriptor-column callback forwarded to selection_example_table.
        seed: Seed forwarded to the strategies.

    Returns:
        The stacked per-strategy tables.
    """
    # The minority set (and hence its nearest-neighbor index) is the same for
    # every strategy, so fit it once here instead of once per strategy.
    minority = np.where(dataset.minority_mask())[0]
    nn = None
    if len(minority) > 0:
        Xz = distance_features(dataset)
        nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1, metric=dataset.distance_metric).fit(
            Xz[minority]
        )
    frames = [
        selection_example_table(dataset, s, budget, describe=describe, seed=seed, nn=nn)
        for s in strategies
    ]
    return pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)

    domain: str,

def baseball_describe(dataset: Dataset, idx: int) -> pd.Series:
    """Return key kinematic features and outcome for one baseball row.

    Args:
        dataset: The baseball Dataset (features must be in CONTINUOUS_FEATURES order).
        idx: Row index.

    Returns:
        Series with exit_velocity, launch_angle, spray_angle, and outcome.
    """
    feat = dataset.feature_names or []
    row: dict = {}
    for name in ("exit_velocity", "launch_angle", "spray_angle"):
        if name in feat:
            row[name] = round(float(dataset.X[idx, feat.index(name)]), 1)
    if dataset.meta is not None and "outcome" in dataset.meta.columns:
        row["outcome"] = dataset.meta.iloc[idx]["outcome"]
    return pd.Series(row)
