  • Exemplary SciPy talk submission (Real-world Numba): https://github.com/scipy-conference/scipy-conference/blob/main/data/talk_submissions/scipy_2019_talk_submission_real_world_numba.md

docs.title: Acquisition: majority-class selection strategies
docs.text:
Given a training Dataset and a budget (how many majority/negative examples are allowed), each strategy in negative_ml.core.selection returns the row indices of the majority examples to keep. Minority examples are always kept in full; the experiment code combines kept minority + selected majority into the final training set. Every strategy shares the same signature, taking a dataset, a budget, and optional keyword arguments and returning an array of row indices, and is registered by name in the STRATEGIES dict so experiments and the CLI can select one by string.

Four strategies vary with the budget (negative_ml.core.selection. BUDGET_VARYING) and are the ones compared throughout the study: random, hard (labeled "decoys" in every figure and script), diversity, and density_diversity. A fifth, as_is, ignores the budget and keeps every majority example; it exists as the full-data reference line, not as a budget-varying strategy.

All four operate over a feature space chosen per dataset: standardized (z-scored) Euclidean distance by default, or raw Hamming distance for domains built from multi-hot/one-hot features (currently only sandwiches), where z-scoring would over-weight rare categories. This is controlled by Dataset.distance_metric and read through negative_ml.core.selection.distance_features, so every strategy below is metric-agnostic.

docs.title: random
docs.text: random_undersample draws budget majority examples uniformly at random, without replacement, using a seeded generator. This is the standard baseline every other strategy is compared against — it reproduces exactly what "just delete some of the majority class" gives you.

docs.title: hard (decoys)
docs.text: hard_examples keeps the majority examples closest to the minority class: it fits a 1-nearest-neighbor index on the minority examples, measures every majority example's distance to its nearest minority neighbor, and keeps the budget majority examples with the smallest such distance. This is the project's operationalization of "near-miss" or boundary examples — inactive molecules that are structurally similar to actives, or baseball hits that just missed being a home run.

docs.title: diversity
docs.text: diversity_selection runs greedy farthest-point (k-center) selection: start from one random majority example, then repeatedly add whichever remaining majority example is farthest (in the chosen metric) from every example already selected. This maximizes coverage of the feature space rather than proximity to the minority class. For very large majority pools, the candidate set is first randomly subsampled to DIVERSITY_POOL_CAP (20,000) to keep the O(n x budget) cost bounded.

docs.title: density_diversity
docs.text: density_aware_diversity clusters the majority pool into budget clusters with MiniBatchKMeans (KMEANS_N_INIT = 3 restarts), then keeps one representative per cluster — the member closest to that cluster's centroid, measured in the dataset's real distance metric rather than the raw Euclidean distance MiniBatchKMeans itself uses internally to fit. This gives coverage like diversity_selection, but weighted by where the data actually is: it does not chase rare outliers the way pure farthest-point selection can, and it keeps roughly one example per "kind" of majority example rather than skewing toward the extremes of the feature space. If MiniBatchKMeans produces empty clusters (so fewer than budget centroids get a representative), the shortfall is filled with a random draw from the unchosen majority pool so every strategy returns exactly the requested budget.

docs.title: What each strategy actually picks
docs.text:
negative_ml.viz.selection_examples builds small inspection tables so the abstract description above can be checked against real picks. At a small per-strategy budget on the 2023 baseball season (home run as the minority class), the four strategies pick visibly different kinds of batted balls:

strategy exit velo launch angle spray angle outcome dist to nearest HR hard (decoys) 108.7 21.0 19.4 double 0.15 hard (decoys) 98.5 23.0 20.8 double 0.16 density_diversity 93.7 26.0 15.4 out 0.58 density_diversity 101.2 9.0 2.9 single 0.63 diversity 92.2 24.0 2.5 out 1.18 diversity 52.5 22.0 5.0 out 3.13 random 96.2 28.0 -27.6 out 0.46 random 102.7 49.0 14.2 out 0.68

decoys picks hard-hit doubles and near-misses that sit right next to the home-run cluster (small distance to the nearest home run). diversity reaches out toward the extremes of the feature space, including a 52.5-mph mishit far from anything else. density_diversity picks typical cluster representatives spread across the batted-ball cloud rather than either extreme. random mirrors the bulk of the data (mostly ordinary outs at unremarkable distances).

The same pattern shows up on the sandwich domain (good sandwich = rating

= 8.5), where decoys and density_diversity both surface sandwiches that sit right at the edge of the good/bad boundary — for example a 6.7-rated peanut-butter-and-provolone sandwich whose nearest good-rated neighbor is only one ingredient swap away — while diversity and random pull from across the full range of ratings and ingredient combinations rather than clustering near that boundary.

docs.title: What question this asks
docs.text:
Every active-learning simulation in this project is pool-based: the full training pool's labels are actually known in advance, and the simulation queries batches from it one at a time, tracking how quickly each condition recovers positive (minority) examples and how model performance evolves. The cold-start experiment (scripts/cold_start_active_learning.py, built on negative_ml.core.active_learning) asks a narrower question than the general active-learning experiment: does the composition of the negatives you start with matter, if everything that happens afterward is a normal, uncurated active-learning loop?

That is a distinct question from "does curating negatives help on every round" (which the broader scripts/active_learning_experiments.py sweeps across four negative compositions applied at every round instead). Cold start isolates the very first labeling decision — how do you choose which negatives to label before you know anything — from everything downstream.

docs.title: Phase 1: the initial bolus
docs.text:
make_cold_start_labeled seeds the initial labeled set:

  • COLD_START_N_POS (1,000) positives are drawn directly from the pool.
  • A random candidate pool of COLD_START_NEG_POOL_SIZE (10,000) negatives is drawn, and one of COLD_START_NEG_STRATEGIES — random, hard (decoys), diversity, or density_diversity, the same four strategies documented in acquisition.md — sub-selects COLD_START_N_NEG (1,000) of them.

The candidate pool passed into the strategy includes the seeded positives alongside the negative pool, so a strategy that needs a minority reference (hard/decoys, which scores by distance to the nearest positive) has one to measure against.

docs.title: Phase 2: workflow rounds
docs.text:
Once the bolus is fixed, run_active_learning simulates COLD_START_N_BATCHES (5) rounds of ordinary active learning, each querying COLD_START_BATCH_SIZE new examples (500 for molecules, 100 for baseball) with one of COLD_START_ACQUISITIONS (random or ucb). Every acquired example — positive or negative — is kept, and the negative composition for training is fixed to "as_is" for every round after the bolus: no further negative curation happens once the study is underway. Any difference in downstream performance is therefore attributable purely to how the initial bolus's negatives were chosen, not to anything that happens afterward.

At every round (including round 0, the state immediately after the bolus is seeded and before any queries), a fresh model is fit on all currently labeled examples and scored on a fixed held-out test set with the standard compute_metrics panel. This produces n_batches + 1 rows per (bolus strategy, acquisition, seed) combination.

docs.title: Acquisition functions
docs.text:
Both COLD_START_ACQUISITIONS strategies are defined in negative_ml.core.active_learning:

  • random_acquisition — uniform random draw from the unlabeled pool. The baseline.
  • ucb_acquisition — Upper Confidence Bound. Scores each unlabeled example as mu + kappa * sigma, where mu is the current model's predicted positive probability (exploitation) and sigma = 1 - |2*mu - 1| is a margin-based uncertainty proxy that peaks at mu = 0.5 (exploration), with kappa = 1.0 balancing the two. This favors examples that are both promising and uncertain, rather than pure top-score exploitation or pure uncertainty sampling.

A third acquisition function, gp_ei_acquisition (a Gaussian process with Expected Improvement), exists in the same module and is used by the broader active_learning_experiments.py sweep, but is not part of the cold-start experiment's COLD_START_ACQUISITIONS.

docs.title: Domains and seeds
docs.text:
The cold-start experiment runs on two domains — molecules (RDKit descriptors, XGBoost, the TRAIN_03_19_2022 pool scored against the TEST_03_19_2022 held-out set) and baseball (trained on the 2023 season pool, scored against the 2024 season, the same cross-season shift used elsewhere). The sandwich domain is not included; its pool is far too small to draw a bolus of 1,000 positives and 1,000 negatives from a 10,000-example candidate pool.

COLD_START_N_SEEDS (3) independent seeds are run per (bolus negative strategy, acquisition) combination, so every (domain, strategy, acquisition) cell has 3 repeats to average over.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
scripts/cold_start_active_learning.py follows the project's decoupled generate/plot convention: generate() runs the full sweep and saves one long result frame per domain (results//data/metrics/ cold_start_active_learning.csv); plot() rebuilds figures from that saved frame without recomputation. Two figure types come out of negative_ml.viz.cold_start_active_learning, each faceted by acquisition strategy (one panel per acquisition) and colored/styled by bolus negative strategy, with a shaded band showing +/- 1 standard deviation across seeds:

  • plot_positives_recovered — cumulative positives labeled versus batch round.
  • plot_performance_curves — a chosen metric (AUROC or AUPRC) versus batch round, with a dashed chance line at 0.5 for AUROC.

docs.title: Data source
docs.text:
The baseball domain uses MLB Statcast batted-ball data, pulled through the pybaseball package (https://github.com/jldbc/pybaseball), which wraps Baseball Savant's public Statcast search. negative_ml.baseball.io.fetch_statcast calls pybaseball's statcast() function for a date range and caches the raw result as parquet under data/raw, so repeat runs read the cached file instead of re-querying Baseball Savant.

Two seasons are used:

  • 2023 (2023-03-30 to 2023-10-01) is the primary training season.
  • 2024 (2024-03-20 to 2024-09-30) is the held-out future year, used to build the chronological cross-season ("hard") evaluation split.

The season date ranges live in negative_ml.baseball.io.SEASONS, and load_season(year, target, binary) is the usual entry point for loading a full season by year.

docs.title: What "batted ball" means here
docs.text:
A raw Statcast pull returns one row per pitch, not one row per batted ball. negative_ml.baseball.io.featurize keeps only rows with a valid launch speed, launch angle, and hit-coordinate landing location (dropna on launch_speed, launch_angle, hc_x, hc_y). That is the operational definition of a batted ball in this project: a pitch that was put into play with tracked exit velocity, launch angle, and landing location.

Concretely, for the 2023 season this drops the raw pull from 720,684 pitch rows to 123,820 batted balls. Everything that is not a tracked batted ball — balls, called strikes, swinging strikes, foul balls without a landing location, and so on — is excluded before featurization even begins.

docs.title: Outcome labeling
docs.text:
Every kept batted ball gets a 5-class outcome via negative_ml.baseball.io.outcome_label: single, double, triple, home_run, or out. The four hit types are read directly off the Statcast events column; anything else (field outs, force outs, sacrifice flies, fielding errors, fielder's choices, double plays, and so on) is folded into the out class. So "out" in this dataset means "not one of the four hit types," not literally "the batter was retired."

2023 season outcome counts (of the 123,820 batted balls):

  • home_run: 5,832 (4.7%)
  • triple: 710 (0.6%)
  • double: 8,223 (6.6%)
  • single: 25,953 (21.0%)
  • out: 83,102 (67.1%)

2024 has a similar shape: 125,847 batted balls, 5,498 home runs (4.4%) and 707 triples (0.6%).

For the binary classification framing that the rest of the study uses, featurize(binary=True, target=...) collapses this to target-vs-rest: y=1 for the chosen target class and y=0 for every other batted ball, including the other three hit types. The default target is home_run, the rare, intuitive minority class. triple is used as a harder target elsewhere in the study (H2/H3 selection comparisons) because it is rarer still and less cleanly separable in exit-velocity/launch-angle space.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
Every batted ball is featurized into ten columns (negative_ml.baseball.io.CONTINUOUS_FEATURES + negative_ml.baseball.io.PITCH_CLASS_FEATURES):

  • exit_velocity, launch_angle — the two kinematic quantities that separate hit types most cleanly.
  • spray_angle — a pull-positive spray angle derived from the Statcast hit coordinates by adjusted_spray_angle. It is adjusted for batter handedness so that, regardless of whether the batter is left- or right-handed, positive always means "pulled" and negative always means "opposite field."
  • plate_x, plate_z — pitch location at the plate.
  • release_speed, release_spin_rate — pitch characteristics.
  • is_fastball, is_breaking, is_offspeed — three 0/1 indicators from pitch_class_indicators, which groups the roughly nine raw Statcast pitch_type codes into three coarse classes rather than one-hot encoding every code individually. A pitch type that doesn't match any group (or is missing) gets all-zero indicators, an implicit "other" class.

Pitch-context columns carry a small residual missing fraction (for example, release_spin_rate is missing on roughly 0.6% of rows); impute_column_medians fills those with the column median once at featurization time so the distance-based selection and clustering code downstream never has to handle NaNs.

docs.title: Evaluation splits
docs.text:
negative_ml.baseball.split.build_splits defines three evaluation regimes, shared by every baseball script:

  • random — a stratified random holdout within the training season.
  • hard — train on the full 2023 season, test on the full 2024 season. A chronological, cross-season distribution shift.
  • park — every batted ball whose home team is in negative_ml.baseball.config.OUTLIER_BALLPARKS (Fenway, Coors Field, Yankee Stadium, Great American Ball Park, Oracle Park, Wrigley Field, and Minute Maid Park) is held out entirely for testing. These parks were chosen for their unusual dimensions and correspondingly different home-run rates (which span roughly 0.030 to 0.061 across parks in the underlying data), so this is a deterministic, park-factor distribution shift rather than a random one.

docs.title: Inspiration
docs.text: The baseball domain, and specifically the idea of curating "near-miss" majority-class examples (batted balls that just missed being a home run) as a deliberate majority-selection strategy, is inspired by Tyler James Burch's hit classifier write-up: https://tylerjamesburch.com/blog/baseball/hit-classifier-3. The exit-velocity/launch-angle scatter in negative_ml.viz.baseball.plot_exit_velo_launch_angle deliberately reproduces the geometry from that post, and the "hard" (decoys) selection strategy in negative_ml.core.selection is this project's generalization of picking majority examples that sit close to the minority class boundary.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
• negative_ml/core/ — domain-agnostic building blocks: the Dataset abstraction, configuration, splitting, selection strategies, evaluation metrics, matched-pair evaluation, active learning, saturation sweeps, the fixed-budget selection sweep, negative-control baselines, and the shared experiment plumbing (EvalSplit, fit_score, positive_scores).
  • negative_ml/molecules/, negative_ml/baseball/, negative_ml/sandwich/ — one package per domain, each following the same internal shape: config.py (domain-specific constants), io.py (loading and featurization into a Dataset), split.py (that domain's evaluation-split builders), and viz.py (domain-specific plotting helpers).
  • negative_ml/models/ — thin builders around scikit-learn / XGBoost estimators, unified behind one task-based factory.
  • negative_ml/viz/ — plotting helpers shared across domains (shared visual style, generic result-curve plotting, matched-pair and active-learning figures) plus the shared styling module.
  • scripts/ — one reproducible generate/plot entry point per experiment, callable standalone or imported by other scripts.
  • negative_ml/cli.py, negative_ml/runner.py, negative_ml/script_io.py — the ad hoc CLI, the domain/path registry it (and the scripts) share, and the argparse/plotting scaffolding the scripts share.

docs.title: The Dataset abstraction
docs.text:
Molecules, baseball batted balls, and sandwich ratings do not resemble each other at all, but the central experiment is identical across all three: hold the minority (or high-value) examples fixed and vary how the majority class is sub-selected. negative_ml.core.dataset.Dataset is the single abstraction that makes this possible — wrapping every domain's features (X), targets (y), task type, optional group ids (for grouped splits), and optional raw metadata (meta) in one dataclass means the splitting, selection, experiment, and evaluation code only has to be written once and works identically across all three domains.

Two fields exist specifically to handle domain quirks without breaking that uniformity:

  • distance_metric ("euclidean" or "hamming") tells every distance-based piece of code (selection strategies, matched-pair discovery) whether to z-score features first (appropriate for continuous features like baseball kinematics or molecule descriptors) or leave them raw and count differing positions (appropriate for the sandwich multi-hot ingredient encoding, where z-scoring would over-weight rare categories).
  • label_y lets a regression Dataset (the sandwich domain, when trained on the continuous rating) carry an independent binary minority definition, so minority_mask()/majority_mask() still work correctly without changing what y actually holds or requiring every caller to pass a threshold.

docs.title: Splits as an injected object, not a parameter
docs.text: negative_ml.core.experiment.EvalSplit bundles a fixed training pool (train_ds) with a held-out test set (X_test, y_test) and a name. Every experiment runner (saturation, sweep/selection, mmp, negative_control) accepts an optional pre-built EvalSplit and falls back to building a default in-dataset split (resolve_split) when none is given. This is what lets the exact same runner code serve two very different regimes — an ordinary in-dataset random or scaffold split, and a cross-dataset split that trains on one dataset and tests on an entirely different one (for example, baseball's "hard" 2023-train/2024-test cross-season split) — without the runners needing to know which regime they're in.

docs.title: Models behind one factory
docs.text:
Every experiment depends on negative_ml.models.base.make_model / model_factory rather than importing XGBoost or scikit-learn directly. make_model takes a task, a model kind, an optional class weight, and any extra hyperparameters, and returns an unfitted estimator for "xgboost" (the default), "ridge" (the sandwich domain's regularized linear model, with an optional top-k F-test feature-selection pipeline), "logistic", or "correlation" (see below). Every returned estimator exposes the same minimal surface the experiment code relies on (fit, and predict_proba or decision_function or predict for scoring), so saturation, selection, and mmp experiments never change when the underlying model does.

CorrelationModel (negative_ml.models.baseline) is a deliberately under-powered single-feature negative control: it scores examples using one feature only, oriented by that feature's correlation sign with the label. It exposes the identical fit/predict_proba surface as every real model, so it flows through the exact same fit_score path in negative_ml.core.negative_control, and its AUROC/AUPRC directly answer "how much signal is in this one feature alone" as a baseline against the full model.

docs.title: Named strategy registries
docs.text: Selection strategies (STRATEGIES in negative_ml.core.selection), acquisition functions (ACQUISITION_FNS in negative_ml.core.active_learning), and domain loaders (DOMAIN_LOADERS in negative_ml.runner) are all plain dicts mapping a string name to a callable with a fixed signature. This is what lets the CLI, the scripts, and the sweep functions select an algorithm by name (e.g. iterate over BUDGET_VARYING, or accept --domain molecules on the command line) instead of importing and branching on concrete functions everywhere.

docs.title: Decoupled generate/plot
docs.text:
Every reproducible script under scripts/ splits into a generate() step (runs the experiment, writes a tidy result frame to results//data/metrics/) and a plot() step (reads that frame back from disk and redraws every figure from it). negative_ml.script_io.run_script and run_sectioned_script provide the shared --generate-only / --plot-only / --section argument scaffolding so every script supports this the same way: 

python scripts/baseball_eda.py                  # generate + plot
python scripts/baseball_eda.py --plot-only       # replot saved artifacts
python scripts/baseball_eda.py --generate-only   # compute, no figures

This means figures can be redrawn (a style tweak, a new color, a relabeled axis) without recomputing anything, and the same saved frames back both the scripts' PNGs and the matching EDA notebooks under notebooks/, so a notebook and its script always draw the same figures from the same data.

docs.title: Result and figure paths
docs.text:
negative_ml.runner defines the on-disk layout every domain and experiment writes to:

results/<domain>/
  data/
    predictions/   metrics/   grids/
  figures/
    eda/   performance/   saturation/   downselection/   negative_control/  ...

data_path, metrics_path, and figure_path build these paths (creating parent directories as needed) so no script hand-assembles a path string, and every domain's outputs land in a predictable, parallel location.

docs.title: The CLI versus the scripts
docs.text: negative_ml.cli (a Typer app) exposes a small set of ad hoc commands (prepare, saturation, selection) for running a single condition quickly. Its results are deliberately written to a "cli_saturation" / "cli_selection" artifact name, distinct from the "saturation" / "selection" artifacts the scripts under scripts/ produce — the CLI runs one condition rather than the scripts' full (split, target, threshold) sweep, so its output frame lacks the tag columns (split, target, threshold, ...) the plotting functions in the scripts expect, and would otherwise silently overwrite the canonical result the notebooks and figures depend on.

docs.title: Shared visual style
docs.text: negative_ml.viz.style centralizes every visual choice so figures produced by different scripts, months apart, still look like one study: the Dark2 categorical palette (used in a fixed order for categorical series, and installed as Matplotlib's default color cycle on import), sequential colormaps for density/probability surfaces, consistent axis despining (style_axes), and a single save_fig helper that fixes the output DPI and crop for every PNG the project writes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: negative_ml.core.config.py holds every constant shared across domains: random seeds, default test fraction, top-k cutoff and score threshold for the metrics, sweep repeat counts, active-learning and cold-start batch sizes/budgets, XGBoost defaults, and figure DPI. Domain-specific constants (OUTLIER_BALLPARKS, the SANDWICH_* family, the MOLECULE_/MORGAN_ family) live in each domain's own config.py instead. The project's AGENTS.md convention is that no other module hard-codes a magic number that belongs in one of these files.

docs.title: Conventions enforced by tooling
docs.text:
The repository's AGENTS.md and pyproject.toml encode a consistent set of conventions, checked in CI (.github/workflows) and expected before every commit:

  • Google-style docstrings on every module, class, and function, with no reStructuredText roles or markdown emphasis inside them; interrogate enforces 100% docstring coverage and pydoclint checks that documented arguments match each function's actual signature.
  • No leading-underscore function names, even for module-internal helpers.
  • ruff is the sole linter, formatter, and import sorter (replacing black/isort/flake8/pylint), configured for pycodestyle + pyflakes + isort rules.
  • pytest with coverage reporting; tests/ contains one file roughly per core/domain module (test_selection.py, test_mmp.py, test_active_learning.py, test_domains.py, test_experiments.py, test_eval.py, test_splitting.py, test_models.py, and so on).

The development environment is a micromamba environment (environment.yml); the base conda/anaconda environment on a typical workstation does not have every dependency (notably pyarrow, needed to read the cached parquet files) installed.

docs.title: Matched pairs
docs.text: A matched pair is one positive (minority) example and one negative (majority) example that are close together in feature space but carry opposite labels. The idea, and the code, live in negative_ml.core.mmp (matched molecular pairs is the chemistry term this generalizes from — a pair of molecules differing by a small structural change that flips activity). Scoring a trained model on matched pairs tests something a global test-set metric cannot: whether the model has learned a genuine, fine-grained decision boundary, or is only picking up on broad class separation that happens to work everywhere except at the boundary.

docs.title: Finding pairs
docs.text:
find_matched_pairs takes a feature matrix and binary labels and, for every positive example, finds its single nearest negative neighbor (scikit-learn's NearestNeighbors with a ball tree). Distance is computed either on z-scored (standardized) features or, for multi-hot domains like sandwiches, raw Hamming distance — the same metric choice used everywhere else in the selection code, and passed in explicitly by the caller.

Positives are then processed from closest to farthest, greedily deduplicated so that no negative example is claimed by more than one pair, and the result is truncated to max_pairs (closest pairs first). The output is a small DataFrame of (idx_pos, idx_neg, dist) rows indexing back into the original arrays.

docs.title: Scoring pairs
docs.text:
score_pairs attaches a fitted model's positive-class scores to a pairs DataFrame: score_pos and score_neg (the model's score for each half of the pair), correct (whether the positive scored higher, as it should), and margin (score_pos - score_neg).

mmp_metrics then reduces a scored-pairs frame to two numbers:

  • pair_auroc — AUROC computed over the pooled positive and negative scores from the matched pairs only (not the whole test set). A random classifier still scores about 0.5 here; a model that perfectly resolves every boundary case scores 1.0.
  • mean_margin — the average score_pos - score_neg across all pairs.

Because matched pairs are deliberately the hardest, closest cross-label examples in the test set, pair_auroc is expected to sit below the model's global test-set AUROC. That gap is the signal the metric is built to surface.

docs.title: Running the comparison
docs.text:
run_mmp_evaluation is the main entry point: for each (selection strategy, seed) combination, it applies a negative_ml.core.selection strategy to the training pool at a fixed budget, fits a fresh model, and scores that model on both the ordinary held-out test set (the standard auroc/auprc/f1 panel) and a pre-computed set of matched pairs drawn from that same test set. The result is one row per (strategy, seed) with both the global metrics and the pairwise ones side by side, which is what makes the comparison meaningful: the same model, same test set, two different views of its performance.

A lighter-weight companion, rescore_examples, fits one model per strategy at a single fixed seed and scores a small saved set of example pairs — used to populate the qualitative example table (see below) without repeating the full multi-seed sweep just to re-derive it.

docs.title: Where this runs
docs.text:
scripts/mmp_experiments.py runs the full pipeline for all three domains, each with its own budget, model, and evaluation split:

  • molecules — RDKit descriptors, the shared XGBoost/ridge model factory, budget 2000, a random 80/20 split, Euclidean distance.
  • baseball — batted-ball kinematics, budget 2000, trained on the full 2023 season and tested on the full 2024 season (the "hard" cross-season split), Euclidean distance.
  • sandwiches — multi-hot ingredients, the feature-selected ridge classifier, budget 80, a random 80/20 split, Hamming distance. Because the dataset is so small, example pairs for the qualitative table are found across the full dataset rather than only the test split.

Each domain also has a describe function (baseball_describe, molecules_describe, sandwiches_describe in negative_ml.viz.mmp) that turns a row index into a short, human-readable summary — kinematics and outcome for a batted ball, scaffold and a few descriptors plus SMILES for a molecule, ingredient list and rating for a sandwich — so the example-pairs figure reads as an actual table of near-miss cases rather than raw feature values.

docs.title: Observed gap between global and pairwise AUROC
docs.text:
Running the pipeline shows the expected gap on both non-molecule domains. Averaged across the four budget-varying strategies:

  • baseball (home run, 2023-train/2024-test): global AUROC ranges from 0.955 (hard/decoys) to 0.991 (random, density_diversity), while pair_auroc ranges only from 0.686 (diversity) to 0.705 (hard/decoys).
  • sandwiches (good >= 8.5 rating, random split): global AUROC ranges from 0.528 (diversity) to 0.600 (random), while pair_auroc ranges from 0.714 (diversity) to 0.762 (random).

In both domains, every strategy's pairwise AUROC sits well below its global AUROC — confirming that the matched-pair cases are, as intended, meaningfully harder than the test set as a whole, even for a model that discriminates the overall classes very well.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text: All metrics live in negative_ml.core.eval. Classification models are scored by compute_metrics, which returns a fixed panel of five values covering two different questions: overall ranking quality, and quality restricted to the top of the ranking. Regression models (currently only the sandwich domain, when trained on the continuous 0-10 rating rather than the good/bad label) are scored by compute_regression_metrics instead, since AUROC and AUPRC are undefined without binary ground truth.

docs.title: Global discrimination
docs.text:
• auroc — area under the ROC curve (sklearn's roc_auc_score). Answers "if I pick a random positive and a random negative, how often does the model score the positive higher?" A value of 0.5 is chance; 1.0 is perfect ranking.
  • auprc — area under the precision-recall curve, computed as average precision (sklearn's average_precision_score). Unlike AUROC, its chance level equals the base rate (the positive fraction), which makes it more informative than AUROC on the heavily imbalanced domains in this study, where the base rate can be a few percent.
  • f1 — f1_at_threshold binarizes the model's scores at a fixed threshold (DEFAULT_THRESHOLD = 0.5 by default) and reports the F1 score at that cutoff.

docs.title: Early retrieval / top-k
docs.text:
These answer a more practical question than global ranking: if only the top k highest-scored examples are actually acted on (the top k molecules get synthesized and tested, the top k prospects get scouted), how good is that shortlist?

  • precision_at_k — the fraction of the top k highest-scored examples that are true positives. Scores are sorted descending and the top k labels are averaged; DEFAULT_TOP_K = 100 by default.
  • enrichment_factor — precision_at_k divided by the overall base rate. An enrichment factor of 5 means the top-k shortlist is five times as enriched for positives as picking randomly would be. Returns 0.0 when the base rate is zero.

compute_metrics returns all five values in one call: auroc, auprc, f1, precision_at_k, and enrichment_factor.

docs.title: Regression metric
docs.text:
• spearman — Spearman rank correlation between the true continuous target and the model's predictions (scipy's spearmanr). This is the regression analog of AUROC/AUPRC: it asks whether the model ranks examples in the same order as the ground truth, without needing a threshold to binarize a continuous target. Returns 0.0 (rather than raising) when either side has zero variance, since the correlation is undefined in that case.

compute_regression_metrics returns {"spearman": ...}.

docs.title: Matched-pair metrics
docs.text: A third family of metrics, pair_auroc and mean_margin, is computed over matched pairs (a positive and a negative example that are close together in feature space) rather than over the whole test set. These are defined in negative_ml.core.mmp and documented separately in matched_pairs.md, since they depend on how the pairs themselves are constructed.

docs.title: How scores are produced
docs.text:
Every metric above takes y_score, a per-example ranking score for the positive class, as input. negative_ml.core.experiment.positive_scores produces that score from a fitted model with a fallback chain: it prefers predict_proba (the positive-class column), falls back to decision_function squashed through a logistic sigmoid (monotonic, so rank-based metrics like AUROC/AUPRC are unaffected, and it maps the model's own decision boundary at margin 0 to a score of 0.5 so the F1 threshold of 0.5 stays meaningful), and falls back to predict() directly when neither is available (used for the raw XGBRegressor case, where the continuous output serves as both a classification ranking score and, for the sandwich domain, the regression prediction itself scored via spearman).

negative_ml.core.experiment.fit_score is the function that actually ties a trained model to a metric panel: it fits a fresh model, scores the held-out test set, and dispatches to compute_regression_metrics when the training Dataset's task is "regression" or to compute_metrics otherwise. Every experiment runner in negative_ml.core (saturation, sweep/selection, mmp, active_learning, negative_control) calls through fit_score or the equivalent inline pattern, so the metric panel reported for one experiment is directly comparable to every other.

docs.title: Data source
docs.text:
The dataset comes from Roll for Sandwich, a game in which each sandwich's ingredients (bread, main, cheese, roughage, a wildcard "wild magic" ingredient, and sauce) are chosen at random and then rated by a human judge on a 0-10 scale. The source workbook is RFS Sandwiches.xlsx, referenced from the project's research plan (https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/11fjXIUbUae35AFNlp-f10t3hSjbq5tiBykLA_IbUojs) and read from data/raw by negative_ml.sandwich.io.read_ratings.

The workbook has one sheet per season. Five seasons (S1 through S5) are read; a sixth season sheet exists in the workbook but has no ratings entered, so it is deliberately excluded (negative_ml.sandwich.io.NUM_SEASONS = 5).

docs.title: Cleaning
docs.text:
Loading a sandwich dataset (sandwich.io.load) runs the raw long frame through several cleaning steps, in order:

  1. read_ratings reads all five season sheets, harmonizes Season 1's "Other / Wild Magic" column header to "Wild Magic" so it lines up with later seasons, concatenates the sheets, and melts the per-season episode columns into a single (Season, Episode) pair.
  2. clean_ratings drops any row with a null field in any column (this also removes the off-season melt copies whose Episode is null), then applies:
  3. normalize_ratings, which repairs harmless rating typos: stray whitespace ("4.9/ 10") and a missing "/10" denominator ("4.6" becomes "4.6/10"). This recovers rows rather than dropping them.
  4. validate_ratings, which drops any row that still doesn't match the expected shape after repair: every ingredient must be a non-null string, the rating must match the regex for a 0-10 value over "/10", and the season must be one of S1-S5. This replaces a Pandera schema used in the original reference notebook, kept out to avoid the extra dependency.
  5. standardize_null_ingredients, which rewrites unrecorded-data placeholders (one or more dashes, e.g. "--") onto that column's canonical "No " label. Without this step, a sandwich whose cheese was left blank and a sandwich whose cheese was explicitly recorded as "No cheese" would one-hot encode into two different features even though both sandwiches have no cheese.
  6. Parsing the cleaned "X.X/10" string into a numeric Clean_Rating column.

docs.title: Featurization
docs.text:
Each of the six ingredient columns (Bread, Main, Cheese, Roughage, Wild Magic, Sauce) is multi-hot encoded by encode_ingredients into one indicator column per observed "Column=Value" combination, so every sandwich row has exactly six ones. After cleaning, this currently produces 239 sandwiches and 843 multi-hot feature columns.

prune_rare_features then drops ingredient-value columns seen in fewer than SANDWICH_MIN_INGREDIENT_COUNT sandwiches. That constant is currently set to 1 (no pruning: every ingredient value that appears at all is kept), after a stricter cutoff of 2 was found to drop too many single-occurrence ingredients the study wanted represented in the model.

Because every feature is a nominal 0/1 indicator, the sandwich Dataset sets distance_metric="hamming" rather than the "euclidean" default used by the other two domains. Hamming distance counts differing positions with every ingredient weighted equally; z-scoring the raw features first (as the euclidean path does) would inflate the weight of rare ingredient values relative to common ones, which is exactly the distortion the sandwich featurization is designed to avoid.

The dataset is natively a regression problem (y is the continuous 0-10 rating). sandwich.io.to_classification recasts it as good-vs-bad classification: a sandwich is "good" (y=1) when its rating is at or above SANDWICH_GOOD_RATING_THRESHOLD (8.5) and "bad" (y=0) otherwise. This is what lets the sandwich domain plug into the same majority-selection and saturation experiments as the (natively classification) molecules and baseball domains.

docs.title: Splits
docs.text:
sandwich.split.build_splits defines three evaluation regimes:

  • random — a stratified random holdout within the full menu.
  • scaffold — a grouped holdout by the Main ingredient (the filling), so entire filling families are held out of training rather than individual sandwiches. This is the sandwich analog of a molecular scaffold split.
  • season — the entire S5 season (the newest) is held out for testing (SANDWICH_TEST_SEASON), a chronological-style shift analogous to baseball's cross-season split.

docs.title: Exploratory results
docs.text:
The rating distribution is skewed high overall, but the exact "good" rate depends on where the good/bad line is drawn. At the threshold actually used throughout the study (rating >= 8.5):

  • 80 of 239 sandwiches (33.5%) are "good."
  • 131 of 239 (54.8%) score at or above 7.
  • 25 of 239 (10.5%) score below 3.

sandwich.config.SANDWICH_GOOD_RATING_THRESHOLDS = [7.5, 8.0, 8.5, 9.0, 9.5] is swept in the downselection scripts to check how sensitive the results are to exactly where this line is drawn.

Ratings by season (mean and count) show some drift over the show's run: S1 has 51 rated sandwiches, S2 has 56, S3 has 26, S4 has 64, and S5 (the held-out test season) has 42.

docs.title: Modeling
docs.text:
Because the dataset is tiny (~240 rows) and very wide (843 multi-hot features), the good-vs-bad classifier is a regularized linear model rather than a tree ensemble: feature_selected_ridge_classifier first keeps the SANDWICH_CLF_TOP_FEATURES (30) features with the strongest univariate F-test association with the label, then fits a RidgeClassifier (L2 penalty SANDWICH_RIDGE_ALPHA = 1.0) on that reduced feature set. Feature selection is refit inside every cross-validation fold so the reported metrics are not contaminated by selecting on the full dataset first. F-test importance was chosen over gradient-boosted "gain" importance because it matches a linear decision boundary; gain importance ranks split usefulness for a tree model and does not transfer.

A single 80/20 holdout is too noisy to trust at this sample size, so scripts/modeling.py scores the good-vs-bad classifier with repeated stratified cross-validation instead: SANDWICH_CV_REPEATS (10) repeats of SANDWICH_CV_FOLDS-fold (5) stratified k-fold, refitting the model from scratch in every fold.

Comparing the ridge classifier against a full-feature XGBoost baseline on this cross-validation protocol gives AUROC 0.558 +/- 0.020 for the ridge classifier and AUROC 0.600 +/- 0.031 for XGBoost, against a chance AUROC of 0.5 and a base rate (chance AUPRC) of about 0.335. The top ingredients selected by the F-test (e.g. Wild Magic=Bacon, Wild Magic=Extra roughage, Sauce=Kewpie mayo) are the ones most linearly associated with a good rating.
